topics.name: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
topics.summary: Alcohols (R–OH) have –OH on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon and are classified 1°/2°/3° by how many other carbons are attached to that carbinol carbon, and by hydric value (mono-, di-, trihydric) according to how many –OH groups are present. Allylic alcohols have –OH on a carbon adjacent to a C=C double bond; benzylic alcohols have it on a carbon adjacent to an aromatic ring — in both cases –OH itself sits on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon, not on the ring or double-bond carbon. Phenols (Ar–OH) instead have –OH bonded directly to an sp<sup>2</sup> aromatic-ring carbon, giving the C–O bond partial double-bond character from resonance. Ethers (R–O–R') are classified simple/symmetrical (identical groups on both sides) or mixed/unsymmetrical (different groups); an aryl alkyl ether like anisole has one aromatic and one alkyl group.
key_formulas: 1°/2°/3° alcohol: count carbons directly bonded to the carbinol carbon
Phenol: –OH on sp² ring carbon; Alcohol: –OH on sp³ carbon
Ether: simple if R = R′, mixed if R ≠ R′
topics.worked_example: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH: the carbinol carbon (bearing –OH) is the CH<sub>2</sub>, which is bonded to only one other carbon (the isopropyl CH) — so this is a primary (1°) alcohol, even though the molecule as a whole is fairly branched.
common_mistakes: Miscounting how many carbons are attached to the carbinol carbon (e.g. overlooking nearby branching) when assigning 1°/2°/3°.
Assuming any ring-containing molecule with –OH is a phenol, without checking whether –OH sits directly on the aromatic ring or on a side-chain sp³ carbon (confusing benzyl alcohol with phenol).
Calling an ether 'simple' without actually comparing its two attached groups, when they are in fact different (making it a mixed ether).

topics.name: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
topics.summary: Alcohols take the suffix '-ol', with the principal chain numbered to give –OH the lowest possible locant (e.g. propan-1-ol); with multiple –OH groups, a multiplying prefix fuses to the suffix (propane-1,2,3-triol). Phenol's –OH-bearing ring carbon is always numbered C1, with substituents named from there (2-chlorophenol); diols use retained names catechol/resorcinol/hydroquinone or systematic benzene-1,2-/1,3-/1,4-diol. Ethers are named substitutively: the longer chain is the parent '-ane', and the shorter O–R group becomes an 'alkoxy' prefix (methoxyethane), unless a retained name applies (anisole). When a carboxylic acid and –OH are both present, IUPAC seniority puts –COOH as the suffix and demotes –OH to a 'hydroxy-' prefix (2-hydroxybenzoic acid for salicylic acid), since carboxylic acids outrank alcohols/phenols in the seniority order.
key_formulas: Principal characteristic group (here, –OH when senior) gets the lowest locant
Phenol numbering: the –OH-bearing ring carbon is always C1
Seniority: carboxylic acid > ... > alcohol/phenol > ether (ether is always named as an 'alkoxy' prefix, never a suffix)
topics.worked_example: (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH: the longest chain containing –OH is four carbons; numbering from the OH end gives OH locant 1, and the isopropyl-derived methyl branch falls on C3 — so the correct name is 3-methylbutan-1-ol, not 2-methylbutan-1-ol.
common_mistakes: Numbering the chain from the wrong end, so –OH doesn't end up with the lowest possible locant.
Giving a trivial/common name (e.g. 'propyl alcohol') when a systematic IUPAC name was specifically requested.
Naming an ether with the longer chain as the alkoxy substituent and the shorter chain as the parent, reversing the correct convention.

topics.name: Nature of the O–H Bond, Hydrogen Bonding and Physical Properties
topics.summary: Alcohols and phenols hydrogen-bond intermolecularly through their O–H, giving them much higher boiling points than alkanes or ethers of comparable molar mass, and appreciable water solubility for short chains (which falls off as the hydrocarbon portion grows). Ethers have no O–H to donate a hydrogen bond, so they cannot hydrogen-bond to themselves (much lower boiling points than isomeric alcohols) but their oxygen lone pairs can still accept a hydrogen bond from water, giving moderate water solubility. A key structural contrast is o- versus p-nitrophenol: the ortho isomer's –OH and –NO<sub>2</sub> are close enough to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond (chelation), lowering its boiling point and making it steam-volatile, while the para isomer's groups are too far apart and instead form an extended intermolecular hydrogen-bond network, raising its boiling point and making it non-steam-volatile.
key_formulas: Boiling point (same mass): ether < alcohol (only alcohol has O–H to hydrogen-bond with itself)
Water solubility needs only ONE hydrogen bond role (donor OR acceptor) — ethers qualify as acceptors only
topics.worked_example: Propan-1-ol (b.p. ≈97°C) and its isomer methoxyethane (b.p. ≈8°C) have identical molar mass, but only propan-1-ol has O–H, so only it can hydrogen-bond to its own kind — explaining the huge boiling-point gap despite the shared molecular formula.
common_mistakes: Assuming boiling-point differences between isomers come from covalent bond strength within a molecule, rather than intermolecular forces between molecules.
Believing an ether's oxygen lone pairs let it hydrogen-bond to other ether molecules just as an alcohol's O–H does, when only O–H can donate a hydrogen bond.
Overlooking whether two substituents are geometrically close enough (as in o-nitrophenol) to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond, versus needing to reach another molecule (as in the para isomer).

topics.name: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
topics.summary: Alkenes give alcohols by acid-catalysed hydration or oxymercuration-demercuration (both Markovnikov, OH to the more substituted carbon; oxymercuration avoids carbocation rearrangement via a bridged mercurinium ion) or by hydroboration-oxidation (anti-Markovnikov, syn addition, no rearrangement). Carbonyl compounds are reduced by NaBH<sub>4</sub> or LiAlH<sub>4</sub> (aldehyde→1°, ketone→2°); LiAlH<sub>4</sub> additionally reduces esters and carboxylic acids to 1° alcohols, while NaBH<sub>4</sub> leaves those groups untouched. Grignard reagents add to carbonyls: formaldehyde always gives a 1° alcohol, other aldehydes give 2° alcohols, ketones give 3° alcohols — but Grignard + CO<sub>2</sub> gives a carboxylic acid, not an alcohol. Haloalkanes are hydrolysed to alcohols by aqueous NaOH/KOH (SN2 for 1°, SN1 for 3°).
key_formulas: Markovnikov (acid hydration, oxymercuration): –OH → more substituted carbon
Anti-Markovnikov (hydroboration-oxidation): –OH → less substituted carbon
Grignard + HCHO → 1° alcohol; + RCHO → 2° alcohol; + R₂C=O → 3° alcohol; + CO₂ → carboxylic acid (not an alcohol)
topics.worked_example: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr + CH<sub>3</sub>CHO, then H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>, gives CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (pentan-2-ol): the propyl group from the Grignard reagent and the methyl group from acetaldehyde both end up attached to the carbinol carbon.
common_mistakes: Confusing hydroboration-oxidation's anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry with oxymercuration/acid hydration's Markovnikov outcome.
Assuming Grignard reagents always give an alcohol product, forgetting that Grignard + CO₂ instead gives a carboxylic acid.
Misidentifying which carbon becomes the carbinol carbon in a Grignard synthesis, leading to the wrong alcohol's structure or class.

topics.name: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
topics.summary: Chlorobenzene is converted to phenol only under very forcing conditions — fusion with NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm (the Dow process) — because the aryl C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character (from chlorine's lone-pair conjugation with the ring) and the planar sp<sup>2</sup> carbon blocks the backside attack an SN2 pathway would need. Benzenesulfonic acid gives phenol by fusion with NaOH followed by acidification. Diazonium salts (from aniline via NaNO<sub>2</sub>/HCl at 273–278 K) hydrolyse readily on mild warming with water, since –N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is an excellent leaving group (departing as stable N<sub>2</sub> gas) unlike the poor leaving group –Cl on an aromatic ring. Industrially, the cumene process (benzene + propene → cumene → cumene hydroperoxide → phenol + acetone) dominates because it yields two valuable products economically.
key_formulas: Chlorobenzene + NaOH (623 K, 300 atm) → phenol (Dow process)
ArSO₃Na + NaOH (fusion), then H⁺ → ArOH
topics.worked_example: Aniline → (NaNO<sub>2</sub>/HCl, 273–278 K) → benzenediazonium chloride → (warm with water) → phenol + N<sub>2</sub>, a mild, low-temperature lab-scale route contrasting with the industrial, high-pressure Dow process.
common_mistakes: Expecting chlorobenzene to hydrolyse to phenol under mild conditions, the way a simple alkyl chloride hydrolyses to an alcohol, without accounting for the aryl C–Cl bond's resistance to substitution.
Confusing diazonium salt hydrolysis (with water, giving phenol) with the Sandmeyer-type reaction (with CuCl, giving chlorobenzene).

Assuming a reagent/condition that works for one phenol-preparation route also works for a structurally different route (e.g. treating sulfonic-acid fusion and haloarene hydrolysis as interchangeable).

topics.name: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
topics.summary: Fischer esterification (alcohol + carboxylic acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) is a reversible condensation; excess alcohol or water removal drives it toward more ester. Acid-catalysed dehydration proceeds via a carbocation (E1), so reactivity follows 3° > 2° > 1° (opposite of SN2 substitution reactivity), and Zaitsev's rule predicts the more substituted alkene as major product; rearrangement via hydride/alkyl shifts can occur if it reaches a more stable carbocation. Oxidation depends on both the oxidant and the alcohol class: PCC is mild and stops a 1° alcohol at the aldehyde; hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>/K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> continue on to the carboxylic acid; a 2° alcohol oxidises to a ketone (and no further); a 3° alcohol resists oxidation entirely under normal conditions, since it has no carbinol C–H for the mechanism to remove.
key_formulas: Dehydration reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° (reverse of SN2 order)
1° alcohol –PCC→ aldehyde; –KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₃ (hot, acidic)→ carboxylic acid
2° alcohol –oxidant→ ketone; 3° alcohol: resists oxidation (no carbinol C–H)
topics.worked_example: Butan-2-ol + acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> gives butan-2-one (oxidation to a ketone); the same butan-2-ol + conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat instead gives but-2-ene as the major (Zaitsev) product (dehydration) — the reagent choice, not the substrate, decides which reaction class occurs.
common_mistakes: Confusing PCC (stops at the aldehyde) with strong oxidants like hot KMnO₄/K₂Cr₂O₃ (which go all the way to the carboxylic acid).
Forgetting that a tertiary alcohol has no carbinol C–H and so cannot be oxidised the normal way, regardless of how strong or how much oxidant is used.
Picking the less-substituted alkene instead of the Zaitsev (more-substituted) product, or reversing the 3°>2°>1° dehydration order with the 1°>2°>3° SN2 order.

topics.name: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
topics.summary: Alcohols react with active metals (Na, K) to release H<sub>2</sub> and form alkoxides; reactivity follows 1° > 2° > 3°, since increasing alkyl substitution both reduces O–H acidity (+I effect) and sterically hinders access to the metal. This is the OPPOSITE order to reactivity with the Lucas reagent (conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl<sub>2</sub>), which follows 3° > 2° > 1° because it depends on carbocation stability (SN1) at the carbinol carbon: tertiary alcohols give near-instant turbidity, secondary within a few minutes, primary only slowly on heating. The two trends are not contradictory — they probe entirely different bonds (O–H acidity versus C–O ionisation). SOCl<sub>2</sub> is often preferred for making alkyl chlorides since its byproducts (SO<sub>2</sub>, HCl) are both gases, unlike PCl<sub>5</sub>'s liquid POCl<sub>3</sub> byproduct, making purification easier.
key_formulas: Na-metal reactivity: 1° > 2° > 3° (O–H acidity/access)
Lucas (HCl/ZnCl₂) reactivity: 3° > 2° > 1° (carbocation stability, opposite bond/mechanism)
ROH + SOCl₂ → RCl + SO₂ + HCl (both gaseous byproducts)
topics.worked_example: Lucas test timing: a tertiary alcohol turns cloudy almost instantly at room temperature; a secondary alcohol within a few minutes; a primary alcohol shows no turbidity at room temperature and needs heating.
common_mistakes: Assuming the Na-metal order (1°>2°>3°) and the Lucas/HX order (3°>2°>1°) should run the same direction, without recognising they involve different bonds and mechanisms.
Misassigning which alcohol class gives immediate Lucas-test turbidity (tertiary) versus which needs heat (primary).
Overlooking that SOCl₂'s byproducts are both gases that escape on their own, unlike PCl₅'s liquid POCl₃ byproduct, when explaining why SOCl₂ is often preferred.

topics.name: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
topics.summary: Phenol (pKa≈10) is far more acidic than a simple alcohol (pKa≈16–18) and even somewhat more acidic than water (pKa≈15.7), because the phenoxide ion is resonance-stabilised by delocalisation into the ring, unlike an alkoxide. Electron-withdrawing groups (EWGs) at ortho/para increase acidity further (direct resonance + induction); electron-donating groups (EDGs) at ortho/para decrease it; substituents at meta act only inductively (weaker effect either way), since the phenoxide's delocalised charge only reaches ortho/para carbons. Multiple EWGs combine roughly additively (picric acid, pKa≈0.4). Phenol is still less acidic than a carboxylic acid (pKa≈4–5), since a carboxylate's two-oxygen resonance delocalises charge even more effectively than a phenoxide's ring delocalisation.
key_formulas: Acidity order: alcohol (pKa≈16–18) < water (≈15.7) < phenol (≈10) < carboxylic acid (≈4–5)
EWG at ortho/para: increases acidity (resonance + induction); EDG at ortho/para: decreases acidity
Meta substitution: inductive effect only (weaker than ortho/para for the same group)
topics.worked_example: p-Cresol < phenol < p-chlorophenol < p-nitrophenol, in increasing acidity: methyl (EDG) decreases acidity below phenol; chlorine's inductive withdrawal slightly outweighs its resonance donation, giving a modest increase; nitro's strong resonance withdrawal gives the largest increase.
common_mistakes: Assuming an electron-donating group always increases acidity (or an EWG always decreases it), reversing the real relationship to phenoxide-ion stabilisation.
Treating meta substitution as having the same strong effect as ortho/para substitution, when meta substituents can only act inductively, not by direct resonance with the phenoxide charge.

Conflating ring-activation (favoured by electron-donating character, relevant to electrophilic substitution) with phenoxide-ion stabilisation/acidity increase (favoured by electron-withdrawing character) — these respond to opposite substituent electronics.

topics.name: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
topics.summary: Phenol's ring is strongly activated (resonance donation from –OH) and ortho/para-directing, reacting with electrophiles far more readily than benzene — e.g. instant reaction with bromine water (no catalyst needed) to give 2,4,6-tribromophenol. Kolbe's reaction (phenoxide + CO<sub>2</sub>, heat/pressure, then acidify) installs –COOH predominantly ortho, giving salicylic acid. The Reimer-Tiemann reaction (phenoxide + CHCl<sub>3</sub>/NaOH, generating electrophilic dichlorocarbene, :CCl<sub>2</sub>, via base-mediated α-elimination) installs –CHO predominantly ortho (after hydrolysis of an intermediate), giving salicylaldehyde. Both reactions specifically require the phenoxide ion (not merely an activated ring, and not an ether like anisole) as the reactive species. Concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> exhaustively nitrates all three activated positions to give picric acid.
key_formulas: Kolbe's: ArOH + NaOH, then CO₂ (heat/pressure), then H⁺ → salicylic acid (ortho-COOH major)
Reimer-Tiemann: ArOH + CHCl₃ + NaOH(aq), heat, then H⁺ → salicylaldehyde (ortho-CHO major)
Phenol + Br₂ (aq, excess, no catalyst) → 2,4,6-tribromophenol (instant, white precipitate)
topics.worked_example: Salicylic acid (from Kolbe's reaction) is acetylated with acetic anhydride on its phenolic –OH to give acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) — two separate named reactions in sequence.
common_mistakes: Confusing Kolbe's reaction (CO₂ electrophile, gives –COOH) with the Reimer-Tiemann reaction (dichlorocarbene electrophile, gives –CHO after hydrolysis).
Forgetting that both Kolbe's and Reimer-Tiemann reactions specifically require the phenoxide ion, so neither works starting from an ether like anisole.
Assuming a second ring substituent's own directing preference overrides –OH's dominant ortho/para-directing influence, rather than recognising –OH remains the stronger director.

topics.name: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
topics.summary: Williamson synthesis (R–X + R'–ONa → R–O–R' + NaX) is an SN2 reaction, working best with a primary alkyl halide; tertiary halides favour E2 elimination instead, so the rule is to put the bulkier group on the alkoxide/phenoxide (nucleophile) and the least hindered group on the halide (electrophile). Aryl halides can never serve as the halide component (SN2-unreactive), so aryl alkyl ethers like anisole need phenoxide + an alkyl halide. Ethers are cleaved by excess hot HI: for primary/secondary dialkyl ethers, I<sup>–</sup> attacks the less hindered carbon (SN2); if a tertiary alkyl group is present, cleavage instead occurs at that more substituted carbon via SN1 (stable carbocation). The aryl C–O bond of an aryl alkyl ether never cleaves — excess HI on anisole always gives phenol + methyl iodide, never iodobenzene + methanol. Ethers can also form via acid-catalysed intermolecular dehydration of two alcohols (lower temperature, excess alcohol), competing with intramolecular dehydration to an alkene at higher temperature.
key_formulas: R–X + R'–ONa → R–O–R' + NaX (best: R = 1°)
Ar–O–R + excess HI → ArOH + RI (the aryl C–O bond never cleaves)
Dialkyl ether + excess HI → cleaves at the less hindered C (SN2), UNLESS a tertiary C is present, then cleaves there instead (SN1)
topics.worked_example: Anisole (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>) + excess HI, heat → phenol + CH<sub>3</sub>I: the resistant aryl C–O bond never breaks, so the methyl side is always the one cleaved.
common_mistakes: Assuming a tertiary alkyl halide is a good Williamson-synthesis substrate because it excels in other, SN1/E1-type reactions (like the Lucas test or dehydration); it in fact favours elimination here.
Believing the aryl C–O bond in an aryl alkyl ether can be cleaved by HI, when its partial double-bond character means only the alkyl side is ever cleaved.

Applying a simple 'always attack the less hindered carbon' (SN2) rule to every ether cleavage, without checking whether one side can instead form a stabilised carbocation (shifting the mechanism to SN1 at the MORE substituted carbon).

topics.name: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
topics.summary: The cumene process starts from benzene + propene (Friedel-Crafts alkylation, AlCl<sub>3</sub>) to give cumene; air oxidation gives cumene hydroperoxide; acid-catalysed rearrangement (1,2-phenyl shift) and cleavage of that single intermediate directly gives phenol and acetone together — making the process economically attractive since both products are valuable. Distinguishing tests: neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> gives a violet/blue/green colour specifically with phenols (not alcohols); the Lucas test (HCl/ZnCl<sub>2</sub>) distinguishes 1°/2°/3° alcohols by reaction-rate; the iodoform test (I<sub>2</sub>/NaOH) is specific to a CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)– or CH<sub>3</sub>CO– unit (positive for ethanol, negative for methanol); bromine water reacts instantly with phenol's activated ring (white ppt) but not with non-ring-activating alcohols like benzyl alcohol. No single test distinguishes every possible sample — each test separates only a specific pair/class of compounds.
key_formulas: Benzene + CH₂=CHCH₃ (AlCl₃) → cumene (isopropylbenzene)
Cumene + O₂ → cumene hydroperoxide, then dil. H⁺ → phenol + acetone (one mechanistic pathway)
FeCl₃ (neutral): phenols → violet/blue/green colour; alcohols → no colour
topics.worked_example: To identify ethanol, phenol, diethyl ether, and tert-butanol among unlabeled samples: Na metal first singles out the ether (no reaction); neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> then singles out phenol (colour) among the rest; the Lucas test finally distinguishes the remaining primary and tertiary alcohols by reaction speed.
common_mistakes: Believing phenol and acetone come from two separate manufacturing steps, rather than from rearrangement and cleavage of the very same cumene hydroperoxide molecule.
Assuming a single test (e.g. just the Lucas test, or just FeCl₃) can distinguish every possible unlabeled sample, rather than recognising each test separates only a specific subset.
Expecting an –OH anywhere in a molecule (e.g. on a benzylic carbon, as in benzyl alcohol) to activate a nearby ring toward fast, catalyst-free bromination the way phenol's ring-attached –OH does.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Classify (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH based on the carbon bearing –OH.
options: Tertiary (3°) alcohol
It cannot be classified as an alcohol because the –OH is on a branched carbon
Primary (1°) alcohol
Secondary (2°) alcohol
questions.explanation: In (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH, the carbinol carbon is bonded to three other carbon atoms (three methyl groups), so it is a tertiary alcohol.
questions.hint: Count how many carbon atoms are directly attached to the carbon bearing –OH.
distractor_logic: Wrongly believes branching at the carbinol carbon disqualifies a compound from being classified as an alcohol at all.
Assumes a compact, single-chain-looking formula must be primary without checking all three attached methyls.
Miscounts the number of carbons attached to the carbinol carbon as two instead of three.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the key structural difference between an alcohol and a phenol?
options: Alcohols always contain a benzene ring while phenols never do.
There is no real structural difference — the names just depend on whether the compound is dissolved in water.
Phenol always has two –OH groups while alcohol always has only one.
In phenol, –OH is attached directly to an sp<sup>2</sup> carbon of an aromatic ring; in alcohol, –OH is attached to an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon.
questions.explanation: Phenols have –OH bonded directly to an sp<sup>2</sup> aromatic-ring carbon; alcohols have –OH on an sp<sup>3</sup> carbon (which may still be part of a molecule containing a ring, e.g. benzyl alcohol is an alcohol, not a phenol, since –OH sits on the side-chain sp<sup>3</sup> carbon).
questions.hint: Look at what kind of carbon the –OH is attached to, not whether a ring is present somewhere in the molecule.
distractor_logic: Reverses the actual definitions of alcohol and phenol.
Treats the alcohol/phenol distinction as a solvent or physical-state difference rather than a structural one.
Falsely generalises hydric value (number of –OH groups) as the defining difference between the two classes.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub> and CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> both belong to which class of ether?
options: Mixed (unsymmetrical) ethers
Cyclic ethers
Aromatic ethers
Simple (symmetrical) ethers
questions.explanation: In both compounds the two alkyl groups attached to O are identical (two CH<sub>3</sub>, or two C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>), so both are simple/symmetrical ethers. A mixed ether has two different groups, e.g. CH<sub>3</sub>–O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>.
questions.hint: Compare the two groups attached on either side of the ether oxygen.
distractor_logic: Misapplies 'mixed ether' to a case where both attached groups are actually identical.
Confuses ordinary open-chain dialkyl ethers with ring-containing cyclic ethers like tetrahydrofuran.
Assumes ether = aromatic ether by default, ignoring that neither compound has a ring.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH?
options: Propan-1-ol
Propan-2-ol
Propyl alcohol
1-Propanol alcohol
questions.explanation: The three-carbon chain (propane) has –OH on the terminal carbon (C1), the lowest possible locant, giving propan-1-ol.
questions.hint: Number the chain to give –OH the lowest locant.
distractor_logic: Misplaces the locant, describing the isomer with –OH on C2 instead of C1.
Gives the common/trivial name instead of the requested IUPAC substitutive name.
Adds a redundant, non-standard 'alcohol' word on top of an already-complete IUPAC name.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of the phenol derivative with a –Cl substituent at the position adjacent (ortho) to –OH?
options: 2-Chlorophenol
o-Chlorobenzene
3-Chlorophenol
4-Chlorophenol
questions.explanation: The ring carbon bearing –OH is numbered C1; the adjacent (ortho) position is C2, so a chlorine there gives 2-chlorophenol.
questions.hint: The carbon bearing –OH is always C1 in a substituted phenol's numbering.
distractor_logic: Drops the phenolic –OH from the name entirely, naming it as a chlorobenzene instead.
Places Cl at the meta position (C3) instead of the ortho position specified.
Places Cl at the para position (C4) instead of the ortho position specified.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: Methyl ethanol
Methoxyethane
Ethoxymethane
Dimethyl ether
questions.explanation: IUPAC substitutive nomenclature names the longer/parent chain as the '-ane' root and the shorter O–R group as an 'alkoxy' substituent: the ethyl group (2C) is the parent (ethane), and –O–CH<sub>3</sub> becomes 'methoxy', giving methoxyethane.
questions.hint: The longer carbon chain becomes the parent '-ane'; the shorter O–R group becomes the 'alkoxy' prefix.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly implies an -OH-bearing 'ethanol' substituted with methyl, rather than a true ether linkage.
Swaps which group is treated as parent chain and which as the alkoxy substituent.
Misnames it as a symmetrical ether despite the two attached groups (methyl and ethyl) being different.

questions.topic: Nature of the O–H Bond, Hydrogen Bonding and Physical Properties
questions.question: Why do alcohols have significantly higher boiling points than alkanes of comparable molecular mass?
options: Alkanes are always gases at room temperature while alcohols are always liquids, so this is simply a definitional difference.
Alcohol molecules form intermolecular hydrogen bonds through their O–H groups, which requires extra energy to break during boiling.
Alcohols always have a much higher molecular mass than alkanes, so the higher boiling point is purely a mass effect.
The C–O single bond in alcohols is much stronger than any C–C or C–H bond in alkanes, which raises the boiling point.
questions.explanation: Boiling overcomes intermolecular forces, not covalent bonds. Alcohols' O–H groups allow hydrogen bonding between molecules, a much stronger intermolecular force than the weak van der Waals forces available to alkanes, so more energy (a higher temperature) is needed to boil them.
questions.hint: Boiling point depends on the forces between molecules, not on the strength of bonds within a single molecule.
distractor_logic: Dodges the actual physical cause with a circular/false claim about physical state.
False generalisation contradicting the question's premise, which already specifies comparable molecular mass.
Confuses intramolecular covalent bond strength (irrelevant to boiling) with intermolecular forces (what actually matters).

questions.topic: Nature of the O–H Bond, Hydrogen Bonding and Physical Properties
questions.question: As alkyl chain length in alcohols increases (e.g. methanol → hexanol), water solubility:
options: Stays exactly constant regardless of chain length, since only –OH determines solubility.
Increases steadily, since a longer chain provides more surface area for hydrogen bonding with water.
Decreases, because the growing hydrophobic hydrocarbon portion outweighs the polar –OH group's ability to hydrogen-bond with water.
Increases only up to butanol and then abruptly becomes zero for all longer alcohols.
questions.explanation: Only the –OH group hydrogen-bonds with water; each added –CH<sub>2</sub>– unit adds hydrophobic character. As the nonpolar portion grows relative to the single –OH, overall water solubility gradually falls (short-chain alcohols are fully miscible; longer-chain alcohols become progressively less soluble).
questions.hint: Only the –OH part is water-loving; the rest of the chain is hydrocarbon and water-repelling.
distractor_logic: Ignores the growing hydrophobic hydrocarbon portion's effect on overall solubility.
Wrongly assumes the whole hydrocarbon chain, not just -OH, participates in hydrogen bonding with water.
Invents a false sharp cutoff instead of the actual gradual decreasing trend.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Which reagent converts propene to propan-2-ol as the major product, following Markovnikov's rule?
options: Dilute H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O (acid-catalysed hydration)
Cold, dilute alkaline KMnO<sub>4</sub>
O<sub>3</sub>, then Zn/H<sub>2</sub>O (ozonolysis)
B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/NaOH (hydroboration-oxidation)
questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed hydration adds H and OH across the double bond via a carbocation intermediate, with OH going to the more substituted carbon (Markovnikov), giving propan-2-ol as the major product.
questions.hint: Markovnikov addition puts –OH on the more substituted carbon; which reagent does that?
distractor_logic: Confuses cold dilute KMnO4 (which gives a vicinal diol, propane-1,2-diol) with simple monohydric alcohol formation.
Confuses ozonolysis, which cleaves the C=C bond into carbonyl fragments, with an addition reaction that preserves the carbon skeleton.
Confuses hydroboration-oxidation's anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry (would give propan-1-ol) with the Markovnikov product asked for.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Which reagent reduces CH<sub>3</sub>CHO (acetaldehyde) to ethanol?
options: PCC
Hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>
NaBH<sub>4</sub>
Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>
questions.explanation: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is a hydride-donating reducing agent that converts the carbonyl C=O of an aldehyde into C–OH, giving the corresponding primary alcohol (ethanol).
questions.hint: You need a reducing agent, not an oxidising or dehydrating one.
distractor_logic: PCC is an oxidising agent used to convert alcohols to aldehydes, the reverse transformation of what's asked.
Hot acidic KMnO4 is a strong oxidant that would further oxidise an aldehyde to a carboxylic acid, not reduce it to an alcohol.
Conc. H2SO4 is a dehydrating/catalytic acid, not a reducing agent, and is irrelevant to carbonyl reduction.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr reacts with formaldehyde (HCHO), followed by acidic hydrolysis. What class of alcohol is formed?
options: Tertiary alcohol
The product is a carboxylic acid, not an alcohol
Primary alcohol
Secondary alcohol
questions.explanation: Formaldehyde is unique among carbonyl compounds in that Grignard addition to it always gives a primary alcohol (here, ethanol) after hydrolysis, since HCHO contributes only H atoms (no extra carbon substituents) to the carbinol carbon.
questions.hint: Formaldehyde is the one aldehyde that behaves specially with Grignard reagents — it always gives this class of alcohol.
distractor_logic: Applies the rule for ketones (which give tertiary alcohols) to formaldehyde, which is not a ketone.
Confuses the HCHO reaction with the separate Grignard + CO2 reaction, which does give a carboxylic acid, not an alcohol.
Applies the general rule for aldehydes-other-than-formaldehyde (which give secondary alcohols) incorrectly to formaldehyde itself.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Alkyl halides are converted into alcohols using aqueous NaOH/KOH via which type of reaction?
options: Elimination exclusively, with no substitution occurring
Electrophilic addition
Nucleophilic substitution (hydrolysis), by SN1 or SN2 depending on the halide's class
Free-radical substitution
questions.explanation: Hydroxide ion (or water) acts as a nucleophile, displacing the halide leaving group at the saturated carbon — an SN2 pathway for primary halides, or SN1 (via a carbocation) for tertiary halides, giving the alcohol.
questions.hint: Think about what kind of nucleophile OH<sup>–</sup> is, and what kind of carbon (saturated, sp<sup>3</sup>) it's attacking.
distractor_logic: Ignores that substitution (not elimination) is the pathway that actually produces the alcohol; elimination is only a competing side reaction giving alkene instead.
Misapplies an addition-reaction category to a substitution occurring at a saturated (not multiply-bonded) carbon.
Confuses the mechanism with free-radical halogenation of alkanes, an unrelated reaction type.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Which classic industrial method converts chlorobenzene directly into phenol by nucleophilic aromatic substitution?
options: Treating chlorobenzene with aqueous HCl
Treating chlorobenzene with dilute NaOH at room temperature
Treating chlorobenzene with Na metal directly (Wurtz-type coupling)
Fusing/heating chlorobenzene with NaOH at 623 K and 300 atm (Dow process)
questions.explanation: The aryl C–Cl bond is unreactive toward ordinary nucleophilic substitution, so very forcing conditions — fusion with NaOH at high temperature and pressure — are needed to displace chlorine with –OH, giving phenol via the Dow process.
questions.hint: The aryl C–Cl bond strongly resists substitution — think about what kind of conditions could still force the reaction.
distractor_logic: Uses the wrong reagent type; substitution here needs a strong nucleophile (OH-) under forcing conditions, not dilute acid.
Too mild; the aryl C-Cl bond is unreactive under such gentle conditions and simply will not undergo substitution.
Na metal with an aryl halide gives a Wurtz-type coupling product (biphenyl), not phenol.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Phenol can be prepared from benzenesulfonic acid by which method?
options: Reduction with H<sub>2</sub>/Pd
Fusion with molten NaOH, followed by acidification
Simple hydrolysis with dilute HCl at room temperature
Reaction with Br<sub>2</sub>/Fe
questions.explanation: Fusing sodium benzenesulfonate with NaOH at high temperature replaces –SO<sub>3</sub>Na with –ONa (sodium phenoxide); subsequent acidification gives phenol.
questions.hint: The –SO<sub>3</sub>H group needs quite forcing conditions to be displaced — dilute acid at room temperature won't do it.
distractor_logic: Hydrogenation/reduction is irrelevant here; -SO3H is not removed by catalytic reduction to give -OH.
Too mild; the sulfonic acid group does not leave under such gentle conditions.
Bromination with Br2/Fe is an unrelated electrophilic substitution reaction, not a way to convert -SO3H into -OH.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Benzenediazonium chloride, when warmed with water, gives which product?
options: Aniline, regenerated unchanged
Phenol, with loss of N<sub>2</sub> gas
Chlorobenzene, via displacement by chloride
Benzene, with loss of N<sub>2</sub> and replacement by H
questions.explanation: Warming a diazonium salt with water hydrolyses the –N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> group, which leaves as N<sub>2</sub> gas while water's oxygen becomes the new C–OH bond, giving phenol.
questions.hint: Water is the nucleophile here — what group does it install where N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> used to be?
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes no reaction takes place, when hydrolysis of the diazonium group is in fact a standard, well-known transformation.
Confuses simple aqueous hydrolysis with the separate Sandmeyer-type reaction (using CuCl), which installs chlorine instead of OH.
Confuses hydrolysis (which installs OH) with a different reagent, H3PO2, which instead replaces the diazonium group with H to give benzene.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Which reagent converts a primary alcohol like ethanol into an aldehyde, stopping at that stage without further oxidation to the acid?
options: NaBH<sub>4</sub>
Hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>
Hot acidic K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>
PCC (pyridinium chlorochromate)
questions.explanation: PCC is a mild, selective oxidant that stops precisely at the aldehyde stage; strong oxidants like hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> or K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> continue on to the carboxylic acid.
questions.hint: You need a mild, selective oxidant that stops early — not a strong one that goes all the way.
distractor_logic: NaBH4 is a reducing agent, not an oxidant; it would not oxidise the alcohol at all.
Too strong; hot acidic KMnO4 is a powerful oxidant that continues past the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid.
Too strong; hot acidic K2Cr2O7 similarly over-oxidises past the aldehyde stage to the carboxylic acid.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: What product forms when propan-2-ol is oxidised with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>?
options: Propan-2-one (acetone)
Propanoic acid
Propan-2-ol is regenerated unchanged
Propene, via dehydration
questions.explanation: A secondary alcohol's carbinol carbon has exactly one H, which is removed along with formation of C=O, giving a ketone (propan-2-one). Unlike primary alcohols, secondary alcohols cannot be oxidised further to a carboxylic acid without breaking a C–C bond.
questions.hint: Secondary alcohols oxidise to a specific carbonyl class that cannot be pushed any further under normal conditions.
distractor_logic: A secondary alcohol cannot be oxidised to a carboxylic acid under normal conditions since that would require breaking a C-C bond.
Denies that oxidation occurs at all, when acidified K2Cr2O7 is in fact a standard, effective oxidant for secondary alcohols.
Confuses oxidation with an entirely different reaction (dehydration), which needs conc. H2SO4/heat, not an oxidant.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: What is the major product when ethanol reacts with acetic acid in the presence of conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> (Fischer esterification)?
options: Ethyl acetate + water
Diethyl ether, via intermolecular dehydration of two ethanol molecules
Ethene, via dehydration of ethanol
Ethyl acetate only, with no other product formed
questions.explanation: Fischer esterification is a condensation reaction: the –OH of the acid and the H of the alcohol combine to form water alongside the ester (ethyl acetate).
questions.hint: Esterification is a condensation reaction — think about what small molecule is always released alongside the ester.
distractor_logic: Confuses esterification (alcohol + carboxylic acid) with intermolecular ether formation (alcohol + alcohol), a different reaction entirely.
Confuses esterification with dehydration to an alkene, a completely different reaction pathway requiring only the alcohol and conc. H2SO4 at high temperature, not a carboxylic acid.
Esterification always releases water as the other product (a condensation reaction), which this option incorrectly omits.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Dehydration of ethanol with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> at around 443 K gives which major product?
options: Ethene (ethylene)
Acetaldehyde
Ethane
Diethyl ether
questions.explanation: At the higher temperature (≈443 K), intramolecular elimination of water dominates, giving ethene; the lower temperature (≈413 K) instead favours the substitution pathway giving diethyl ether.
questions.hint: This is the higher of the two characteristic ethanol/H2SO4 temperatures — which pathway (elimination or substitution) does that favour?
distractor_logic: Confuses dehydration (elimination, using conc. H2SO4 alone) with oxidation, which requires a separate oxidising agent.
Dehydration removes water to form an unsaturated alkene, not a fully saturated alkane like ethane.
This is instead the major product at the lower characteristic temperature (~413 K), via a different (substitution) pathway.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Which class of alcohol resists oxidation by common oxidising agents like acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> under normal conditions?
options: Secondary alcohols
All alcohols resist oxidation equally, regardless of class
Tertiary alcohols, e.g. 2-methylpropan-2-ol
Primary alcohols
questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols have no hydrogen on the carbinol carbon, so the usual oxidation mechanism (removing that H while forming C=O) is unavailable; oxidising a tertiary alcohol under normal conditions does not occur without breaking a C–C bond, which requires much more vigorous conditions.
questions.hint: Oxidation of an alcohol needs a hydrogen on the carbon bearing –OH — which class lacks that hydrogen?
distractor_logic: Secondary alcohols are in fact readily oxidised (to the corresponding ketone).
Denies the well-established, class-dependent oxidation trend that specifically exempts tertiary alcohols under normal conditions.
Primary alcohols are in fact readily oxidised (first to aldehyde, then further to carboxylic acid).

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: What happens when ethanol reacts with sodium metal?
options: Sodium hydroxide is formed along with ethane
Sodium ethoxide forms and H<sub>2</sub> gas is evolved: 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>OH + 2Na → 2C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONa + H<sub>2</sub>
No visible reaction occurs, since alcohols are neutral compounds unreactive to metals
Sodium ethoxide forms, but no gas is evolved
questions.explanation: The acidic O–H hydrogen is displaced by sodium, forming sodium ethoxide and releasing H<sub>2</sub> gas (visible as effervescence) — the same type of reaction alcohols and phenols both give with active metals.
questions.hint: Compare this to how sodium reacts with water — the alkyl group's oxygen keeps its bond intact.
distractor_logic: Misassigns the products; the alkyl group stays attached to oxygen forming alkoxide, it does not split off as ethane.
Denies the well-known reactivity of the acidic O-H bond with active metals like sodium.
Misses that H2 gas is a directly observable (and characteristic) product of this reaction.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: What reagent combination is known as the Lucas reagent, used to distinguish 1°, 2°, and 3° alcohols?
options: Conc. HBr + red phosphorus
Conc. HCl + anhydrous ZnCl<sub>2</sub>
Dilute HCl + NaOH
Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> + KMnO<sub>4</sub>
questions.explanation: The Lucas reagent is a mixture of concentrated HCl and anhydrous ZnCl<sub>2</sub> (a Lewis acid catalyst that helps ionise the C–O bond), used because the rate of turbidity (alkyl chloride formation) differs sharply by alcohol class.
questions.hint: This reagent works by helping the alcohol's C–O bond ionise — think of a Lewis-acid catalyst paired with a hydrogen halide.
distractor_logic: This is a different halogenation reagent combination (used to generate alkyl bromides via phosphorus halides in situ), not the specific Lucas reagent.
Dilute HCl alone (without ZnCl2 as catalyst) is too weak to differentiate alcohol classes usefully, and adding NaOH would simply neutralise it.
This combination resembles oxidation reagents, unrelated to the Lucas test's halide-substitution chemistry.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: In the Lucas test, which class of alcohol reacts fastest, with turbidity appearing almost immediately at room temperature?
options: All three classes react at exactly the same rate
A tertiary alcohol
A primary alcohol
A secondary alcohol
questions.explanation: Tertiary alcohols form the most stable carbocation, so they ionise (SN1) fastest, giving near-instant turbidity; primary alcohols react slowest (needing heat, via a sluggish SN2-type pathway), with secondary alcohols intermediate.
questions.hint: Think about which class of alcohol forms the most stable carbocation intermediate.
distractor_logic: Contradicts the entire premise/purpose of the Lucas test, which exists specifically because the three classes react at markedly different rates.
Primary alcohols actually react slowest, needing heating, since they require an SN2-type pathway rather than a fast SN1 pathway.
Secondary alcohols react at an intermediate rate (typically a few minutes), not as fast as tertiary.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Which is more acidic, phenol or ethanol, and why (at a basic level)?
options: Phenol, because the phenoxide ion formed after loss of H<sup>+</sup> is stabilised by resonance delocalisation into the aromatic ring, while ethoxide has no such stabilisation.
Phenol is more acidic only because it smells different from ethanol, and smell correlates directly with acid strength.
Ethanol, because alkyl groups are electron-withdrawing, stabilising the ethoxide ion more than the phenoxide ion.
Phenol and ethanol are equally acidic, since both possess a single –OH group with an identical type of O–H bond.
questions.explanation: After losing H<sup>+</sup>, phenol's negative charge can delocalise into the aromatic ring by resonance, spreading out and stabilising the phenoxide ion; ethoxide has no comparable delocalisation pathway, so it remains a much weaker (less stabilised, less readily formed) conjugate base.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the negative charge on the conjugate base of each compound after it loses H<sup>+</sup>.
distractor_logic: A nonsensical, chemically irrelevant 'explanation' with no real basis in acid-strength reasoning.
Reverses the actual electronic character of alkyl groups; they are electron-donating (+I), which destabilises negative charge rather than stabilising it.
Ignores the vastly different degree of stabilisation available to each conjugate base, despite the superficially similar O-H bond.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Which type of substituent, at the ortho or para position of phenol, generally increases its acidity relative to unsubstituted phenol?
options: Only substituents at the meta position affect acidity; ortho/para substituents have no effect
An electron-withdrawing group (EWG), such as –NO<sub>2</sub>
An electron-donating group (EDG), such as –CH<sub>3</sub>
Any substituent, regardless of electronic character, simply by adding molecular weight
questions.explanation: An EWG at ortho/para withdraws electron density from the ring by both induction and resonance, further stabilising the phenoxide ion's negative charge and increasing acidity relative to unsubstituted phenol.
questions.hint: Think about which type of substituent would help stabilise (spread out) the negative charge on the phenoxide ion even further.
distractor_logic: Reverses which positions have the strongest effect; ortho/para substitution (with a direct resonance pathway) has the strongest influence, while meta substitution is comparatively weak, not absent.
EDGs generally decrease phenol's acidity, not increase it, since they push additional electron density toward an already-negative phenoxide.
Ignores the electronic (not mass-based) basis of the effect entirely.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Which is more acidic: phenol or p-nitrophenol?
options: p-Nitrophenol
Phenol
Neither is acidic at all
They are equally acidic
questions.explanation: –NO<sub>2</sub> at the para position is a strong electron-withdrawing group that stabilises the phenoxide ion via resonance, making p-nitrophenol considerably more acidic than phenol.
questions.hint: Nitro is a strong electron-withdrawing group — what does that do to acidity when placed at para?
distractor_logic: Reverses the actual order; -NO2 at the para position is a strong EWG that increases, not decreases, acidity via resonance withdrawal.
Factually wrong; phenols are weakly acidic compounds, capable of reacting with strong bases like NaOH.
Ignores the significant acidifying effect of the para-nitro substituent relative to unsubstituted phenol.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Does phenol react with aqueous NaOH?
options: Only under extremely high temperature and pressure, unlike an ordinary acid-base reaction
Yes, but it forms an ester, not sodium phenoxide
No — phenols are neutral, non-acidic compounds
Yes — phenol reacts with NaOH to form sodium phenoxide and water
questions.explanation: Phenol is acidic enough to be neutralised by a strong base like NaOH at room temperature, forming sodium phenoxide and water — a standard acid-base reaction, not an esterification.
questions.hint: Phenol is a weak acid — what would you expect a weak acid to do when mixed with a strong base?
distractor_logic: Overstates the difficulty of what is actually a mild, room-temperature acid-base neutralisation.
Misidentifies the type of product; this is an acid-base neutralisation giving a salt (phenoxide), not an esterification.
Denies phenol's real, well-established acidity and its standard reaction with strong bases.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Phenol reacts with CO<sub>2</sub> and NaOH under Kolbe's reaction conditions (heat, pressure), followed by acidification. What is the product?
options: Salicylaldehyde
Picric acid
Salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid)
Benzoic acid
questions.explanation: Kolbe's reaction carboxylates the phenoxide ion, predominantly at the ortho position, giving (after acidification) salicylic acid, 2-hydroxybenzoic acid.
questions.hint: This reaction installs a –COOH group, predominantly at the ortho position relative to –OH.
distractor_logic: Confuses Kolbe's reaction (giving a carboxylic acid via CO2) with the Reimer-Tiemann reaction (giving an aldehyde via CHCl3).
Confuses Kolbe's reaction (carboxylation with CO2) with nitration, an entirely different electrophile and reaction.
Misses the -OH group's presence entirely and the characteristic ortho-carboxylation pattern of this specific reaction.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Phenol reacts with CHCl<sub>3</sub> and aqueous NaOH, heat, followed by acidification — the Reimer-Tiemann reaction. What is the product?
options: Benzyl alcohol
2,4,6-Trichlorophenol
Salicylic acid
Salicylaldehyde (2-hydroxybenzaldehyde)
questions.explanation: Dichlorocarbene, generated in situ from CHCl<sub>3</sub> and base, attacks the phenoxide ring (predominantly ortho); hydrolysis of the resulting intermediate gives salicylaldehyde.
questions.hint: This reaction's electrophile comes from CHCl3, and installs a –CHO group, not –COOH.
distractor_logic: An unrelated product that doesn't reflect the actual dichlorocarbene-based mechanism/electrophile involved here.
Confuses formation of an electrophilic carbene intermediate (which ultimately installs -CHO) with simple direct ring chlorination.
Confuses the Reimer-Tiemann reaction (which gives an aldehyde) with Kolbe's reaction (which gives a carboxylic acid).

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: What is the product when phenol reacts with excess bromine water (no solvent)?
options: No reaction occurs
p-Bromophenol only
Benzene, via loss of the –OH group
2,4,6-Tribromophenol (white precipitate), immediately
questions.explanation: Phenol's ring is strongly activated by –OH, so excess bromine water substitutes at all three available activated (ortho/ortho/para) positions essentially instantly, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol — a classic test for phenol.
questions.hint: Phenol's ring is strongly activated, and there's excess Br2 available — how many positions get substituted?
distractor_logic: Incorrect; phenol's ring is strongly activated (not deactivated) toward electrophilic substitution, which is exactly why this reaction is so fast and complete.
Describes the product of controlled monobromination (using CS2 as solvent, low temperature), not what excess bromine water in water gives.
Invents an unrelated defunctionalisation (loss of -OH) that is not part of this reaction at all.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Which position(s) does phenol's –OH group direct an incoming electrophile to, in electrophilic aromatic substitution?
options: Ortho and para positions
Meta position only
Only the para position, never ortho
All six ring positions equally, with no preference
questions.explanation: –OH is a strong ortho/para director, donating electron density into the ring by resonance specifically at those positions, making them the preferred sites for electrophilic attack.
questions.hint: –OH's lone-pair resonance donation into the ring specifically boosts electron density at two particular types of position.
distractor_logic: Reverses phenol's actual directing behaviour; -OH is an ortho/para director, not a meta director.
Phenol directs to both ortho and para positions, not exclusively para.
Denies phenol's strong, well-documented directing effect toward specific ring positions.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Which reaction converts an alkyl halide and a sodium alkoxide into an ether?
options: Fischer esterification
Wurtz reaction
Friedel-Crafts alkylation
Williamson ether synthesis: R–X + R'–ONa → R–O–R' + NaX
questions.explanation: Williamson synthesis is the standard SN2-based method for making an ether: the alkoxide's oxygen displaces the halide from the alkyl halide.
questions.hint: You need the reaction where an alkoxide acts as a nucleophile toward an alkyl halide.
distractor_logic: Gives an ester (from an acid + alcohol), not an ether.
Gives a C-C coupled alkane (two alkyl halides + Na), unrelated to forming a C-O-C ether linkage.
Installs an alkyl group directly on an aromatic ring using AlCl3, unrelated to forming an ether linkage.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: In Williamson synthesis, which type of alkyl halide gives the best (highest-yield) substitution results?
options: A primary alkyl halide
A vinylic halide (halogen on a C=C carbon)
A tertiary alkyl halide
An aryl halide (halogen directly on an aromatic ring)
questions.explanation: A primary alkyl halide readily undergoes clean SN2 substitution with the bulky alkoxide nucleophile, without the competing elimination that tertiary substrates favour.
questions.hint: This reaction needs backside (SN2) attack — which class of halide is least sterically hindered for that?
distractor_logic: Vinylic halides do not undergo SN2 substitution at all under normal conditions.
Favours E2 elimination instead of substitution under these strongly basic (alkoxide) conditions, giving mostly alkene, not ether.
Aryl halides are essentially unreactive toward SN2 substitution.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: What happens when diethyl ether is heated with excess concentrated HI?
options: The ether undergoes dehydration to give an alkene
The ether is oxidised to two molecules of acetic acid
The C–O bond is cleaved, giving two molecules of ethyl iodide (plus water)
The ether is unaffected, since ethers are generally unreactive toward all reagents
questions.explanation: Excess hot HI cleaves ether C–O bonds; for a simple symmetrical dialkyl ether like diethyl ether, this gives two molecules of the corresponding alkyl iodide plus water.
questions.hint: Ethers do react with excess strong hydrogen halides — think about what bond in the ether gets broken.
distractor_logic: Dehydration is a reaction of alcohols (removing water); ethers have no -OH group to remove in this way.
Confuses cleavage (a substitution-type reaction breaking C-O bonds) with oxidation, which would require an oxidising agent, not HI.
Denies the well-known cleavage reaction of ethers with strong hydrogen halides like excess HI.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: When anisole is heated with excess HI, which bond breaks — the aryl C–O bond or the alkyl (methyl) C–O bond?
options: The aryl C–O bond breaks, giving iodobenzene + methanol
Neither bond breaks; anisole is unreactive toward HI
The alkyl (methyl) C–O bond breaks, giving phenol + methyl iodide
Both C–O bonds break simultaneously
questions.explanation: The aryl C–O bond has partial double-bond character (from resonance) and strongly resists cleavage; the alkyl C–O bond breaks instead, giving phenol and methyl iodide.
questions.hint: One of these two C–O bonds has partial double-bond character, making it much harder to break.
distractor_logic: Incorrect; the aryl C-O bond's partial double-bond character makes it strongly resist cleavage, so it is essentially never the one that breaks.
Denies the well-established cleavage reaction of aryl alkyl ethers with excess hot HI.
Overstates that the resistant aryl C-O bond also breaks; only the alkyl C-O bond cleaves under these conditions.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Ethers can also be made by acid-catalysed intermolecular dehydration of two alcohol molecules. Which condition favours ether formation over alkene formation, for the same alcohol and conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>?
options: Lower reaction temperature, with excess alcohol present
Higher reaction temperature
Adding water to the reaction mixture before heating
A large excess of conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> relative to alcohol
questions.explanation: At the lower characteristic temperature with excess alcohol, the intermolecular substitution pathway (giving the ether) is favoured over the intramolecular elimination pathway that dominates at higher temperature.
questions.hint: Two separate ethanol/H2SO4 outcomes are possible — one is favoured by milder heat and plenty of alcohol.
distractor_logic: This instead favours the competing intramolecular elimination pathway, giving alkene as the major product.
Adding water would hinder both dehydration pathways by diluting the acid catalyst and shifting the water-releasing equilibrium backward, not specifically favour ether formation.
A large excess of acid relative to alcohol (opposite of excess alcohol) does not favour the intermolecular (two-alcohol-molecule) pathway needed for ether formation.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: What are the two industrial starting materials for the cumene process?
options: Toluene and propene
Benzene and ethene
Benzene and propene
Phenol and acetone
questions.explanation: Benzene undergoes Friedel-Crafts alkylation with propene (AlCl<sub>3</sub> catalyst) to give cumene (isopropylbenzene), the starting point for the rest of the process.
questions.hint: Think about what aromatic and alkene combination, via Friedel-Crafts alkylation, gives isopropylbenzene (cumene).
distractor_logic: Wrong aromatic starting material; the cumene process specifically uses benzene, not toluene.
Wrong alkene; propene (not ethene) is needed to give the isopropyl group characteristic of cumene.
These are actually the PRODUCTS of the cumene process, not its starting materials.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: What are the two products of the cumene process, after cumene hydroperoxide is treated with dilute acid?
options: Cumene and hydrogen peroxide
Phenol and acetone
Phenol and formaldehyde
Benzene and propanone
questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed rearrangement and cleavage of cumene hydroperoxide gives phenol and acetone as the two final products.
questions.hint: This process is valued industrially precisely because it gives two useful products from one pathway — name them.
distractor_logic: These are an intermediate/reagent used earlier in the process, not its final products.
Wrong carbonyl byproduct; acetone (not formaldehyde) is the actual co-product of this process.
Misidentifies phenol as unreacted benzene rather than the actual hydroxylated product formed.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Which correctly describes the neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> test for distinguishing phenols from alcohols?
options: Both alcohols and phenols give an identical coloration, making the test non-distinguishing
Phenols give a characteristic violet/blue/green coloration; alcohols give no such coloration
Neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> distinguishes primary from secondary alcohols, not phenols from alcohols
Alcohols give a characteristic coloration with neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> while phenols do not
questions.explanation: Phenols form a coloured complex with Fe<sup>3+</sup> that simple alcohols do not form, making neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> a useful, selective test specifically for phenols.
questions.hint: This is a test that reacts specifically with the phenolic functional group, not with ordinary alcohols.
distractor_logic: Denies the test's actual usefulness and selectivity for phenols specifically over alcohols.
Misapplies the test's actual purpose; it distinguishes phenols (which react) from alcohols (which don't), not among different alcohol classes.
Reverses which class of compound actually gives the colour reaction; it is phenols, not alcohols, that respond to this test.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Which test distinguishes ethanol (positive) from methanol (negative), based on a CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)– or CH<sub>3</sub>–CO– structural unit?
options: The Lucas test
The iodoform test (yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> precipitate with I<sub>2</sub>/NaOH)
The neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> test
The Lucas test, but with the results reversed for these two alcohols
questions.explanation: Ethanol has the required CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)– structural unit and gives a positive iodoform test (yellow CHI<sub>3</sub> precipitate); methanol lacks this unit and tests negative.
questions.hint: This test is specific to a particular structural pattern involving a methyl group next to a carbon bearing OH (or a carbonyl).
distractor_logic: The Lucas test distinguishes alcohol classes (1°/2°/3°) by reaction rate with HCl/ZnCl2, unrelated to the specific CH3-CH(OH)- structural requirement being tested here.
The neutral FeCl3 test distinguishes phenols from alcohols/other compounds, unrelated to the CH3-CH(OH)- structural requirement being tested here.
Misapplies the Lucas test's actual purpose and reverses which of the two alcohols would even be relevant to it.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Anisole (methoxybenzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>) is classified as:
options: A simple ether, since only one substituent group is really attached
A phenol derivative, since it is structurally related to phenol by substitution
A tertiary alcohol, since the oxygen is attached to a ring carbon
An aryl alkyl (mixed, aromatic) ether
questions.explanation: Anisole has an aromatic ring on one side of the ether oxygen and a methyl group on the other — two different groups make it a mixed (unsymmetrical) ether. It has no –OH at all, so despite looking related to phenol, it is not a phenol.
questions.hint: Anisole has no –OH group — check what functional group is actually present.
distractor_logic: Miscounts the two different groups (aryl and methyl) attached to O as if only one substituent were present.
Confuses a compound with no –OH (ether linkage) for a phenol, based only on structural resemblance.
Confuses an ether oxygen bonded to two carbons with a carbinol carbon that actually bears –OH.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Which pair correctly matches an alcohol's hydric classification with an example, based on the number of –OH groups present?
options: Monohydric alcohol — CH<sub>2</sub>OH–CHOH–CH<sub>2</sub>OH (glycerol)
Dihydric alcohol — HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>OH (ethylene glycol)
Trihydric alcohol — HOCH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>OH (ethylene glycol)
Dihydric alcohol — CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>OH (ethanol)
questions.explanation: Ethanol has 1 –OH (monohydric), ethylene glycol has 2 –OH groups (dihydric), and glycerol has 3 –OH groups (trihydric).
questions.hint: Literally count the –OH groups written in each structure.
distractor_logic: Undercounts glycerol's three –OH groups as only one.
Overcounts ethylene glycol's –OH groups as three when only two are actually present.
Miscounts ethanol's single –OH group as two, perhaps confused by the word 'di' appearing elsewhere.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: An allylic alcohol has its –OH group attached to a carbon that is:
options: Adjacent to an aromatic ring (i.e. benzylic) rather than a double bond
Directly adjacent to a carbon–carbon double bond, e.g. CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH
Directly part of an aromatic ring
The double-bond carbon itself, as in an enol
questions.explanation: 'Allylic' means the carbinol (sp<sup>3</sup>) carbon is adjacent to a C=C double bond, as in prop-2-en-1-ol, CH<sub>2</sub>=CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH. If –OH sat on the double-bond carbon itself, that would be an enol, not an allylic alcohol.
questions.hint: 'Allylic' refers to position relative to a C=C bond, not to the double-bond carbon itself.
distractor_logic: Confuses allylic classification (relative to a double bond) with benzylic classification (relative to an aromatic ring).
Describes the structural feature of phenol, not an allylic alcohol.
Confuses allylic position (adjacent to C=C) with vinylic position (on the C=C carbon itself, i.e. an enol).

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the IUPAC name of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub>CH–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH?
options: Isopentyl alcohol
2-Methylbutan-1-ol
3-Methylbutan-1-ol
3-Methylbutan-4-ol
questions.explanation: The longest chain containing the –OH carbon has four carbons, numbered from the OH end for the lowest locant (butan-1-ol); the branch then falls on C3, giving 3-methylbutan-1-ol.
questions.hint: Number from the end nearer –OH so the principal group gets the lowest locant, then locate the branch from that same end.
distractor_logic: Gives the trivial/common name instead of the requested systematic IUPAC name.
Misassigns the branch's locant as C2 instead of C3 by numbering from the wrong end.
Gives –OH the wrong (higher) locant instead of the lowest possible one available.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of catechol (the simplest ortho-dihydroxybenzene, with no other substituents)?
options: Benzene-1,2-diol
Benzene-1,3-diol
Benzene-1,4-diol
1,2-Dihydroxybenzol
questions.explanation: Catechol has two –OH groups on adjacent ring carbons (ortho), giving locants 1,2: benzene-1,2-diol. Benzene-1,3-diol is resorcinol (meta) and benzene-1,4-diol is hydroquinone (para).
questions.hint: 'Catechol' = ortho-dihydroxybenzene; match that ortho relationship to locants 1,2.
distractor_logic: Names the meta-dihydroxybenzene isomer (resorcinol) instead of the ortho one (catechol) actually described.
Names the para-dihydroxybenzene isomer (hydroquinone) instead of the ortho one (catechol) actually described.
Uses 'benzol', a non-IUPAC name, instead of the correct root 'benzene'.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Applying the 'principal group gets lowest locant' rule, what is the IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–Br?
options: 1-Bromobutan-3-ol
4-Bromo-2-butanol
4-Bromobutan-2-ol
2-Bromobutan-4-ol
questions.explanation: –OH (the principal characteristic group, expressed as suffix '-ol') gets priority for the lowest locant over the bromo substituent. Numbering from the OH end gives OH at C2 and Br at C4: 4-bromobutan-2-ol.
questions.hint: The suffix group (-ol) always outranks substituent prefixes (like bromo) when assigning the lowest locant.
distractor_logic: Numbers from the wrong end, giving -OH a higher locant (3) than the lower one (2) actually available.
Uses outdated locant placement (number before the parent name) instead of current IUPAC style (number immediately before the suffix).
Gives -OH the highest possible locant instead of prioritising it for the lowest one.

questions.topic: Nature of the O–H Bond, Hydrogen Bonding and Physical Properties
questions.question: Diethyl ether and butan-1-ol are structural isomers (both C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O) with very different boiling points (ether ≈35°C, alcohol ≈118°C). Why?
options: Butan-1-ol has an O–H bond enabling intermolecular hydrogen bonding between its own molecules; diethyl ether has no O–H bond and so cannot hydrogen-bond to other ether molecules.
Both compounds should have identical boiling points since isomers always share identical physical properties.
Diethyl ether has a lower boiling point simply because it has a smaller total molecular surface area, unrelated to hydrogen bonding.
Butan-1-ol's higher boiling point is due to its C–O bond being much stronger than the ether's two C–O bonds combined.
questions.explanation: Same formula and molar mass, but only the alcohol's O–H bond permits strong, directional intermolecular hydrogen bonding between like molecules. Ether oxygen has lone pairs but no attached H to donate, so ether-ether interactions stay weak, giving it a far lower boiling point despite an identical molecular formula.
questions.hint: Compare which of the two isomers actually has an O–H bond available for hydrogen bonding to itself.
distractor_logic: False; isomers share molecular formula but can differ enormously in physical properties depending on which functional groups are present.
Overlooks that the two isomers have identical molecular formula/mass, so surface-area differences are not the real driver; the actual cause is hydrogen-bonding capability.
Mistakes intramolecular covalent bond strength (irrelevant to boiling) for the true cause, intermolecular hydrogen bonding.

questions.topic: Nature of the O–H Bond, Hydrogen Bonding and Physical Properties
questions.question: Ethers are only weakly-to-moderately soluble in water (roughly comparable to isomeric alcohols) despite having no O–H bond themselves. Why?
options: Ethers dissolve in water purely via van der Waals forces, with no hydrogen bonding involved at all.
Ether molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other just as alcohols do, giving similar solubility by the same mechanism.
Ethers are actually completely insoluble in water; any apparent solubility data reflects experimental error.
The ether oxygen's lone pairs can accept a hydrogen bond from water's O–H, even though ether molecules cannot hydrogen-bond to each other.
questions.explanation: An ether cannot donate a hydrogen bond (no O–H), but its oxygen lone pairs can accept one from water's O–H. This one-sided hydrogen bonding gives ethers moderate water solubility, similar to isomeric alcohols, even though ether-ether self-association is essentially absent (hence their much lower boiling points).
questions.hint: Solubility in water only requires the ether to accept a hydrogen bond from water — not to hydrogen-bond with itself.
distractor_logic: Overlooks the genuine hydrogen-bond-accepting role of the ether oxygen's lone pairs with water molecules.
Incorrect; ethers cannot hydrogen-bond to each other since none have an O-H to donate, unlike alcohols.
Factually wrong; low-molecular-weight ethers do show appreciable water solubility.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Oxymercuration-demercuration of propene [Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O, then NaBH<sub>4</sub>] gives which alcohol, and why is it often preferred over direct acid-catalysed hydration?
options: Propan-2-ol (Markovnikov product); preferred because it proceeds through a bridged mercurinium ion rather than a free carbocation, avoiding the rearranged byproducts common with acid-catalysed hydration.
Propan-1-ol (anti-Markovnikov product), by the same mechanistic logic as hydroboration-oxidation.
A roughly equal mixture of propan-1-ol and propan-2-ol, since the mercurinium ion opens non-selectively.
Propan-2-ol, preferred only because the reagents are cheaper, with no real mechanistic advantage.
questions.explanation: Oxymercuration proceeds through a bridged (three-membered) mercurinium ion rather than a free carbocation, so it still gives the Markovnikov product (OH on the more substituted carbon) but without the risk of carbocation rearrangement seen in ordinary acid-catalysed hydration.
questions.hint: Oxymercuration gives the same regiochemistry (Markovnikov) as acid hydration, but through a different, rearrangement-free intermediate.
distractor_logic: Confuses oxymercuration's Markovnikov regiochemistry with hydroboration-oxidation's anti-Markovnikov outcome.
Incorrectly claims non-selective ring-opening; the mercurinium ion still opens regioselectively to give the Markovnikov product.
Misses the actual mechanistic reason (a bridged ion avoiding free-carbocation rearrangement) for the reagent's usefulness.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Which reagent sequence converts but-1-ene into butan-1-ol (anti-Markovnikov, syn addition)?
options: B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub> (or BH<sub>3</sub>·THF), then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/NaOH
Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O (acid-catalysed hydration)
LiAlH<sub>4</sub>, then aqueous H<sub>3</sub>O<sup>+</sup>
Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O, then NaBH<sub>4</sub>
questions.explanation: Hydroboration-oxidation adds boron to the less hindered (terminal) carbon in a concerted, syn fashion, and oxidation replaces B with OH with retention of configuration, giving the anti-Markovnikov alcohol, butan-1-ol.
questions.hint: You need the one method that places –OH on the less substituted (terminal) carbon.
distractor_logic: Confuses acid-catalysed hydration (Markovnikov, giving butan-2-ol) with the anti-Markovnikov method asked for.
Misapplies LiAlH4, a carbonyl/ester-reducing agent, to an alkene hydration context where it has no role.
Confuses oxymercuration (Markovnikov, giving butan-2-ol) with the anti-Markovnikov method asked for.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Reduction of an ester, R–COOCH<sub>3</sub>, with excess LiAlH<sub>4</sub> followed by aqueous workup gives:
options: An aldehyde, R–CHO, as the final isolated product
A primary alcohol, R–CH<sub>2</sub>OH, along with methanol
A carboxylic acid, R–COOH
A ketone
questions.explanation: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a strong hydride reducing agent that fully reduces esters, releasing the alkoxy portion as an alcohol (here methanol) and reducing the acyl portion all the way to a primary alcohol, R–CH<sub>2</sub>OH.
questions.hint: LiAlH4 is a strong enough reducing agent to go all the way — it doesn't stop partway.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly stops the reduction at the aldehyde stage; excess LiAlH4 over-reduces all the way to the primary alcohol.
Confuses reduction (which adds hydride, giving alcohol) with hydrolysis, which would be a different reaction giving back acid and alcohol without reduction.
Misapplies a ketone-forming outcome (relevant to limited Grignard addition to acid chlorides under special conditions) to straightforward ester reduction by LiAlH4.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: R–MgX reacts with dry CO<sub>2</sub>, followed by acidic hydrolysis. What is the product?
options: A primary alcohol, since CO<sub>2</sub> behaves like formaldehyde toward Grignard reagents
A carboxylic acid, R–COOH — not an alcohol
No reaction occurs, since Grignard reagents cannot react with dry ice
A secondary alcohol, matching the general pattern seen for aldehydes
questions.explanation: Grignard reagents add to the electrophilic carbon of CO<sub>2</sub> to give a magnesium carboxylate, which on acidic workup yields a carboxylic acid, R–COOH — a well-known chain-extension route to acids, not an alcohol-forming reaction.
questions.hint: This is a common reagent-matching trap: not every Grignard reaction gives an alcohol.
distractor_logic: Misapplies formaldehyde's unique 1°-alcohol-forming behaviour to CO2, which actually gives a carboxylate/carboxylic acid instead.
False; RMgX + CO2 is a standard, well-established reaction used for one-carbon chain extension to a carboxylic acid.
CO2 is not an aldehyde and does not follow the aldehyde-to-secondary-alcohol pattern.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Why does converting chlorobenzene to phenol (Dow process) require much harsher conditions (623 K, 300 atm) than hydrolysing an alkyl chloride to an alcohol?
options: The harsh conditions exist only because chlorobenzene is completely insoluble in NaOH solution under any conditions, so temperature/pressure serve purely to improve solubility.
