The aryl C–Cl bond has partial double-bond character (from chlorine lone-pair conjugation with the ring), and the sp<sup>2</sup> carbon resists backside nucleophilic attack, making it far less reactive than an ordinary sp<sup>3</sup> alkyl C–Cl bond.
Chlorobenzene reacts just as readily as an alkyl chloride; the harsh conditions are used purely to speed up the reaction for economic reasons, not due to any real electronic resistance.
Aryl halides are actually more reactive than alkyl halides toward nucleophilic substitution; the harsh conditions are simply a historical artifact of the original process.
questions.explanation: Resonance donation of a chlorine lone pair into the aromatic ring gives the aryl C–Cl bond partial double-bond character, strengthening and shortening it, while the planar sp<sup>2</sup> geometry blocks the backside attack an SN2-type pathway would need — together making aryl halides intrinsically far less reactive toward nucleophilic substitution than alkyl halides.
questions.hint: Think about the hybridisation of the ring carbon bearing chlorine, and where the chlorine's lone pair can go.
distractor_logic: Misidentifies an assumed solubility issue as the cause, rather than the intrinsic unreactivity of the aryl C-Cl bond itself.
Denies the genuine electronic reason (bond character and blocked backside attack) for the forcing conditions actually required.
Reverses the actual relative reactivity of aryl versus alkyl halides toward nucleophilic substitution.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Which sequence correctly prepares phenol from aniline via diazonium salt chemistry?
options: Aniline → direct treatment with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature → phenol
Aniline → (NaNO<sub>2</sub>/HCl, 273–278 K) → benzenediazonium chloride → (Cu/HCl) → phenol + N<sub>2</sub>
Aniline → (NaNO<sub>2</sub>/HCl at 350 K) → phenol directly, with no diazonium intermediate
Aniline → (NaNO<sub>2</sub>/HCl, 273–278 K) → benzenediazonium chloride → (warm with water/dilute acid) → phenol + N<sub>2</sub>
questions.explanation: Aniline is diazotised at low temperature (273–278 K, since diazonium salts decompose above this range) to give the diazonium salt; subsequent warming with water hydrolyses this to phenol, releasing N<sub>2</sub> gas.
questions.hint: Diazonium salts are only stable at low temperature and need a specific, later hydrolysis step to reach phenol.
distractor_logic: Skips diazotisation entirely and misapplies dilute HNO3 (a nitration reagent used on phenol/other substrates), not a valid route from aniline to phenol.
Misapplies Sandmeyer-type Cu/HCl conditions, which give chlorobenzene, not the hydrolysis conditions that actually give phenol.
Ignores that diazonium salts are unstable above about 283 K and would decompose before controlled hydrolysis to phenol could occur.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Why is the cumene process the dominant industrial route to phenol, rather than direct routes like the Dow process?
options: Both processes are essentially equally used industrially worldwide, with no dominant method.

It is economically efficient because it produces two commercially valuable products (phenol and acetone) from cheap starting materials (benzene and propene), whereas the Dow process consumes chlorine and needs very harsh, energy-intensive conditions.
It is preferred purely because it involves fewer total chemical steps than the Dow process, regardless of economics or by-products.
The Dow process is actually cheaper overall, but the cumene process is used only because chlorobenzene is banned in most countries.
questions.explanation: The cumene process converts cheap benzene and propene into two valuable products — phenol and acetone — in an economically efficient sequence, making it far more attractive than the Dow process, which consumes chlorine and requires very energy-intensive conditions to make just phenol.
questions.hint: Think about what the cumene process yields as a bonus, beyond just phenol itself.
distractor_logic: Factually understates the cumene process's dominant, widely-used industrial role for phenol production.
Both routes are multi-step; the real advantage is the valuable co-product (acetone) and overall economics, not simply step count.
Invents an unsupported regulatory reason rather than citing the actual economic/by-product rationale.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: How does oxidising a primary alcohol with PCC differ from oxidising it with hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub>?
options: PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage; hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> is a strong oxidant that continues all the way to the carboxylic acid.
Both reagents give identical products (carboxylic acid), since both are simply classified as 'oxidising agents'.
PCC gives the carboxylic acid directly, while hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> stops at the aldehyde.
Neither reagent can oxidise a primary alcohol; both require a secondary alcohol substrate.
questions.explanation: PCC's mildness is exactly why it is chosen when the aldehyde product needs to be isolated without further oxidation; hot acidic KMnO<sub>4</sub> is much stronger and drives the reaction all the way to the carboxylic acid.
questions.hint: One of these two reagents is specifically valued in synthesis for stopping the reaction early — which one, and at what stage?
distractor_logic: Ignores the real, exam-relevant strength/selectivity difference between the two oxidants.
Reverses the actual relative strength/selectivity of the two oxidants.
Factually wrong; both reagents are classically used specifically to oxidise primary alcohols.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: In acid-catalysed dehydration of butan-2-ol, which alkene is the major product according to Zaitsev's rule?
options: But-1-ene (the less substituted, terminal alkene)
An equal 50:50 mixture of but-1-ene and but-2-ene
But-2-ene (the more substituted, internal alkene)
2-Methylpropene, via a skeletal rearrangement
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule predicts the more substituted (more stable) alkene as the major E1 dehydration product; the secondary carbocation from butan-2-ol loses a proton preferentially from the side giving the more substituted double bond, but-2-ene.
questions.hint: Zaitsev's rule favours the more highly substituted (more stable) alkene as the major product.
distractor_logic: Picks the less-substituted (Hofmann-type) alkene instead of the Zaitsev major product actually favoured under acid-catalysed dehydration.
Ignores that Zaitsev's rule predicts a clear major/minor product distribution, not an equal 50:50 mixture.
Invents an unnecessary and incorrect carbon-skeleton rearrangement; no rearrangement is needed to reach the stable major alkene here.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Which correctly ranks the reactivity of 1°, 2°, and 3° alcohols toward acid-catalysed dehydration?
options: 3° > 2° > 1°
All three classes dehydrate at identical rates under acid catalysis
2° > 3° > 1°
1° > 2° > 3°
questions.explanation: Acid-catalysed dehydration proceeds via carbocation formation (E1); since carbocation stability follows 3° > 2° > 1°, so does dehydration reactivity — the reverse of the SN2 substitution reactivity order (1° > 2° > 3°), which instead depends on steric accessibility, not carbocation stability.
questions.hint: Dehydration proceeds through a carbocation intermediate — which class of alcohol forms the most stable one?
distractor_logic: Ignores that carbocation stability (which differs sharply by class) is exactly what controls the rate in this E1-type mechanism.
Places tertiary alcohols incorrectly below secondary, when tertiary carbocations are actually the most stable and form fastest.
This is actually the reactivity order seen in SN2 substitution, not in E1 dehydration.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: How does esterification with a carboxylic acid (Fischer esterification) differ from esterification using an acid chloride?
options: Acid chlorides cannot react with alcohols to form esters at all; only carboxylic acids can be used for ester synthesis.

Fischer esterification (alcohol + carboxylic acid, H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) is reversible and typically needs water removal or excess reagent to reach completion; the acid chloride reaction is essentially irreversible, proceeding rapidly with HCl released, without needing a catalyst.
Both reactions are equally reversible, requiring identical conditions (catalytic acid, water removal) to reach completion.
Fischer esterification is irreversible while the acid chloride reaction is the one that's reversible and equilibrium-limited.
questions.explanation: Fischer esterification is a genuine equilibrium (ester + water ⇌ acid + alcohol), so its yield benefits from removing water or using excess reagent; acid chlorides react with alcohols essentially irreversibly (releasing HCl), making that route faster and more complete without needing a catalyst.
questions.hint: Think about which of the two reactions can run backward (hydrolyse) under the same conditions it was formed in.
distractor_logic: Factually wrong; acid chlorides are commonly used specifically because they react readily and irreversibly with alcohols to give esters.
Ignores the fundamentally different, essentially irreversible nature of the acid chloride + alcohol reaction.
Reverses which of the two reactions is reversible and which is not.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Why does a tertiary alcohol dehydrate faster than a primary alcohol under the same acid-catalysed conditions?
options: Tertiary alcohols dehydrate faster only because they are generally less soluble in the acidic reaction medium, forcing a faster reaction to compensate.
The tertiary carbocation intermediate is much more stable (greater hyperconjugation and inductive electron donation from three alkyl groups) than a primary carbocation, so it forms much faster.
Tertiary alcohols dehydrate faster because their O–H bond is intrinsically weaker due to more electronegative surrounding atoms, unrelated to any carbocation.
There is actually no real difference in dehydration rate between alcohol classes; any apparent difference is measurement error.
questions.explanation: Dehydration's rate-determining step is formation of the carbocation; a tertiary carbocation is stabilised by hyperconjugation and the electron-donating inductive effect of three alkyl groups, so it forms far more readily (faster) than a primary carbocation.
questions.hint: Think about what actually forms in the rate-determining step of acid-catalysed dehydration, and how stable that intermediate is for each alcohol class.
distractor_logic: Invents an irrelevant solubility-based explanation rather than citing the actual carbocation-stability reason.
Misattributes the rate difference to O-H bond strength rather than to the stability of the carbocation intermediate that actually forms in the rate-determining step.
Denies the well-established, mechanistically grounded reactivity trend between alcohol classes.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: Why does reactivity of alcohols toward sodium metal follow the order 1° > 2° > 3°?
options: Tertiary alcohols react fastest with sodium because their bulky alkyl groups stabilise the alkoxide product, making the reaction most favourable.
Reactivity with sodium metal depends only on molecular weight, with heavier alcohols reacting faster regardless of class.
All alcohols react with sodium at essentially the same rate, since O–H bond strength is nearly identical across 1°, 2°, and 3° alcohols.

Alkyl groups are electron-donating (+I effect) and increasingly bulky going from 1° to 3°, both reducing O–H bond acidity and hindering approach to the metal surface, so reactivity decreases with increasing substitution.
questions.explanation: Both electronic (+I, destabilising the alkoxide/reducing O–H acidity) and steric (hindering access to the metal surface) effects increase from 1° to 3°, so reactivity with Na decreases in that same direction: 1° > 2° > 3°.
questions.hint: Think about how increasing alkyl substitution affects both O–H acidity and steric access to the metal.
distractor_logic: Reverses the actual observed reactivity trend (1°>2°>3°), which is driven by +I and steric effects disfavouring bulkier alcohols, not favouring them.
Ignores the actual electronic/steric basis of the trend, substituting an unrelated and incorrect molecular-weight-based rule.
Denies the real (if modest) rate differences that do exist and are attributable to the +I and steric effects of the alkyl groups.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: Why doesn't the Lucas test usefully distinguish methanol from ethanol, even though it clearly distinguishes 1°/2°/3° alcohols of similar overall size?
options: Methanol and ethanol actually do show a clear, useful difference because methanol behaves like a tertiary alcohol due to its small size.
The Lucas test only works on aromatic alcohols (phenols), not on any aliphatic alcohols including methanol and ethanol.
The Lucas test cannot be performed on small alcohols at all because they are too volatile to remain in the test tube during the reaction.

The Lucas test differentiates alcohols by carbocation stability (i.e. by substitution class: 1°/2°/3°), not by carbon count; methanol and ethanol are both primary-type (unstabilised carbocation character), so both react slowly/not at all, giving no useful timing distinction between them.
questions.explanation: The Lucas test's discriminating power comes from differences in carbocation stability across substitution classes; two primary-type alcohols of similar (low) carbocation-stabilising ability, like methanol and ethanol, both react too slowly to be usefully distinguished from each other by this test.
questions.hint: Think about what property (substitution class, not carbon count) actually determines how the Lucas test discriminates between alcohols.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly claims a class change for methanol; it remains primary-type, reacting slowly like other primary alcohols, not like a tertiary one.
Factually wrong; the Lucas test is specifically an aliphatic-alcohol classification test and does not apply to phenols at all.
Invents an unrelated volatility-based explanation rather than the actual mechanistic reason, which is carbocation stability by substitution class.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: Which reagent converts an alcohol into the corresponding alkyl chloride while releasing only gaseous byproducts (SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl), making purification easy?
options: Thionyl chloride, SOCl<sub>2</sub> (the Darzens procedure)
PCl<sub>3</sub>
PCl<sub>5</sub>
Conc. HCl alone (without ZnCl<sub>2</sub> or another catalyst)
questions.explanation: SOCl<sub>2</sub> reacts with an alcohol to give the alkyl chloride plus SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl, both gases that escape the reaction mixture, leaving a clean product with minimal purification needed.
questions.hint: Which reagent's byproducts are both gases, escaping the mixture on their own?
distractor_logic: PCl3 gives H3PO3 as a byproduct, which is not a gas and also complicates purification.
PCl5 gives POCl3 (a liquid) alongside HCl, which complicates purification unlike SOCl2's fully gaseous byproducts.

Reacts too slowly with most alcohols (especially 1°) without a catalyst like ZnCl2 to be a practical general-purpose chlorinating method, and offers no purification advantage even where it does react.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Why is phenol more acidic than water, despite both compounds having an O–H bond attached to a similarly-sized group?
options: Phenol is actually less acidic than water, since aromatic rings are generally electron-donating and destabilise any adjacent negative charge.
Phenol and water are equally acidic, since their pKa values are essentially identical.
Phenol is more acidic than water solely because phenol has a higher molecular weight.

Phenoxide (phenol's conjugate base) is stabilised by resonance delocalisation of its negative charge into the aromatic ring, an option unavailable to hydroxide (water's conjugate base); this extra stabilisation makes phenol lose a proton more readily than water.
questions.explanation: Phenol's pKa (≈10) is markedly lower than water's (≈15.7); the difference is due to resonance delocalisation of the phenoxide ion's charge into the ring, a stabilisation pathway water's conjugate base (hydroxide) simply does not have.
questions.hint: Compare what happens to the negative charge on each conjugate base — only one of them has a ring to delocalise into.
distractor_logic: Both parts are wrong: phenol IS more acidic than water, and aromatic rings can indeed help stabilise (not destabilise) an adjacent negative charge via resonance.
Factually incorrect; there is a significant, well-documented pKa gap between phenol and water.
Misattributes the acidity difference to an irrelevant physical property (molecular weight) rather than the actual electronic/resonance basis.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Why does an electron-donating group (EDG) like –OCH<sub>3</sub> at the para position generally decrease phenol's acidity, even though –OCH<sub>3</sub> can also withdraw some electron density inductively?
options: –OCH<sub>3</sub>'s dominant effect at para is resonance donation of its own lone pair into the ring, which competes with (and partially cancels) the ring's ability to delocalise the phenoxide's negative charge, net destabilising phenoxide and decreasing acidity despite the modest inductive withdrawal.
–OCH<sub>3</sub>'s effect on acidity depends only on its molecular size blocking the ring sterically, not on any electronic effect at all.
–OCH<sub>3</sub> always increases phenol's acidity regardless of position, since oxygen-containing groups are inherently acidifying.
–OCH<sub>3</sub> has no measurable effect on phenol's acidity at any position, since its inductive and resonance effects always cancel out exactly.
questions.explanation: –OCH<sub>3</sub>'s resonance donation into the ring is the dominant effect at para, working against (not helping) phenoxide charge delocalisation; the net result is a real, measurable decrease in acidity compared to phenol itself, despite a small opposing inductive-withdrawal contribution.
questions.hint: Weigh –OCH<sub>3</sub>'s two competing electronic effects (resonance donation vs inductive withdrawal) — which one dominates at the para position?
distractor_logic: Ignores the electronic (resonance/inductive) basis of the effect entirely in favour of an unsupported steric explanation.
Overgeneralises; the resonance-donating character of -OCH3 at ortho/para specifically works against phenoxide stabilisation, decreasing (not increasing) acidity there.
Overstates a precise, exact cancellation that does not occur; the net effect is a real, measurable decrease in acidity.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Why is the acidifying effect of a substituent (e.g. –NO<sub>2</sub>) generally weaker at the meta position of phenol than at ortho or para?
options: Meta-substituted phenols are always less acidic than unsubstituted phenol itself, regardless of the substituent's electronic character, since meta substitution is inherently deactivating in every case.

Direct resonance delocalisation of the phenoxide's negative charge only reaches the ortho and para carbons; a meta substituent cannot interact with that charge through resonance and can only exert its (generally weaker) inductive effect, giving a smaller acidifying effect than the same group at ortho/para.
Meta substitution has a stronger acidifying effect than ortho/para substitution, since meta positions are further from any steric clash with –OH.
There is no real positional difference; ortho, meta, and para substitution all affect phenol's acidity identically.
questions.explanation: Drawing out the phenoxide ion's resonance structures shows the negative charge appearing only on the ortho and para ring carbons (and the oxygen); a meta substituent has no direct resonance overlap with that charge and so contributes acidifying strength through induction alone, a weaker effect than direct resonance withdrawal.
questions.hint: Draw the resonance structures of the phenoxide ion — which ring carbons actually carry the delocalised negative charge?
distractor_logic: Overgeneralises; a meta EWG still modestly increases acidity via induction alone, it's just a smaller increase than the same EWG at ortho/para, not a decrease below unsubstituted phenol.
Reverses the actual relative magnitude of the effect; ortho/para substitution (via direct resonance) has the stronger effect, not meta (inductive-only).
Denies the actual resonance-structure-based reason (charge delocalises specifically to ortho/para carbons, not meta) for the well-documented positional dependence.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Rank the acidity of phenol, o-cresol (2-methylphenol), and o-nitrophenol.
options: Phenol > o-nitrophenol > o-cresol
All three are equally acidic
o-Cresol > phenol > o-nitrophenol
o-Nitrophenol > phenol > o-cresol
questions.explanation: –NO<sub>2</sub> (an EWG) increases acidity above phenol, while –CH<sub>3</sub> (an EDG) decreases it, giving the order o-nitrophenol > phenol > o-cresol.
questions.hint: Sort by substituent electronic character: which is an EWG, which is an EDG, and which has neither?
distractor_logic: Places the strongly-acidifying nitro-substituted phenol below unsubstituted phenol, when EWGs like -NO2 should increase, not decrease, acidity relative to phenol itself.
Ignores the real, substituent-dependent acidity differences at play between these three specific compounds.
Reverses the entire order; this would require the EDG (methyl) to increase acidity and the EWG (nitro) to decrease it, exactly backwards from their actual electronic effects.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Why does phenol undergo electrophilic aromatic substitution more readily than benzene itself?
options: Phenol reacts more slowly than benzene, since –OH is electron-withdrawing and deactivates the ring.

The oxygen lone pair on –OH delocalises into the ring by resonance, increasing electron density (especially at ortho/para), making the ring more reactive toward electrophiles than benzene's ring alone.
Phenol and benzene actually react at identical rates in electrophilic substitution, since both have the same core benzene ring.
Phenol reacts faster only because it has a higher molecular weight, making it a bigger target for electrophiles to hit.
questions.explanation: –OH's lone pair conjugates with the ring, increasing electron density at ortho/para positions and making the ring considerably more nucleophilic (reactive toward electrophiles) than benzene, whose ring has no such activating substituent.
questions.hint: Think about what –OH's lone pair can do to the ring's electron density through resonance.
distractor_logic: Reverses -OH's actual electronic character; -OH is a net electron donor via resonance (despite a small opposing inductive withdrawal), making it a ring activator, not a deactivator.
Ignores the substantial rate-enhancing effect that -OH's resonance donation provides relative to unsubstituted benzene.
Misattributes reactivity to an irrelevant physical property (molecular weight) rather than the actual electronic (resonance donation) cause.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Why does Kolbe's reaction on phenol give predominantly the ortho-carboxylation product (salicylic acid) rather than the para product, even though –OH directs to both positions?
options: Ortho selectivity arises because CO<sub>2</sub> is a much bulkier electrophile than typical halogenating or nitrating agents, and bulky electrophiles always prefer the position closest to the directing group.

The reaction proceeds through a phenoxide ion where the incoming CO<sub>2</sub> electrophile is thought to be held close to the ortho position by coordination with the sodium counter-ion (a cyclic-type intermediate), favouring ortho attack over para under these specific conditions.
The reaction actually gives roughly equal amounts of ortho and para product, with 'Kolbe's reaction' referring only to the general reaction type, not to any particular regioselectivity.
Para attack is actually sterically impossible for CO<sub>2</sub> in this reaction, so ortho is the only geometrically available position at all.
questions.explanation: A coordination/chelation effect between the sodium phenoxide's cation and the incoming CO<sub>2</sub> is thought to hold the electrophile close to the ortho position, giving the characteristic ortho-selectivity of Kolbe's reaction under the specific conditions (heat, pressure) actually used.
questions.hint: Think about what role the sodium counter-ion of the phenoxide salt might play in positioning the incoming CO2.
distractor_logic: Misattributes the selectivity to a generic sterics-favours-proximity rule rather than the actual coordination/chelation-based explanation specific to this reaction.
Understates the well-documented ortho-selectivity that is characteristic of Kolbe's reaction as actually carried out industrially/in the lab.

Overstates that para attack is completely impossible; -OH does direct to both positions in principle, but ortho is specifically favoured here due to the phenoxide/CO2 coordination effect, not an absolute geometric block on para.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Which reagent set correctly gives picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) from phenol?
options: Phenol + Br<sub>2</sub> water (excess), giving picric acid as the tribrominated analogue
Phenol + CHCl<sub>3</sub>/NaOH (Reimer-Tiemann conditions), giving picric acid via a carbene-mediated nitration pathway
Phenol + dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature, giving picric acid directly in one mild step
Phenol + concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> (often with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>), giving exhaustive nitration at all three activated (2,4,6) positions
questions.explanation: Concentrated HNO<sub>3</sub> under forcing conditions drives nitration all the way to the trinitro stage, filling all three activated (2,4,6) positions to give picric acid; dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> at room temperature only achieves mononitration (o-/p-nitrophenol).
questions.hint: Full trinitration needs much more forcing conditions than the mild, dilute-acid nitration that gives only mononitrophenols.
distractor_logic: Confuses bromination (which gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol, a halogenated compound) with nitration (which is what actually gives picric acid).
Conflates two entirely different named reactions/electrophiles; Reimer-Tiemann installs -CHO via dichlorocarbene, unrelated to nitro-group installation.
Dilute HNO3 at room temperature actually gives only a mixture of mono-nitrated products (o- and p-nitrophenol), not the fully trinitrated picric acid.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Why does phenol react with bromine water instantly at room temperature (no catalyst needed), while benzene requires a Lewis acid catalyst (e.g. FeBr<sub>3</sub>) to react with bromine at all?
options: Phenol's ring is strongly activated by –OH's resonance donation, making it reactive enough toward the mild electrophile Br<sub>2</sub> without any catalyst; benzene's unactivated ring needs a Lewis acid to polarise Br<sub>2</sub> into a stronger electrophile first.
Phenol reacts faster with bromine only because it is more soluble in water than benzene, unrelated to any ring-activation effect.
Phenol and benzene actually require identical reaction conditions with bromine, and any apparent difference is due to experimental impurities in typical phenol samples.
Benzene actually reacts faster than phenol with bromine water, but this is masked in typical lab demonstrations by phenol's distinctive white precipitate making its reaction seem faster.
questions.explanation: An activated ring (phenol) can react with a comparatively weak, unpolarised electrophile like Br<sub>2</sub> directly; an unactivated ring (benzene) needs a Lewis acid catalyst to generate a stronger electrophile (Br<sup>+</sup>-like species) before reaction can proceed.
questions.hint: Compare how activated each ring is toward electrophiles, and what that implies about how strong an electrophile each one needs.
distractor_logic: Substitutes an irrelevant solubility-based explanation for the real electronic (ring-activation) cause of the reactivity difference.
Denies the well-documented, mechanistically grounded reactivity difference between an activated (phenol) and unactivated (benzene) aromatic ring toward the same electrophile.
Denies the real, correctly-observed reactivity difference by inventing an experimental-artifact explanation instead.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Why does Williamson synthesis work poorly (favouring elimination instead) when a tertiary alkyl halide is used with a strong alkoxide base?
options: Alkoxides are strong, bulky bases/nucleophiles, and tertiary alkyl halides are highly prone to E2 elimination under strongly basic conditions (and sterically hindered toward SN2 backside attack), so elimination (giving alkene) dominates over the desired substitution.
Tertiary alkyl halides give excellent SN2 substitution with alkoxides because the tertiary carbon's extra alkyl groups stabilise the transition state.
Alkoxides are too weak a nucleophile to react with any alkyl halide, tertiary or otherwise, which is why Williamson synthesis never works with any substrate.
Tertiary alkyl halides simply do not react with alkoxides at all under any conditions, so no product forms.
questions.explanation: Both structural features of a tertiary halide work against SN2: severe steric hindrance blocks backside attack, and the strong, bulky alkoxide base readily promotes E2 elimination instead, so alkene (not ether) dominates.
questions.hint: A tertiary alkyl halide with a strong base is a classic setup for a specific competing elimination mechanism.
distractor_logic: Misapplies 'stabilisation' in a way that actually favours elimination (via carbocation-like character) over the desired SN2 substitution, which tertiary substrates in fact strongly disfavour due to steric hindrance to backside attack.
Contradicts the premise that Williamson synthesis is a standard, effective method (specifically with primary halides); alkoxides are perfectly capable nucleophiles for SN2 with unhindered substrates.
Factually wrong; tertiary alkyl halides do react with strong bases like alkoxides, just predominantly via elimination rather than the desired substitution.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: To synthesise tert-butyl methyl ether, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–O–CH<sub>3</sub>, via Williamson synthesis while avoiding the elimination side-reaction, which reagent pairing should be used?
options: Methyl chloride, CH<sub>3</sub>Cl, + tert-butyl alcohol (without converting it to the alkoxide first)
Sodium tert-butoxide, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–ONa, + methyl iodide, CH<sub>3</sub>I
tert-Butyl iodide + sodium tert-butoxide (two tertiary reagents)
tert-Butyl chloride, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Cl, + sodium methoxide, CH<sub>3</sub>ONa
questions.explanation: The classic Williamson rule: pair the more hindered group as the alkoxide (nucleophile) and the least hindered (here, methyl) group as the alkyl halide (electrophile), so SN2 is favoured over E2.
questions.hint: Put the bulky group on the nucleophile (alkoxide) side, and the least hindered group on the electrophile (alkyl halide) side.
distractor_logic: A neutral alcohol is a poor enough nucleophile that this combination would react extremely slowly or not at all compared to using the deprotonated alkoxide.
Pairs two bulky, hindered reagents together, virtually guaranteeing elimination rather than the desired SN2 substitution due to severe steric hindrance on both sides.
Pairs a hindered, elimination-prone tertiary alkyl halide with a strong base, which would favour E2 elimination (giving isobutylene) over the desired substitution.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: When 2-ethoxy-2-methylpropane, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, is heated with excess HI, which products form, and why?
options: Both C–O bonds remain fully intact, and HI addition simply protonates the ether oxygen with no further bond cleavage occurring.
The ether cleaves via SN2 exclusively, always giving the less hindered ethyl iodide and 2-methylpropan-2-ol regardless of which side is more substituted.
The reaction gives 2-methylpropene and ethanol as the sole products, via an E1-type elimination rather than any substitution at all.

2-Methylpropan-2-yl iodide [(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–I] and ethanol, since the more substituted (tertiary) C–O bond breaks preferentially through an SN1-like pathway, as the tertiary carbon readily forms a stable carbocation.
questions.explanation: With a tertiary alkyl group present, cleavage proceeds via a faster SN1 pathway at the more substituted carbon (which forms a stable carbocation), giving the tertiary iodide and ethanol, rather than simply defaulting to attack at the less hindered ethyl side.
questions.hint: One side of this ether can form a very stable carbocation — that changes which mechanism (and which side) dominates.
distractor_logic: Ignores that excess strong acid (HI) with its good nucleophile (I-) does in fact cleave ether C-O bonds under these classic 'ether cleavage' conditions, not just protonate reversibly.

Overlooks that with a tertiary alkyl group present, cleavage instead proceeds via a faster SN1 pathway at the more substituted carbon, giving the tertiary iodide, not simply defaulting to attack at the less hindered side.

Misapplies an elimination pathway here; the well-established outcome for a tertiary-group-containing ether cleaved by excess HI is substitution (SN1) at the more substituted carbon, giving the alkyl iodide, not elimination to an alkene.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Why do primary/secondary alkyl-alkyl ether cleavages by excess HI typically proceed via SN2 (I<sup>–</sup> attacking the less hindered carbon), while ethers with a tertiary alkyl group typically cleave via SN1 (at the more substituted carbon)?
options: The choice between SN1 and SN2 in ether cleavage depends entirely on the concentration of HI used, not on the alkyl groups' substitution pattern at all.

The dominant pathway is whichever is faster for the specific substrate: without a sufficiently stable carbocation accessible (primary/secondary only), SN2 at the less hindered carbon is faster; once a tertiary alkyl group is present, its very stable carbocation makes SN1 there the faster pathway instead.
The mechanism is always SN2 regardless of substrate, with no exceptions for any degree of substitution.
The mechanism is always SN1 regardless of substrate, with I<sup>–</sup> simply attacking whichever carbocation happens to form fastest, even for simple primary-primary ethers.
questions.explanation: Mechanism selection tracks carbocation accessibility: primary carbons cannot readily form carbocations, so SN2 dominates there; once a tertiary carbon (capable of a stable carbocation) is present, the faster SN1 pathway at that carbon takes over instead.
questions.hint: Ask which mechanism is actually faster for a given substrate, based on whether a stable carbocation is accessible at all.
distractor_logic: Ignores the well-established substrate-structure-dependence (carbocation stability) of this mechanistic switch, substituting an unrelated concentration-based explanation.
Denies the well-documented mechanistic switch to SN1 that occurs specifically when a sufficiently stable (typically tertiary) carbocation becomes accessible.
Overstates SN1 dominance; primary carbons do not readily form carbocations at all, so primary-primary (or primary-secondary) ether cleavage genuinely proceeds via SN2, not SN1.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Why can't Williamson synthesis make di-tert-butyl ether directly from (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Cl + (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–ONa?
options: Both reagents are maximally hindered around the reacting carbon/oxygen, blocking the necessary SN2 backside attack essentially completely; E2 elimination (giving isobutylene, favoured by the strong, bulky base) dominates overwhelmingly instead.
The reaction fails only because tert-butoxide is too weak a base/nucleophile to react with any alkyl halide at all.
The reaction actually proceeds smoothly via SN2 in this case, because both groups being identical (both tert-butyl) somehow favours, rather than hinders, backside nucleophilic attack.
Di-tert-butyl ether cannot exist as a stable compound under any circumstances, regardless of synthetic method.
questions.explanation: Having bulky groups on BOTH the nucleophile and the electrophile makes SN2 backside attack essentially impossible, so the strong, bulky tert-butoxide base instead promotes E2 elimination of the tert-butyl chloride, giving isobutylene rather than the desired ether.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the feasibility of backside (SN2) attack when both reacting partners are maximally bulky.
distractor_logic: Mischaracterises tert-butoxide, which is in fact a strong (if bulky) base/nucleophile; the specific problem here is steric hindrance to SN2, which favours E2 instead, not a general lack of basicity/nucleophilicity.

Incorrectly claims that having two identical, bulky groups favours SN2, when in fact having two bulky groups on both the nucleophile and the electrophile makes backside attack especially difficult, not easier.
Factually wrong framing; the issue is specifically the failure of THIS synthetic method (Williamson, via SN2) for this substrate combination, not an inherent instability of the ether itself.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Why do the cumene process's phenol and acetone come from a single mechanistic pathway, rather than two entirely separate manufacturing routes?
options: Acetone is actually formed first, and phenol is subsequently made FROM the acetone in a second separate step.
The two products are entirely coincidental byproducts that happen to form in the same reactor but through completely unrelated, independent reaction pathways.
Phenol is made from cumene hydroperoxide in one step, and acetone is made completely separately by oxidising leftover unreacted propene in a different reactor.

Both products arise from the acid-catalysed rearrangement and cleavage of the very same intermediate, cumene hydroperoxide, in a single reaction step — a phenyl group migration followed by hydrolytic cleavage directly gives phenol and acetone together.
questions.explanation: A 1,2-phenyl shift within cumene hydroperoxide, followed by hydrolytic cleavage of the resulting intermediate, directly yields both phenol and acetone from the same starting molecule in one mechanistic sequence.
questions.hint: Trace both products back to the same single starting molecule, cumene hydroperoxide, rather than two separate reactors.
distractor_logic: Reverses/misorders the mechanism; both products emerge together from cleavage of the same rearranged intermediate, not sequentially from one another.
Denies the genuine shared-intermediate mechanism (rearrangement/cleavage of one single molecule) that produces both products together.
Invents an unrelated, incorrect second manufacturing route for acetone that has no connection to the actual cumene hydroperoxide rearrangement mechanism.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Why is the cumene process considered more industrially favourable than a hypothetical route that made phenol alone, with no useful co-product?
options: It is actually less efficient than simpler routes, but is used anyway purely for historical/traditional reasons unrelated to genuine efficiency.

It converts cheap benzene and propene entirely into two commercially valuable products (phenol and acetone) in one integrated process, minimising waste and maximising value extracted from the starting materials.
It uses fewer total atoms in its starting materials than any alternative process, regardless of what happens to those atoms during the reaction.
Atom economy/by-product value is irrelevant to industrial process selection; only reaction speed determines which process is chosen.
questions.explanation: Turning both fragments of cumene hydroperoxide into sellable products, rather than treating one as waste, is a major economic advantage — a hypothetical phenol-only route would waste the acetone-forming fragment entirely.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to the 'other half' of cumene hydroperoxide in a route that only wanted phenol.
distractor_logic: Denies the real, substantive economic/efficiency advantage that having a valuable co-product provides.
Misapplies 'atom economy' as simply meaning 'fewer starting atoms' rather than the actual concept of how much of the starting material ends up as useful product rather than waste.
