questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: A student proposes distinguishing phenol from benzyl alcohol using bromine water. Which correctly predicts and explains the result?
options: Neither compound reacts with bromine water under any circumstances, since bromine water is used only for detecting unsaturation in alkenes.
Benzyl alcohol reacts faster than phenol with bromine water, since its –OH is more accessible on the flexible side-chain.

Phenol reacts instantly with excess bromine water, giving a white precipitate of 2,4,6-tribromophenol (its ring is strongly activated by –OH); benzyl alcohol's –OH sits on the side-chain, not the ring, so it does not activate the ring the same way and does not react in this fast, precipitate-forming manner.
Both compounds react identically with bromine water, giving the same tribromo precipitate, since both contain a benzene ring.
questions.explanation: Only phenol's –OH is directly attached to (and activates) the aromatic ring; benzyl alcohol's –OH is on a side-chain carbon and doesn't confer the same ring-activating effect, so only phenol reacts readily with bromine water.
questions.hint: Compare exactly where the –OH group sits in each molecule — directly on the ring, or on a side-chain carbon?
distractor_logic: Misapplies bromine water's alkene-testing use to this entirely different phenol-testing context, where excess bromine water instead performs ring substitution on the strongly activated phenol ring.
Reverses the actual reactivity comparison; phenol's ring-activating -OH, not benzyl alcohol's side-chain -OH, is what drives the fast bromine water reaction.
Ignores that benzyl alcohol's -OH is not directly attached to (and therefore does not activate) the ring in the way phenol's -OH does.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: How do methanol's industrial and biological hazards connect back to the primary-alcohol oxidation chemistry discussed elsewhere in this chapter?
options: Just as a primary alcohol is oxidised stepwise to an aldehyde and then a carboxylic acid by common oxidants, the body's alcohol dehydrogenase enzyme oxidises methanol the same way (to formaldehyde, then formic acid); it is this metabolic oxidation, producing toxic intermediates, that makes methanol dangerous to ingest.
Methanol's industrial hazards are purely about its flammability, with no connection at all to alcohol oxidation chemistry.
Methanol's toxicity is completely unrelated to any chemistry covered in this chapter, arising instead from an entirely different, unrelated biological mechanism.
Methanol is actually LESS hazardous than ethanol precisely because it cannot undergo the same oxidation sequence that ethanol undergoes in the body.
questions.explanation: Methanol undergoes the same general type of stepwise oxidation (alcohol → aldehyde → acid) that any primary alcohol undergoes, but its specific intermediates (formaldehyde, formic acid) are considerably more toxic than ethanol's, making the connection to ordinary oxidation chemistry directly relevant to its hazard.
questions.hint: Methanol's metabolism in the body follows the very same alcohol-to-aldehyde-to-acid pattern covered for primary alcohols generally.
distractor_logic: Denies the genuine, medically established connection between ordinary primary-alcohol oxidation chemistry and methanol's specific toxicological mechanism.
Denies the direct, chapter-relevant connection between primary-alcohol oxidation chemistry and methanol's actual toxicological pathway.
Factually wrong; methanol undergoes essentially the same type of oxidation sequence as ethanol, but its specific oxidation products are considerably more toxic than ethanol's.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Which statement about hybridisation and bonding in phenol is correct?
options: Phenol has no resonance structures involving the oxygen lone pair, since the ring is already fully aromatic and cannot accept more electron density.
The C–O bond in phenol is longer than in alcohols because aromatic rings generally weaken every bond attached to them.
Oxygen in phenol is sp<sup>3</sup> hybridised exactly as in alcohols, so the C–O bond lengths in phenol and ethanol are essentially identical.
The C–O bond in phenol has partial double-bond character because an oxygen lone pair delocalises into the aromatic ring, making it shorter than the alcoholic C–O bond.
questions.explanation: One oxygen lone pair conjugates with the ring π-system, giving the phenolic C–O bond partial double-bond character. This shortens the bond relative to the (non-conjugated, sp<sup>3</sup>) alcoholic C–O bond, and also increases O–H bond polarity, contributing to phenol's higher acidity.
questions.hint: Think about where the oxygen lone pairs can delocalise when attached to an aromatic ring versus a saturated carbon.
distractor_logic: Misunderstands that aromatic rings can still act as resonance acceptors for a substituent's lone pair, as seen in phenol, aniline and anisole.
Reverses the actual trend and invents a nonexistent general 'aromatic rings weaken all attached bonds' effect.
Ignores that resonance delocalisation into the ring changes the effective bond order/length compared to an ordinary sp3 C-O bond.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Compound X, molecular formula C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O, does not react with sodium metal to liberate hydrogen gas. Which class does X most likely belong to?
options: A secondary alcohol
A tertiary alcohol
An ether, e.g. diethyl ether or methyl propyl ether
A primary alcohol
questions.explanation: Reaction with Na (2 R–OH + 2Na → 2 R–ONa + H<sub>2</sub>↑) requires an acidic O–H bond, present in alcohols of every class (1°, 2°, 3°), which all react (just at different rates). An isomeric ether such as C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> has no O–H bond and is inert to Na.
questions.hint: Sodium metal reacts specifically with the O–H bond — which class of C<sub>4</sub>H<sub>10</sub>O isomer lacks that bond entirely?
distractor_logic: Ignores that secondary alcohols also react with Na (just somewhat more slowly), contradicting the given observation.
Ignores that tertiary alcohols still possess an O-H bond and still react with Na, only more slowly, contradicting a stated total absence of reaction.
Ignores that primary alcohols readily evolve H2 with Na, contradicting the given 'no reaction' observation.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Which IUPAC name is correct for HO–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH (glycerol)?
options: 1,2,3-Trihydroxypropane
Propane-2,1,3-triol
Propan-1,2,3-ol
Propane-1,2,3-triol
questions.explanation: With three –OH groups as the sole principal functional group, the multiplying prefix 'tri' fuses with '-ol' to give the suffix '-triol', with locants cited in ascending order: propane-1,2,3-triol.
questions.hint: Three identical principal-group substituents require the 'tri' multiplying prefix fused to the suffix, with locants listed lowest-to-highest.
distractor_logic: Names all -OH groups as 'hydroxy' prefixes, when -OH is the sole principal group here and should be the suffix, not a prefix.
Lists the locants out of the required ascending numerical order.
Uses the singular suffix '-ol' instead of the required multiplying form '-triol' for three identical principal groups.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: A benzene ring carries both –OH and –COOH at adjacent positions (this is salicylic acid). Which naming approach is IUPAC-correct?
options: Both groups are expressed together as suffixes, giving 'benzoic-ol acid'.
Since both are oxygen-containing groups of similar priority, either name is equally acceptable.
It should be named as a substituted phenol, e.g. 2-carboxyphenol, since –OH is generally the senior aromatic functional group.
–COOH outranks –OH in seniority, so the parent is named as a substituted benzoic acid, with –OH as a 'hydroxy' prefix: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid.
questions.explanation: IUPAC seniority places carboxylic acids above alcohols/phenols. When both are present, –COOH becomes the parent suffix ('-oic acid') and –OH is demoted to a 'hydroxy-' prefix: 2-hydroxybenzoic acid.
questions.hint: When two different characteristic groups are present, only the higher-seniority one becomes the suffix; the other becomes a prefix.
distractor_logic: Invents a suffix combination ('-ol acid') that is not valid IUPAC style; only the single most senior group is expressed as suffix.
Incorrectly assumes no defined seniority order exists between carboxylic acid and phenol/alcohol groups.
Reverses the actual IUPAC seniority order, which places carboxylic acid above phenol/alcohol, not the other way round.

questions.topic: Nature of the O–H Bond, Hydrogen Bonding and Physical Properties
questions.question: Based on the diagram, which correctly explains why o-nitrophenol is steam-volatile with a markedly lower boiling point than p-nitrophenol?
options: o-Nitrophenol has a lower boiling point simply because ortho-substituted benzenes are always less symmetric and therefore always boil lower than their para isomers.

In o-nitrophenol, –OH and –NO<sub>2</sub> are close enough to form an intramolecular hydrogen bond (chelation), leaving little capacity for intermolecular association; p-nitrophenol's groups are too far apart for this, so its molecules hydrogen-bond intermolecularly instead, raising its boiling point.
Both isomers form identical intramolecular hydrogen bonds, so the volatility difference must come from crystal packing effects unrelated to hydrogen bonding.
p-Nitrophenol is steam-volatile because its –NO<sub>2</sub> group is a stronger electron-withdrawing group at the para position, which lowers its boiling point directly through induction.
questions.explanation: The ortho arrangement lets –OH and –NO<sub>2</sub> form a 6-membered intramolecular H-bonded ring (chelate), which is energetically self-contained — it doesn't need other molecules, so o-nitrophenol has fewer intermolecular attractions, a lower boiling point, and can be carried over with steam. The para isomer's groups are too far apart for this and must hydrogen-bond intermolecularly instead, raising its boiling point and eliminating steam-volatility.
questions.hint: Look at whether –OH and –NO<sub>2</sub> in each diagram are close enough to bond with each other directly, or must reach across to a different molecule.
distractor_logic: Invents a general 'ortho = lower boiling' rule not grounded in the actual hydrogen-bonding cause shown in the diagram.
Denies that ortho vs para geometry changes whether intramolecular bonding is even possible, which is the actual determining factor.
Misattributes a volatility effect (which is really about hydrogen-bonding pattern) to an unrelated inductive/acidity argument.

questions.topic: Nature of the O–H Bond, Hydrogen Bonding and Physical Properties
questions.question: Rank ethanol, water and diethyl ether in order of increasing boiling point, with correct reasoning.
options: Diethyl ether (≈35°C) < ethanol (≈78°C) < water (≈100°C) — ether has no O–H hydrogen bonding at all; water's smaller size and two O–H bonds per molecule give a more extensive hydrogen-bond network than ethanol's single, alkyl-diluted O–H.
Diethyl ether < water < ethanol — correctly placing ether lowest but ranking water below ethanol.
Ethanol < diethyl ether < water — ranking the non-hydrogen-bonding ether above ethanol.
Water < ethanol < diethyl ether — reversing the entire order.
questions.explanation: Only ethanol and water have O–H bonds capable of intermolecular hydrogen bonding; ether has none, giving it by far the lowest boiling point. Between ethanol and water, water's smaller size and greater H-bond-donor/acceptor density (2 O–H bonds + 2 lone pairs per small molecule, versus ethanol's single O–H diluted by a bulky ethyl group) let it form a more extensive network, giving water the highest boiling point.
questions.hint: First separate out the one compound with no O–H at all, then compare how 'diluted' the O–H hydrogen bonding is by the attached hydrocarbon group.
distractor_logic: Correctly isolates ether as lowest but wrongly ranks water below ethanol despite water's more extensive hydrogen-bond network.
Incorrectly ranks the non-hydrogen-bonding ether above ethanol, when ether's inability to self-associate should place it lowest.
Ignores that water hydrogen-bonds most extensively of the three, placing it lowest instead of highest.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Which combination of Grignard reagent and carbonyl compound, followed by acidic hydrolysis, correctly gives pentan-2-ol, CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>?
options: CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr (n-propylmagnesium bromide) + CH<sub>3</sub>CHO (acetaldehyde)
Excess CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + CH<sub>3</sub>COOC<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> (ethyl acetate)
CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>MgBr (ethylmagnesium bromide) + CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO (propanal)
CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + CH<sub>3</sub>–CO–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub> (butan-2-one)
questions.explanation: Adding the propyl group of the Grignard reagent to the carbonyl carbon of acetaldehyde places –OH and an H on that carbon, flanked by CH<sub>3</sub> (from acetaldehyde) and propyl (from the Grignard reagent): CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, exactly pentan-2-ol.
questions.hint: Work out exactly which carbon becomes the carbinol carbon, and which two groups end up attached to it, for each option.
distractor_logic: Excess Grignard with an ester adds twice, giving a tertiary alcohol (2-methylbutan-2-ol) via double addition, not the secondary alcohol asked for.
This pairing actually places -OH at C3 (giving pentan-3-ol), not C2, since the ethyl and propanal-derived groups are symmetric about the carbinol carbon.
A ketone reagent gives a tertiary alcohol (2-methylbutan-2-ol here), not the secondary alcohol pentan-2-ol asked for.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Which sequence converts but-1-ene into butan-1-ol while structurally avoiding any risk of carbocation rearrangement, and why does it avoid that risk?
options: Conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O, then heat — proceeds through a secondary carbocation that could rearrange, and in any case gives butan-2-ol, not butan-1-ol.
HBr, then aqueous NaOH — HBr addition proceeds via a carbocation risking rearrangement, and substitution afterwards would again give butan-2-ol.
Hg(OAc)<sub>2</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O, then NaBH<sub>4</sub> — also avoids rearrangement via a bridged ion, but gives the Markovnikov product butan-2-ol, not butan-1-ol.

B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/NaOH — the concerted, four-centred transition state adds B and H in one step without ever forming a free carbocation, so no hydride/alkyl shifts can occur.
questions.explanation: Hydroboration-oxidation's concerted, syn-addition mechanism never generates a free carbocation, so it is inherently rearrangement-free, and its anti-Markovnikov regiochemistry places OH on the terminal carbon, correctly giving butan-1-ol.
questions.hint: Only one listed method both avoids a free carbocation intermediate AND gives the anti-Markovnikov (terminal) alcohol needed here.
distractor_logic: Correctly identifies the rearrangement risk of acid-catalysed hydration but the reaction gives the wrong (Markovnikov) regiochemistry for the target alcohol regardless.
Correctly identifies a carbocation-mediated (rearrangement-prone) pathway, but the final substitution step would give the wrong alcohol (butan-2-ol) in any case.
Correctly avoids rearrangement via a bridged mercurinium ion, but still gives the Markovnikov product, not the anti-Markovnikov butan-1-ol asked for.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Which statement correctly distinguishes the reducing power/selectivity of NaBH<sub>4</sub> versus LiAlH<sub>4</sub> for preparing alcohols?
options: NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces aldehydes and ketones to alcohols but does not reduce esters or carboxylic acids under normal conditions; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a stronger, less selective agent that reduces aldehydes, ketones, esters, and carboxylic acids all the way to alcohols.
Neither reagent can reduce ketones; both are used exclusively for reducing esters to alcohols.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> reduces carboxylic acids and esters efficiently, while LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is limited to aldehydes and ketones only.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> and LiAlH<sub>4</sub> are fully interchangeable in every synthetic situation, since both are simply 'hydride reducing agents'.
questions.explanation: NaBH<sub>4</sub> is the milder hydride source, useful when esters/acids elsewhere in a molecule must be left untouched; LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is considerably more reactive and will reduce esters and carboxylic acids (as well as aldehydes/ketones) all the way to the corresponding alcohols.
questions.hint: One of these reagents is deliberately chosen in synthesis specifically because it leaves esters/acids untouched — which one, and why?
distractor_logic: Incorrect on both counts; both reagents readily reduce ketones, among their most common substrates, and neither is limited to esters only.
Reverses the actual relative reactivity/selectivity of the two reagents toward esters and acids.
Denies the real, exam-relevant selectivity difference between the two hydride reagents.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Compare (i) chlorobenzene fused with NaOH at 623 K/300 atm and (ii) benzenediazonium chloride warmed with water, both giving phenol. Which correctly compares their reaction character?
options: (i) is a genuine nucleophilic aromatic substitution at an otherwise-unreactive aryl C–Cl bond needing forcing conditions; (ii) proceeds far more easily on mild warming because –N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is an excellent leaving group that departs as stable N<sub>2</sub> gas, driving the reaction even at low temperature.
Route (i) is not really a substitution at all, but a radical chain reaction initiated by heat.
Route (ii) actually requires harsher conditions than route (i), since diazonium salts are generally very stable and unreactive at any temperature.
Both routes proceed by an identical mechanism and require identical forcing conditions, since both start from an aromatic ring bonded to a leaving group.
questions.explanation: The two leaving groups behave very differently: –Cl on an aromatic ring is a poor leaving group needing forcing conditions to be displaced, whereas –N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is an outstanding leaving group (departing as inert, stable N<sub>2</sub> gas), so diazonium hydrolysis proceeds readily under mild warming.
questions.hint: Compare how good a leaving group –Cl is on an aromatic ring versus how good a leaving group –N<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> is.
distractor_logic: Misidentifies harsh-condition aryl halide hydrolysis as a radical process rather than nucleophilic aromatic substitution.
Factually reverses diazonium salt behaviour; diazonium salts are notoriously unstable/reactive on warming, which is exactly why hydrolysis proceeds so readily.
Ignores the very different leaving-group ability and reaction ease of -N2+ (excellent, giving N2 gas) versus -Cl (poor leaving group on an aromatic ring).

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: Why can't a simple SN2-type hydrolysis (mild aqueous NaOH, gentle heat) convert chlorobenzene to phenol the way it converts a primary alkyl chloride to a primary alcohol?
options: Chlorobenzene fails to react with mild aqueous NaOH only because chlorine is too large an atom to ever be displaced by hydroxide.
SN2 substitution actually does occur readily on chlorobenzene under mild conditions; the harsh Dow-process conditions are simply an obsolete, no-longer-necessary method.
The aromatic ring has no real effect on the reaction mechanism; mild hydrolysis fails only because chlorobenzene is a liquid rather than a solid.

SN2 needs backside nucleophilic attack on the carbon bearing the leaving group, but that carbon in chlorobenzene is part of the planar, sp<sup>2</sup> aromatic ring, sterically and electronically blocking backside attack; combined with the aryl C–Cl bond's partial double-bond character, this makes the ordinary SN2 pathway essentially unavailable.
questions.explanation: Backside (SN2) attack requires an accessible carbon opposite the leaving group; the planar aromatic ring geometrically blocks this, and resonance-donated double-bond character in the C–Cl bond further strengthens it — together ruling out the mild SN2 pathway that works fine for sp<sup>3</sup> alkyl halides.
questions.hint: Think about the geometry backside attack requires, and whether that geometry is even accessible on a flat aromatic ring.
distractor_logic: Misattributes the resistance purely to chlorine's atomic size, when chlorine is in fact readily displaced from sp3 alkyl chlorides under similarly mild conditions.
Denies the accepted mechanistic understanding that aryl halides genuinely resist ordinary SN2/SN1 pathways under mild conditions.
Invents an irrelevant physical-state explanation, ignoring the real electronic/steric cause rooted in ring geometry and bond character.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: A student treats 3,3-dimethylbutan-2-ol with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat expecting straightforward dehydration. What complication is likely, and what does it reveal about acid-catalysed dehydration in general?
options: The secondary carbocation formed here is already the most stable possible intermediate for this substrate, so no rearrangement would occur.
Rearrangement would only be possible via a 1,2-hydride shift, never via an alkyl (methyl) group shift, so this particular substrate cannot rearrange at all.
No rearrangement is possible in dehydration reactions under any circumstances, since only bonds directly involved in the C–OH being lost can be affected.

The initially formed secondary carbocation can undergo a 1,2-methyl shift to a more stable tertiary carbocation, so the major product may be a rearranged alkene — showing that E1-type dehydration can proceed with skeletal rearrangement whenever a more stable carbocation is accessible via a shift.
questions.explanation: This substrate is a classic rearrangement-prone case: the secondary carbocation formed initially sits adjacent to a carbon bearing a methyl group that can migrate (1,2-methyl shift) to give a more stable tertiary carbocation, so the major dehydration product often reflects this rearranged cation.
questions.hint: Check whether an adjacent carbon can donate a group via a 1,2-shift to reach a more stable carbocation.
distractor_logic: Overlooks that an adjacent carbon here can donate a methyl group via a 1,2-shift to reach a more stable tertiary cation — a classic rearrangement-prone pattern.
Incorrectly rules out alkyl-group shifts, when 1,2-methyl (and other alkyl) shifts are equally well-documented alongside hydride shifts.
Denies the well-documented possibility of 1,2-hydride/alkyl shifts in carbocation intermediates formed during E1 dehydration.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Which reagent converts propan-1-ol all the way to propanoic acid, and which single mild-oxidant alternative would instead stop the sequence at propanal?
options: Hot acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> (or K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) gives propanoic acid; PCC alone stops the oxidation at propanal.
NaBH<sub>4</sub> gives propanoic acid, while PCC over-oxidises further to propanoic anhydride.
Hot acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> stops at propanal, while PCC continues on to propanoic acid.
Both hot acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub> and PCC give exactly the same final product, propanoic acid, differing only in reaction rate.
questions.explanation: Strong oxidants like hot acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>/K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> push a primary alcohol all the way to the carboxylic acid; PCC, being deliberately mild, is the classic choice when the reaction must be stopped at the aldehyde stage.
questions.hint: One reagent is a strong oxidant; the other is specifically chosen in synthesis for stopping early.
distractor_logic: Misapplies NaBH4 (a reducing, not oxidising, agent that would not oxidise an alcohol at all) and invents a nonexistent 'over-oxidation to anhydride' outcome for PCC.
Reverses the actual relative oxidising strength/selectivity of the two reagents.
Denies PCC's well-established selectivity for stopping precisely at the aldehyde stage.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Why is esterification (alcohol + carboxylic acid) an equilibrium reaction, and what practical technique shifts it toward more ester product?
options: The only way to increase ester yield is to lower the reaction temperature as much as possible, since esterification is exothermic and cooling favours the forward direction regardless of concentration effects.
Adding more water to the reaction mixture increases ester yield by diluting the acid catalyst and letting it work more efficiently.

Esterification is reversible (ester + water can hydrolyse back to acid + alcohol under the same acidic conditions); using excess alcohol or continuously removing water (e.g. by distillation) shifts the equilibrium toward more ester, by Le Chatelier's principle.
Esterification is not actually reversible at all; any observed hydrolysis of esters back to acid and alcohol must be a completely separate, unrelated reaction.
questions.explanation: Fischer esterification and ester hydrolysis are the forward and reverse of the same acid-catalysed equilibrium; removing water (a product) or adding excess alcohol (a reactant) pushes the equilibrium toward the ester side, per Le Chatelier's principle.
questions.hint: Think of esterification and hydrolysis as the forward and reverse of one equilibrium — what shifts an equilibrium toward products?
distractor_logic: Overstates a minor thermal effect while ignoring the standard, more effective Le Chatelier approaches (excess reagent, water removal) actually used in practice.
Reverses the actual effect; adding water shifts the equilibrium backward (toward hydrolysis), decreasing ester yield, not increasing it.
Denies the well-established equilibrium nature of Fischer esterification.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Which correctly tracks the change in oxidation level of the relevant carbon across propan-1-ol → propanal → propanoic acid?
options: Propan-1-ol to propanal is an oxidation, but propanal to propanoic acid is actually a reduction, reversing the trend partway through.
Only the final step (propanal to propanoic acid) is an oxidation; converting propan-1-ol to propanal requires no oxidising agent, occurring spontaneously in air.

Each step is a genuine oxidation of that carbon (from C–OH, to C=O with one C–H remaining, to C bonded to two oxygens with no C–H left), consistent with using progressively stronger oxidants (mild PCC for step 1, or strong KMnO<sub>4</sub>/K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> to go directly from alcohol to acid).
The oxidation state of the relevant carbon does not change across this sequence; only the alcohol's O–H bond is affected in each step.
questions.explanation: Both transformations change the carbon's bonding environment and increase its oxidation level, which is exactly why both genuinely require an oxidising agent — a mild one (PCC) if isolating the aldehyde, or a strong one (KMnO<sub>4</sub>/K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) to reach the acid directly.
questions.hint: Track how many oxygens (and how many C-H bonds) are on that specific carbon at each stage.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly claims a reduction step; both transformations in this sequence are oxidations, each requiring an oxidising agent.
Understates that alcohol-to-aldehyde conversion does require a genuine (if mild) oxidising agent such as PCC; it doesn't happen spontaneously without one.
Incorrect; both alcohol-to-aldehyde and aldehyde-to-acid steps do change the carbon's bonding environment/oxidation state, which is precisely why both require an oxidising agent.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: For converting (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH cleanly to (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–Cl with minimal side products, how do conc. HCl/ZnCl<sub>2</sub> (Lucas reagent) and SOCl<sub>2</sub>/pyridine compare?
options: Neither reagent can convert a tertiary alcohol to a tertiary chloride at all; only primary and secondary alcohols can undergo this transformation.

SOCl<sub>2</sub> always gives significant rearrangement for tertiary substrates because it proceeds exclusively via a free carbocation mechanism, just like the Lucas reagent, so there is no meaningful advantage to choosing it here.

SOCl<sub>2</sub>/pyridine is generally preferred for a tertiary alcohol like this — it proceeds through a chlorosulfite intermediate under comparatively less strongly acidic, less carbocation-prone conditions than the Lucas reagent, which (being strongly acidic) can promote elimination side-products with tertiary substrates.

Lucas reagent is always the cleaner method for any alcohol class, since it is specifically designed as a classification/distinguishing reagent, so it should always be preferred over SOCl<sub>2</sub> for actual synthesis.
questions.explanation: Lucas reagent's strongly acidic, SN1-type conditions readily form the tertiary carbocation but also risk competing elimination for a tertiary substrate; SOCl<sub>2</sub> with pyridine proceeds under milder, less strongly acidic conditions with reduced carbocation character, generally giving a cleaner substitution outcome for tertiary alcohols.
questions.hint: Think about which method's conditions are more strongly acidic/carbocation-prone, and how that risk plays out specifically for a tertiary substrate.
distractor_logic: Factually wrong; tertiary alcohols readily react with the Lucas reagent (fastest, via SN1) among all classes, and can also react with SOCl2.
Overstates that SOCl2 always proceeds via a free carbocation; with pyridine present, the mechanism can proceed with less carbocation character than the strongly acidic Lucas conditions.

Misunderstands that Lucas reagent's role is primarily diagnostic (distinguishing alcohol classes via reaction rate); its strongly acidic, carbocation-forming conditions are precisely why it is not typically the preferred general preparative method, especially for tertiary substrates.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: A 1° alcohol and a 3° alcohol are both treated with HBr (no ZnCl<sub>2</sub> catalyst added). How do their expected mechanisms and relative rates compare?
options: Neither alcohol reacts with HBr in the absence of ZnCl<sub>2</sub>, since ZnCl<sub>2</sub> is an absolutely required catalyst for any alcohol-to-alkyl-halide conversion.
The primary alcohol reacts faster than the tertiary alcohol because primary alkyl halide products are more stable than tertiary ones, so the reaction proceeds preferentially through that pathway.

The tertiary alcohol reacts readily via SN1 (forming a stable tertiary carbocation captured by Br<sup>–</sup>); the primary alcohol reacts much more slowly, needing an SN2-type pathway that is comparatively sluggish without a catalyst like ZnCl<sub>2</sub> to help ionise the C–O bond.
Both alcohols react at essentially the same rate via SN1 regardless of class, since HBr alone is a strong enough acid to protonate any alcohol equally well.
questions.explanation: Ionisation to a carbocation (the rate-determining step for SN1) is highly class-dependent, strongly favouring tertiary substrates; primary alcohols lack this stabilisation and must instead rely on a slower SN2-type pathway, especially without a catalyst to assist C–O ionisation.
questions.hint: Protonation of the alcohol happens either way — the real difference is in what happens next, and how easily each substrate can form a carbocation.
distractor_logic: Incorrect; ZnCl2 is specifically needed to accelerate the otherwise-slow reaction with primary/secondary alcohols, but tertiary alcohols react readily with HX even without it.
Reverses the actual observed reactivity order (tertiary reacts faster than primary with HX under typical, uncatalysed conditions) and conflates product stability with reaction rate/mechanism.
Ignores that the rate-determining ionisation step to form a carbocation is highly class-dependent (favouring tertiary), not something HBr protonation alone equalises.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Rank phenol, p-cresol, p-chlorophenol, and p-nitrophenol in order of INCREASING acidity, and justify using substituent electronic effects.
options: p-Cresol < p-chlorophenol < phenol < p-nitrophenol — placing unsubstituted phenol above the chlorine-substituted phenol.

p-Cresol < phenol < p-chlorophenol < p-nitrophenol — methyl (EDG) decreases acidity below phenol; chlorine's inductive withdrawal outweighs its weaker resonance donation, giving a modest increase over phenol; nitro is a powerful resonance-withdrawing EWG, giving the largest increase.
Phenol < p-cresol < p-chlorophenol < p-nitrophenol — placing the EDG-substituted p-cresol above unsubstituted phenol.
p-Nitrophenol < p-chlorophenol < phenol < p-cresol — the reverse order.
questions.explanation: Methyl (EDG) decreases acidity relative to phenol; chlorine's strong inductive electron-withdrawal outweighs its weaker resonance lone-pair donation, giving a net (modest) acidity increase over phenol; nitro's powerful resonance withdrawal gives by far the largest increase — hence p-cresol < phenol < p-chlorophenol < p-nitrophenol.
questions.hint: Weigh each substituent's competing inductive and resonance effects, then rank net electron-withdrawing strength.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly places unsubstituted phenol above the chlorine-substituted phenol, when chlorine's net inductive-withdrawal effect at para makes p-chlorophenol somewhat more acidic than phenol itself, not less.
Incorrectly places the EDG-substituted p-cresol above unsubstituted phenol in acidity, when an EDG should decrease (not increase) acidity relative to phenol.
Reverses the entire acidity order, effectively treating EWGs as acid-weakening and the EDG as acid-strengthening, the opposite of their actual electronic roles.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid, pKa ≈0.4) is dramatically more acidic than phenol (pKa ≈10) or even a mononitrophenol (pKa ≈7). What explains this large cumulative effect?
options: Each nitro group independently withdraws electron density from the ring by both induction and resonance, and their effects are roughly additive; with three strongly electron-withdrawing groups all at ortho/para positions (all able to directly stabilise the phenoxide's negative charge via resonance), the cumulative stabilisation is very large, making picric acid an unusually strong organic acid.
Picric acid's extreme acidity has nothing to do with its nitro substituents; it is due to an entirely different functional group not present in ordinary phenol.
Only one of the three nitro groups actually contributes to the acidifying effect; the other two are purely decorative substituents with no electronic influence.
The dramatic acidity increase is due to steric strain from having three substituents crowded onto the ring, unrelated to any electronic/resonance effect.
questions.explanation: All three nitro groups sit at ortho/para positions capable of direct resonance interaction with the phenoxide's negative charge, and their electron-withdrawing effects (induction + resonance) combine roughly additively, giving picric acid its dramatically enhanced acidity relative to mono- or unsubstituted phenol.
questions.hint: Check the positions of all three nitro groups relative to the –OH-bearing carbon — are they all in resonance-accessible positions?
distractor_logic: Incorrect; picric acid's core structure IS phenol with three added nitro groups, and it is precisely those nitro groups that cause its dramatically increased acidity.
Denies that all substituents capable of resonance interaction with the ring contribute to the cumulative effect, when in fact all three ortho/para-positioned nitro groups do so.
Substitutes an unsupported steric explanation for the actual, well-established electronic (inductive + resonance withdrawal) cause.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: A student claims: '–OH is electron-donating by resonance (as seen in phenol's own ring-activating effect for electrophilic substitution), so it should also make the phenolic O–H bond itself MORE acidic through that same resonance mechanism.' Evaluate this claim.
options: The claim is entirely correct as stated: resonance donation from -OH directly makes the O–H bond weaker and more acidic in exactly the same way it activates the ring toward electrophiles.

The claim conflates two different roles of the same resonance interaction: -OH's lone-pair donation into the ring (in neutral phenol) activates the ring toward electrophiles, but it is the SEPARATE resonance stabilisation of the phenoxide ion, occurring only AFTER deprotonation, that is the real source of phenol's enhanced acidity — not any direct 'acidifying donation' into the intact O–H bond of neutral phenol.
The claim is correct only for para-substituted phenols, not for unsubstituted phenol itself.
The claim is entirely wrong; -OH's resonance donation has no connection whatsoever to phenol's acidity, and the two phenomena are completely unrelated.
questions.explanation: Ring activation (in neutral phenol) and phenoxide stabilisation (after deprotonation) both trace back to oxygen lone-pair delocalisation, but they are distinct events at different stages; phenol's enhanced acidity comes from the phenoxide ion's resonance stabilisation after proton loss, not from a direct 'acidifying' resonance donation while the O–H bond is still intact.
questions.hint: Separate what's happening in neutral phenol (before losing H<sup>+</sup>) from what's happening in the phenoxide ion (after losing H<sup>+</sup>).
distractor_logic: Conflates the resonance donation happening in neutral phenol (which activates the ring) with the separate, stabilising resonance delocalisation that occurs specifically in the phenoxide ion after deprotonation.
Invents an unnecessary substituent requirement; -OH's ring-activating resonance donation and its role in phenoxide stabilisation both occur in unsubstituted phenol as well.
Overstates the disconnect; both phenomena do trace back to the same underlying lone-pair delocalisation, even though the claim's specific causal mechanism is not quite right.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, dichlorocarbene (:CCl<sub>2</sub>) is generated in situ from CHCl<sub>3</sub> and strong base. Which correctly describes the mechanism and why the ortho product predominates?
options: The final product retains both chlorine atoms from the original dichlorocarbene, giving a dichloromethyl-substituted phenol as the isolated product, not an aldehyde.
The carbene :CCl<sub>2</sub> is a nucleophile that attacks an electron-poor position on the ring, specifically targeting the position ortho to –OH (treated here as electron-withdrawing).
Dichlorocarbene is generated by simple homolytic cleavage of a C–Cl bond in CHCl<sub>3</sub> under heat, with no base involvement in its formation at all.

NaOH deprotonates the acidic CHCl<sub>3</sub>, and the resulting CCl<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup> undergoes α-elimination (losing Cl<sup>–</sup>) to generate electrophilic :CCl<sub>2</sub>, which attacks the electron-rich phenoxide ring (predominantly ortho); hydrolysis of the resulting dichloromethyl intermediate then gives salicylaldehyde.
questions.explanation: Base-mediated α-elimination from CHCl<sub>3</sub> generates the electrophilic carbene :CCl<sub>2</sub>, which attacks the electron-rich phenoxide ring (ortho-favoured, by an effect analogous to Kolbe's reaction); the resulting dichloromethyl intermediate is then hydrolysed to the aldehyde, salicylaldehyde.
questions.hint: Track the full sequence: how is the carbene made, what kind of species is it, and what happens to the two chlorines after it attacks the ring?
distractor_logic: Overlooks the essential hydrolysis step that converts the initially-formed dichloromethyl intermediate into the final aldehyde (-CHO) group, releasing chloride ions.
Misidentifies both the carbene's electrophilic (not nucleophilic) character and -OH's actual electron-donating (not withdrawing) role in activating this ring.
Omits the essential role of strong base (NaOH) in first deprotonating CHCl3 before alpha-elimination can generate the carbene.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: How do the electrophiles and conditions of Kolbe's reaction and the Reimer-Tiemann reaction compare, and why do both give predominantly ortho-substitution on phenol?
options: Neither reaction actually proceeds through a phenoxide ion intermediate; both react with neutral phenol directly, with the ring's inherent –OH-directing effect being solely responsible for ortho selectivity.

Kolbe's reaction uses CO<sub>2</sub> as electrophile (attacking phenoxide under heat/pressure) to install –COOH; Reimer-Tiemann uses dichlorocarbene, :CCl<sub>2</sub> (from CHCl<sub>3</sub>/NaOH), to eventually install –CHO; despite different electrophiles, both proceed through a phenoxide ion intermediate and are believed to favour ortho attack via similar coordination/proximity effects with the phenoxide oxygen.
Kolbe's reaction gives predominantly para substitution, while Reimer-Tiemann gives predominantly ortho substitution, so their regioselectivity is actually opposite.
Both reactions use exactly the same electrophile, CO<sub>2</sub>, differing only in the base used, which is why they give similar ortho selectivity.
questions.explanation: Both reactions are run under basic conditions that generate the phenoxide ion, and both are believed to owe their ortho-preference to a coordination/proximity effect between the phenoxide oxygen and the incoming electrophile, even though the electrophiles themselves (CO<sub>2</sub> versus :CCl<sub>2</sub>) are chemically quite different.
questions.hint: Identify the actual electrophile in each named reaction first, then look for what the two mechanisms have in common regarding the phenoxide ion.
distractor_logic: Overlooks that both reactions are specifically carried out under basic conditions that generate the phenoxide ion, which plays a role beyond simply being 'phenol with -OH still directing'.
Misstates Kolbe's reaction's actual regioselectivity, which favours ortho, matching (not opposing) Reimer-Tiemann's ortho preference.
Incorrectly claims the two reactions share the same electrophile, when Kolbe's reaction uses CO2 while Reimer-Tiemann uses dichlorocarbene, a fundamentally different species.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: A phenol derivative already bearing a strong electron-withdrawing group (e.g. –NO<sub>2</sub>) at the para position is subjected to Kolbe's reaction conditions. What outcome is expected, and why?
options: The reaction is completely blocked and cannot occur at all once any second substituent is present on the ring, regardless of its electronic character.
The reaction proceeds much faster than with unsubstituted phenol, since –NO<sub>2</sub> additionally activates the ring toward all types of substitution reactions.
The reaction proceeds identically to unsubstituted phenol, since Kolbe's reaction depends only on the presence of –OH/–O<sup>–</sup> and is completely unaffected by any other ring substituents.

The reaction proceeds much less readily (lower yield/slower) than with unsubstituted phenol, because the existing –NO<sub>2</sub> group withdraws electron density from the ring, reducing the phenoxide ring's reactivity toward the CO<sub>2</sub> electrophile, even though –OH itself is still present and still directs to its own ortho/para positions.
questions.explanation: A second electron-withdrawing substituent lowers the overall electron density (nucleophilicity) of the ring, slowing electrophilic attack by CO<sub>2</sub> even though –OH is still present and still an ortho/para director in principle.
questions.hint: Think about the ring's overall electron density with two substituents present, one donating (–OH) and one withdrawing (–NO<sub>2</sub>).
distractor_logic: Overstates that any second substituent entirely blocks the reaction; the reaction can still occur (just less readily with an EWG present), it is not an absolute block.
Reverses -NO2's actual electronic character; it is a ring deactivator (electron-withdrawing), which would slow, not speed up, further electrophilic substitution.

Ignores that a second, electron-withdrawing substituent measurably reduces the ring's overall nucleophilicity/reactivity toward electrophilic attack, regardless of -OH's continued directing influence.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Based on the diagram, isopropyl methyl ether, (CH3)2CH–O–CH3, is treated with excess HI. Which bond cleaves preferentially, and what are the major products?
options: Neither bond cleaves under these conditions, since isopropyl methyl ether is specifically resistant to HI cleavage.
The bond to the primary/methyl carbon cleaves preferentially, giving methyl iodide + propan-2-ol as major products.
The bond to the secondary (isopropyl) carbon cleaves preferentially, via an SN1-favoured pathway, giving isopropyl iodide + methanol as major products.
Both C–O bonds cleave with exactly equal probability, giving a precise 50:50 statistical mixture of all possible products.
questions.explanation: A secondary carbocation, though less stable than a tertiary one, is still considerably more accessible than requiring the methyl carbon to ionise, so cleavage is directed preferentially to the isopropyl side, giving isopropyl iodide and methanol.
questions.hint: Compare how easily each side of this ether could form a carbocation — the secondary carbon has a real advantage here.
distractor_logic: Denies the well-established general reactivity of dialkyl ethers (with no aryl group present) toward cleavage by excess hot HI.

Misapplies the general 'less hindered carbon reacts' SN2 rule uniformly; once a secondary (or tertiary) carbon is present, some degree of SN1 character shifts cleavage toward the more substituted carbon instead.

Understates that a secondary carbon, having somewhat greater carbocation-forming ability than a primary carbon, does show a genuine (if not absolute) preference for cleavage at that more substituted site.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Which correctly ranks the general suitability of the alkyl halide component for clean Williamson synthesis (favouring SN2 substitution over competing E2 elimination), from best to worst?
options: Secondary > methyl > primary > tertiary
Tertiary > secondary > primary > methyl
Methyl > primary > secondary > tertiary
All four classes work equally well in Williamson synthesis
questions.explanation: Increasing substitution increases both steric hindrance to SN2 backside attack and the tendency toward competing E2 elimination, so suitability for clean Williamson substitution decreases from methyl/primary down to tertiary.
questions.hint: Think about how steric hindrance to backside attack, and tendency toward elimination, change as substitution increases.
distractor_logic: Places secondary above methyl/primary, when methyl and primary halides are in fact the best (least hindered, least elimination-prone) substrates for SN2-based Williamson synthesis.
Reverses the actual order; increasing substitution increases both steric hindrance to SN2 and elimination tendency, making tertiary the WORST choice, not the best.
Ignores the well-established substrate-dependence of SN2 versus E2 competition, which is governed significantly by the alkyl halide's own structure.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: A synthesis target is benzyl ethyl ether, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>. Which Williamson synthesis reagent pairing correctly and reliably gives this product?
options: Ethyl chloride, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–Cl, + sodium phenoxide, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONa

Benzyl chloride, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–Cl (readily undergoes SN2, since the benzylic position is activated, not hindered, by the adjacent ring), + sodium ethoxide, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONa
Chlorobenzene, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–Cl, + sodium ethoxide, C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONa
Benzyl alcohol, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH (without converting it to its sodium salt), + ethyl chloride directly
questions.explanation: Benzylic halides react readily via SN2 (the adjacent aromatic ring stabilises the transition state), making benzyl chloride a good electrophile; paired with sodium ethoxide, this correctly gives benzyl ethyl ether, with the ether oxygen attached to the benzylic CH<sub>2</sub>.
questions.hint: Make sure the oxygen ends up attached to the CH<sub>2</sub> group, not directly to the aromatic ring itself.
distractor_logic: This combination would actually give phenyl ethyl ether (an aryl alkyl ether), not the target benzyl ethyl ether, which requires the oxygen attached to a benzylic CH2, not directly to the ring.
Incorrectly uses an ARYL halide rather than the required benzylic (side-chain) halide; aryl C-Cl bonds are essentially unreactive toward the SN2 mechanism Williamson synthesis requires.
A neutral alcohol is too weak a nucleophile to react efficiently with an alkyl halide without first being deprotonated to the corresponding alkoxide.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: tert-Butyl ethyl ether, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub>, is treated with just ONE equivalent of cold, dilute HI (mild conditions, not excess hot HI). Which correctly predicts the major products?
options: The tertiary C–O bond is still cleaved preferentially, giving tert-butyl iodide + ethanol, because the tertiary carbocation forms so readily (low activation energy) that it remains kinetically preferred even under comparatively mild conditions.
Under mild conditions, cleavage instead favours the ethyl (primary) C–O bond via SN2, switching mechanism compared to what would happen with excess hot HI.
Both C–O bonds cleave with equal probability under mild conditions, unlike under forcing conditions where selectivity would instead emerge.
No cleavage occurs at all under mild/limited conditions; ether cleavage strictly requires excess, hot, concentrated HI in every case.
questions.explanation: The tertiary carbocation's low activation energy for formation makes that pathway kinetically favoured regardless of whether conditions are mild or forcing, so the same regiochemical preference (cleavage at the tertiary carbon) is expected either way.
questions.hint: Ask whether the ease of forming the tertiary carbocation actually depends on how forcing the reaction conditions are.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes milder conditions favour a mechanistic switch toward the primary carbon; the tertiary carbocation pathway remains kinetically favourable even under milder conditions.
Reverses the actual relationship; regioselectivity for the more stabilised (tertiary) carbocation pathway would be expected under both mild and forcing conditions here, not only under forcing ones.

Overstates the necessity of forcing conditions specifically for THIS substrate; a highly stabilised tertiary carbocation can form and react even under comparatively milder conditions than a less activated substrate would need.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Which combination of test results correctly and uniquely distinguishes four unlabeled samples — ethanol, phenol, diethyl ether, and 2-methylpropan-2-ol — using Na metal, neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub>, and the Lucas test together?
options: Na metal alone is sufficient, since each of the four compounds is claimed to evolve a different, distinguishable volume of H<sub>2</sub> gas allowing full identification.
Neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub> alone distinguishes all four samples, since each compound is claimed to give a differently coloured response.

Na metal: ethanol, phenol, and tert-butanol evolve H<sub>2</sub>; diethyl ether does not (identifies the ether). Neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub>: phenol alone gives a violet/blue/green colour among the remaining three (identifies phenol). Lucas test on the remaining two: tert-butanol gives immediate turbidity (tertiary); ethanol shows no turbidity at room temperature, reacting only slowly on heating (primary) — distinguishing the final two.
A single test, the Lucas test alone, is sufficient to distinguish all four samples simultaneously without needing Na metal or FeCl3 at all.
questions.explanation: Each test narrows the field by a different criterion: Na metal separates the ether (no O–H) from the rest; FeCl<sub>3</sub> then isolates phenol from the remaining alcohols; the Lucas test finally distinguishes the primary and tertiary alcohols by their very different reaction rates.
questions.hint: No single test here does the whole job — work out which specific pair of compounds each test actually separates.
distractor_logic: Overstates what Na metal reactivity alone can reveal; while it distinguishes the ether from the three O-H-containing compounds, it cannot on its own distinguish phenol from the two alcohols.
Overstates FeCl3's discriminating power; it specifically and only detects phenols, giving no distinguishing colour reaction among the three non-phenolic samples.

Overlooks that the Lucas test specifically distinguishes alcohol CLASSES and gives no distinguishing signal for phenol (not typically classified this way) or diethyl ether (which lacks an O-H bond needed for the Lucas mechanism at all).

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: A researcher needs to confirm both that a sample is a tertiary alcohol AND that it contains no separate CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)– unit elsewhere in the molecule. How should the Lucas test and iodoform test be sequenced to get both pieces of information cleanly?
options: Only the Lucas test is actually necessary, since a positive (immediate) Lucas result for a tertiary alcohol automatically also proves the absence of any CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)– unit elsewhere in the molecule.
Only the iodoform test is actually necessary, since a negative iodoform result automatically also proves the sample is a tertiary alcohol.

Run them as two entirely separate portions of the sample, since the reagents (conc. HCl/ZnCl<sub>2</sub> for Lucas; I<sub>2</sub>/NaOH for iodoform) would interfere with each other if combined in one vessel — a positive (immediate turbidity) Lucas test on one portion confirms tertiary classification, while a negative iodoform test on the other portion confirms the absence of that structural unit.
Both tests can be safely combined into a single reaction vessel and run simultaneously, since their reagents (acidic Lucas reagent and basic iodoform reagent) are chemically compatible.
questions.explanation: Lucas reagent is strongly acidic while iodoform reagent is strongly basic; combining them in one vessel would cause them to neutralise/interfere with each other, so each test must be run on a separate portion of the sample to get a clean, individually interpretable result for each unrelated structural question.
questions.hint: Check whether the two reagent systems (strongly acidic vs strongly basic) could actually coexist cleanly in the same reaction vessel.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes tertiary classification at the carbinol carbon says anything about unrelated structural features (like a separate CH3-CH(OH)- unit) elsewhere in the same molecule; these are independent structural questions.

Incorrectly assumes the absence of a CH3-CH(OH)-/CH3-CO- unit says anything about the classification of the carbinol carbon actually bearing the -OH group being investigated; these are again independent questions.
Incorrectly claims compatibility between a strongly acidic reagent system (Lucas) and a strongly basic one (iodoform/NaOH), which would in fact neutralise/interfere with each other if combined.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: The ceric ammonium nitrate (CAN) test gives a red coloration for alcohols but brown/green for phenols. Could this result be explained, in general terms, by the same acidity/electronic concepts used elsewhere in this chapter to distinguish alcohols from phenols?
options: Alcohols and phenols would be expected to give IDENTICAL CAN test results, since both possess a similar-looking oxygen atom capable of the same type of coordination to cerium.
The CAN test works purely because phenols are coloured compounds to begin with, while alcohols are colourless, with no actual chemical reaction occurring in either case.

No connection exists whatsoever; the CAN test result is due to an entirely different type of chemistry (redox behaviour) completely unrelated to any acid-base/electronic reasoning used elsewhere in the chapter.

Yes, in a general sense — the test relies on differently-coloured cerium(IV)-alkoxide/aryloxide coordination complexes, and the differing electronic character of an alcohol's oxygen (more electron-rich, non-delocalised) versus a phenol's oxygen (partially delocalised into the ring, more readily deprotonated/coordinated given phenol's greater acidity) plausibly underlies the visually distinguishable complexes, echoing the same electronic distinction responsible for their differing acidities.
questions.explanation: Even though the CAN test itself is a coordination-complex-formation reaction rather than a simple acid-base reaction, the underlying electronic difference between an alcohol's and a phenol's oxygen (the same distinction responsible for their differing acidities) plausibly contributes to why the two give visually distinguishable complexes.
questions.hint: Ask what property of the oxygen atom itself — in an alcohol versus a phenol — would matter for forming a coordination complex with a metal ion.
distractor_logic: Ignores the well-documented, genuinely distinguishable colours the CAN test gives for the two classes, and dismisses the real electronic difference between an alcohol's and a phenol's oxygen.
Misdescribes the CAN test as merely observing pre-existing colour rather than an actual coordination/complex-formation reaction between the substrate and the cerium reagent.

Overstates the disconnect; even a coordination-complex-forming test still depends on the oxygen's availability/electronic character, a property genuinely related to the acidity/electron-donating differences discussed elsewhere.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: A compound with formula C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O reacts with Na metal to release H<sub>2</sub> gas but gives no colour with neutral FeCl<sub>3</sub>. What is its most likely structure and class?
options: A cresol (methylphenol)
o-Cresol
Anisole, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>
Benzyl alcohol, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–OH — a primary, benzylic alcohol, not a phenol
questions.explanation: C<sub>7</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O isomers include cresols (phenols), anisole (an ether) and benzyl alcohol. Reaction with Na (H<sub>2</sub> evolved) rules out anisole, which has no O–H. A negative FeCl<sub>3</sub> test rules out phenolic structures like cresols. Benzyl alcohol fits both: it's an alcohol (O–H on the sp<sup>3</sup> benzylic carbon), not a phenol.
questions.hint: Use both clues together — Na reactivity needs O–H; the FeCl<sub>3</sub> colour test is specific to phenols.
distractor_logic: A phenol like cresol would react with Na, but would also give a positive (violet/blue) FeCl3 colour, contradicting the given negative test.
Same error as the cresol option — a phenolic isomer would test positive with FeCl3, contradicting the data.
Anisole has no O-H bond at all and would not react with Na, contradicting the given H2 evolution.

questions.topic: Classification and Structure of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: Which statement correctly links molecular structure to the large boiling-point gap between propan-1-ol (≈97°C) and its isomer methoxyethane, CH<sub>3</sub>–O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> (≈8°C)?
options: Both should have nearly identical boiling points since they are structural isomers with the same molecular formula.
Propan-1-ol's O–H allows intermolecular hydrogen bonding between alcohol molecules; the ether has no O–H to hydrogen-bond with itself, despite identical molar mass.
Methoxyethane should boil higher because ether oxygen is more electronegative and forms stronger dipole interactions than an alcohol's O–H.
Propan-1-ol should boil lower because branching at the ether's oxygen increases its van der Waals contact area above the alcohol's.
questions.explanation: Both are C<sub>3</sub>H<sub>8</sub>O isomers with equal molar mass, but only propan-1-ol has an O–H bond capable of a network of intermolecular hydrogen bonds, dramatically raising its boiling point over the isomeric ether, which lacks O–H and relies only on weaker dipole and van der Waals forces.
questions.hint: Same formula, same mass — the deciding factor is whether O–H hydrogen bonding is possible.
distractor_logic: Ignores that boiling point depends on intermolecular forces present, not merely on sharing the same molecular formula.
Overstates ordinary dipole-dipole interaction strength relative to true O-H hydrogen bonding, which the ether cannot form.
Invents an irrelevant branching/surface-area argument while ignoring that the ether has no O-H to hydrogen bond with at all.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>–CH(OH)–CH(CH<sub>3</sub>)–CH<sub>2</sub>–CH<sub>3</sub>, applying the lowest-locant rule to both the –OH and the methyl branch?
options: 2-Methylpentan-4-ol
3-Methylpentan-2-ol
Pentan-2-ol-3-methyl
3-Methylpentan-4-ol
questions.explanation: The parent chain is five carbons (pentane); –OH gets priority for the lowest locant. Numbering from the end nearer –OH places OH at C2 and the methyl branch at C3: 3-methylpentan-2-ol.
questions.hint: Try numbering from both ends and pick whichever gives –OH (the suffix group) the lower locant.
distractor_logic: Numbers from the wrong end, giving -OH a higher locant than the alternative direction allows.
Uses non-standard suffix-then-prefix word order instead of the correct combined name format.
Fails to give -OH the lowest possible locant (2, not 4) when numbering from the correct end.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: 2,4,6-Trinitrophenol (picric acid) is the product of exhaustive nitration of phenol. Which explanation correctly accounts for this specific substitution pattern rather than, say, 2,3,5-?
options: Nitration of phenol occurs randomly at all six ring positions, and 2,4,6-trinitrophenol is just the major product isolated by chance after purification.
The 2,4,6-pattern results from steric control only, since positions 3 and 5 are simply 'too crowded' regardless of electronic effects.
Nitro groups direct later substitution to their own ortho/para positions, so the 2,4,6-pattern arises purely from –NO<sub>2</sub> directing further –NO<sub>2</sub> groups, independent of –OH.
–OH is an ortho/para director, so successive nitrations under forcing conditions fill the activated ortho (2,6) and para (4) positions relative to C1–OH.
questions.explanation: –OH strongly activates and directs incoming NO<sub>2</sub><sup>+</sup> to its own ortho (2,6) and para (4) positions via resonance donation of its lone pair into the ring. With excess conc. HNO<sub>3</sub>, all three activated positions get nitrated, giving 2,4,6-trinitrophenol.
questions.hint: Think about which positions –OH itself directs electrophiles to, and how that plays out over three successive substitutions.
distractor_logic: Denies that any directing effect controls regiochemistry, which is factually incorrect for an activated, ortho/para-directing ring.
Dismisses the real electronic (resonance) directing effect of -OH in favour of an unsupported purely steric explanation.
Ignores that -OH is present from the start and dominates directing; also -NO2 is actually a meta-director, which would work against this pattern if taken alone.

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CH<sub>3</sub>, and which physical-property consequence correctly follows from that structure?
options: 1-Ethoxypropane; and since ether oxygen still has lone pairs, it hydrogen-bonds with other ether molecules just as strongly as alcohols hydrogen-bond with each other.
Ethyl propyl ether; the correct IUPAC substitutive name for this compound.
1-Ethoxypropane; having no O–H bond, it cannot hydrogen-bond with molecules of itself, giving it a much lower boiling point than isomeric alcohols of similar mass.
Propoxyethane; and because ethers are more polar than alcohols overall, it should boil higher than a comparable alcohol.
questions.explanation: The 3-carbon chain (propane) is the parent, with –O–C<sub>2</sub>H<sub>5</sub> ('ethoxy') as substituent: 1-ethoxypropane. Lacking O–H, it cannot self-associate by hydrogen bonding, so its boiling point is much lower than isomeric or similarly-sized alcohols, though it can still weakly accept H-bonds from water.
questions.hint: Name it first (longer chain = parent), then reason about O–H bonding from the functional group actually present.
distractor_logic: Names the compound correctly but wrongly claims ether-ether hydrogen bonding is as strong as alcohol-alcohol bonding; ethers have no O-H donor and cannot hydrogen-bond to each other.
Gives the functional-class (common) name rather than the requested IUPAC substitutive name.
Gets both the parent-chain choice wrong (should be the 3-carbon chain) and the boiling-point trend backwards (ethers boil lower than isomeric alcohols, not higher).

questions.topic: IUPAC Nomenclature of Alcohols, Phenols and Ethers
questions.question: 'p-Cresol' is the common name for a methylphenol. Which IUPAC name correctly matches it, and why?
options: 4-Methylbenzenol — using 'benzenol' instead of the retained IUPAC parent name 'phenol'.
4-Methylphenol — 'para' means the methyl group sits directly opposite (C4) the –OH-bearing carbon, which is always numbered C1 in phenol.
2-Methylphenol — matching 'para' to the ortho (C2) position instead of the para (C4) position.
1-Methyl-4-hydroxybenzene — treating –OH as a prefix and methyl's carbon as C1, instead of letting the senior –OH group anchor numbering at C1.
questions.explanation: 'Cresol' is the retained common name for methylphenol; 'para' specifies the methyl substituent is opposite (C4) the –OH-bearing carbon (always C1 in phenol's own numbering). The IUPAC name is therefore 4-methylphenol.
questions.hint: In phenol's own numbering, the –OH carbon is always C1; 'para' means directly opposite, i.e. C4.
distractor_logic: Uses a non-standard parent name 'benzenol' instead of the correct retained IUPAC name 'phenol'.
Mismatches the common name (which specifies para) with an IUPAC name placing the methyl group ortho instead.
Incorrectly treats -OH as a prefix and numbers methyl's carbon as C1, when -OH is the senior/only functional group and should anchor the numbering and be the suffix, not a prefix.

questions.question: A mixture of o- and p-nitrophenol is separated by steam distillation. Which combination correctly explains both (a) why separation is possible, and (b) which isomer is more acidic and why?
options: (a) is correct, but (b) is reversed: o-nitrophenol is claimed more acidic because 'ortho substituents are always more acidifying than para ones' as a blanket rule.
Both isomers are equally acidic since –NO<sub>2</sub>'s electron-withdrawing strength doesn't depend on ring position, and separation is only about differing melting points, not volatility.

(a) o-Nitrophenol's intramolecular H-bonding makes it steam-volatile while p-nitrophenol's intermolecular H-bonding makes it non-volatile; (b) p-nitrophenol is actually more acidic, since its –NO<sub>2</sub> conjugates directly with the phenoxide through the ring, an effect partly reduced in the ortho isomer where the intramolecular H-bond competes for the same electron density.
Steam distillation separates them because p-nitrophenol has a lower molecular weight, not because of any hydrogen-bonding difference.
questions.explanation: Physically, intramolecular chelation (ortho) versus intermolecular association (para) explains the volatility difference exploited in steam distillation. Electronically, the para position allows direct resonance conjugation of –NO<sub>2</sub> with the phenoxide oxygen through the ring, giving stronger phenoxide stabilisation than the ortho isomer (where the effect is partly used up in the intramolecular H-bond); p-nitrophenol is therefore somewhat more acidic than o-nitrophenol, though both are far more acidic than phenol itself.
questions.hint: Separate the physical (volatility/H-bonding) reasoning from the electronic (resonance/acidity) reasoning — both trace back to the same ortho-vs-para geometry.
distractor_logic: Invents an oversimplified positional rule instead of the correct resonance/intramolecular-H-bond-competition explanation.
Denies both established effects: the positional dependence of resonance withdrawal, and steam-volatility as the actual basis for separation.
Misattributes the separation to molecular weight, which is identical for both isomers (constitutional isomers), instead of the true volatility/H-bonding cause.

questions.question: Which statement correctly connects an alcohol's carbon classification (1°/2°/3°) to the typical boiling-point trend among isomeric alcohols of the same molecular formula (e.g. butan-1-ol vs butan-2-ol vs 2-methylpropan-2-ol)?
options: All isomeric alcohols of the same molecular formula must have identical boiling points because they have the same number and type of hydrogen-bonding groups.
Boiling-point trends among 1°/2°/3° isomeric alcohols are unpredictable and show no consistent pattern.

Boiling point generally decreases from primary to tertiary (1° > 2° > 3°) because increased branching near –OH reduces surface area for van der Waals contact and can sterically hinder efficient hydrogen bonding, even though all three can form O–H hydrogen bonds.
Tertiary alcohols boil highest among isomers because their extra alkyl branching adds extra polarity to the O–H bond.
questions.explanation: 1°, 2°, and 3° alcohols of the same formula can all hydrogen-bond via O–H, but as branching increases the molecule becomes more compact/spherical, reducing intermolecular contact area and hindering H-bond geometry, so boiling points generally fall in the order 1° > 2° > 3° for isomeric alcohols (e.g. butan-1-ol 118°C > butan-2-ol 100°C > 2-methylpropan-2-ol 82°C).
questions.hint: All three isomers can hydrogen-bond — the differentiating factor here is molecular shape/branching, not hydrogen-bonding ability itself.
distractor_logic: Ignores that molecular shape/branching still measurably affects boiling point among isomers sharing identical hydrogen-bonding groups.
Denies the well-established general trend (1° > 2° > 3°) seen across isomeric alcohol series.
Misattributes a steric/surface-area effect to a nonexistent increase in O-H polarity; branching actually tends to lower, not raise, boiling point.

questions.question: An ester is reduced by LiAlH<sub>4</sub> to a primary alcohol, which is then treated with PCC. What is the final product, and what does this reveal about PCC's oxidising strength?
options: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> reduces the ester fully to a 1° alcohol; PCC then oxidises that alcohol only as far as the corresponding aldehyde, since PCC is a mild oxidant that stops at the aldehyde stage.
PCC has no effect on primary alcohols at all, so the alcohol from the LiAlH4 step remains the unchanged final product.
LiAlH<sub>4</sub> only partially reduces the ester to an aldehyde, so PCC then has nothing further left to oxidise.
PCC oxidises the 1° alcohol all the way to the carboxylic acid, taking the molecule back to the same oxidation level as (part of) the original ester.
questions.explanation: LiAlH<sub>4</sub> is a strong enough hydride source to fully reduce the ester to the primary alcohol; PCC, being a mild, selective oxidant, then stops precisely at the aldehyde stage rather than continuing on to the carboxylic acid. The overall two-step sequence is a net reduction of the ester, not a round trip back to it.
questions.hint: Match each reagent to its known strength: one is a strong, exhaustive reducing agent; the other is a deliberately mild, stage-stopping oxidant.
distractor_logic: Factually wrong; PCC is specifically used to oxidise 1° alcohols to aldehydes, so it clearly does react with the alcohol from the first step.
Misunderstands that LiAlH4, being a strong/excess hydride source, reduces esters fully to the 1° alcohol rather than stopping at an intermediate aldehyde.
Misapplies KMnO4/K2Cr2O7-type strong-oxidant behaviour (which goes to the acid) to PCC, which is specifically mild and stops at the aldehyde.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Hydrolysis of a tertiary alkyl halide with aqueous NaOH to give a tertiary alcohol is typically run under mild conditions. Why, and what competing pathway does this avoid?
options: Strong heating and concentrated base actually favour substitution over elimination for tertiary halides, so mild conditions are used only for cost reasons.

Tertiary halides react with hydroxide predominantly via SN1 and readily undergo E1 elimination as a competing pathway (especially with heat or strong base), so mild, weakly basic aqueous conditions favour substitution (alcohol) over elimination (alkene).
Tertiary halides only react via SN2, so steric hindrance — not elimination — is the sole competing concern, unrelated to base strength or temperature.
Tertiary halides do not undergo any competing elimination reaction, so reaction conditions have no effect on the product distribution obtained.
questions.explanation: Tertiary carbons undergo SN1 substitution through a stable carbocation, but that same carbocation is also prone to E1 elimination, particularly favoured by heat and strong base. Mild aqueous conditions therefore steer the outcome toward the substitution (alcohol) product rather than the alkene.
questions.hint: Think about what a tertiary carbocation intermediate can do besides simply being attacked by a nucleophile.
distractor_logic: Reverses the actual selectivity trend; forcing conditions (heat, concentrated/strong base) favour elimination, not substitution.
Misassigns tertiary substrates to the SN2 mechanism, when they overwhelmingly favour SN1/E1 due to steric hindrance to backside attack and carbocation stability.
Denies the well-known SN1/E1 competition that is especially pronounced for tertiary substrates.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Alcohols
questions.question: Which combination correctly prepares 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tert-butyl alcohol) by Grignard synthesis, and what general rule does it illustrate?
options: CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + propanone (acetone, CH<sub>3</sub>COCH<sub>3</sub>), then acidic hydrolysis — illustrating that Grignard reagents react with ketones to give tertiary alcohols.

CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + propanal (CH<sub>3</sub>CH<sub>2</sub>CHO), then acidic hydrolysis — this actually gives butan-2-ol, a secondary alcohol, since aldehydes other than formaldehyde give secondary alcohols.
CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + CO<sub>2</sub>, then acidic hydrolysis — this gives acetic acid, a carboxylic acid, not any alcohol at all.
CH<sub>3</sub>MgBr + formaldehyde (HCHO), then acidic hydrolysis — this gives ethanol, a primary alcohol, not the target tertiary alcohol.
questions.explanation: A ketone's carbonyl carbon already carries two carbon substituents; adding a third (from the Grignard reagent) gives a carbinol carbon bonded to three carbons — a tertiary alcohol. Acetone + methylmagnesium bromide gives exactly (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH, 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
questions.hint: Count how many carbon substituents the carbonyl carbon already has before the Grignard group is added.
distractor_logic: Correctly names what a non-formaldehyde aldehyde gives (secondary alcohol) but this is not the reagent pairing that yields the target tertiary alcohol.
Correctly identifies the Grignard-plus-CO2 outcome (a carboxylic acid) but this is not an alcohol-forming route at all, let alone the target tertiary alcohol.
Correctly names formaldehyde's unique primary-alcohol outcome but this does not give the target tertiary alcohol.
