questions.question: 2-Methylpropene is treated separately with (a) dil. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O and (b) B<sub>2</sub>H<sub>6</sub>, then H<sub>2</sub>O<sub>2</sub>/NaOH. Which correctly names both alcohol products and identifies which method gives which?
options: (a) acid-catalysed hydration is Markovnikov, giving 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary); (b) hydroboration-oxidation is anti-Markovnikov, giving 2-methylpropan-1-ol (primary) — the same starting alkene gives two different alcohols, of two different classes, purely depending on which method is used.
(a) gives 2-methylpropan-1-ol and (b) gives 2-methylpropan-2-ol.
Neither method can hydrate 2-methylpropene at all, since it is too hindered/symmetrical an alkene to undergo either type of addition.
Both methods give the identical product, 2-methylpropan-2-ol, since 2-methylpropene only has one possible addition product regardless of mechanism.
questions.explanation: 2-Methylpropene's unsymmetrical double bond (one CH<sub>2</sub>= carbon, one =C(CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>2</sub> carbon) gives genuinely different major products depending on regiochemistry: Markovnikov addition (acid hydration) puts –OH on the more substituted carbon (tertiary alcohol), while anti-Markovnikov addition (hydroboration-oxidation) puts it on the less substituted carbon (primary alcohol).
questions.hint: Identify which carbon of the unsymmetrical double bond is more substituted, then apply each method's known regiochemistry.
distractor_logic: Swaps which method gives which regiochemical outcome, reversing the Markovnikov/anti-Markovnikov assignments.
Factually wrong; 2-methylpropene is a standard, reactive substrate for both hydration methods.
Incorrect; the two methods have opposite regiochemistry, and 2-methylpropene's unsymmetrical double bond gives genuinely different major products from each.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: In the cumene process, cumene hydroperoxide rearranges and cleaves under dilute acid to give phenol and acetone in one step. Why is acetone (not propan-2-ol) the co-product?
options: Acetone and phenol are unrelated co-products formed from two completely separate cumene molecules reacting independently.
Dilute acid simply hydrolyses two different ester-like linkages within cumene hydroperoxide, one giving phenol and a separate one giving acetone, with no rearrangement step involved.
Propan-2-ol is the initial product, which is then spontaneously oxidised by atmospheric O<sub>2</sub> in a second, separate step to give the acetone found in commercial phenol production.

Acid-catalysed rearrangement proceeds through migration of the phenyl group to the adjacent oxygen; the resulting intermediate collapses directly, on hydrolysis, into phenol plus acetone (a ketone) — acetone forms directly from this cleavage, not via a separate alcohol-oxidation step.
questions.explanation: The mechanism involves a 1,2-phenyl shift from carbon to the adjacent peroxide oxygen, generating an intermediate that fragments on hydrolysis directly into phenol and acetone from the very same cumene hydroperoxide molecule — a single concerted rearrangement/cleavage pathway, not a two-molecule or two-step oxidation process.
questions.hint: Both products come from the same starting molecule via one rearrangement-then-cleavage mechanism, not from a separate later oxidation.
distractor_logic: Incorrect; both phenol and acetone come from the very same cumene hydroperoxide molecule cleaving into two fragments within one mechanistic pathway.
Omits the essential rearrangement (1,2-phenyl shift) step that is mechanistically central to how these two specific products form together.
Invents an unnecessary second oxidation step; acetone is formed directly within the same acid-catalysed cleavage mechanism, not from oxidising an isolated alcohol.

questions.topic: Methods of Preparation of Phenols
questions.question: How does phenol's greater acidity (compared to an ordinary alcohol) make diazonium-salt hydrolysis a practical lab-scale route to pure phenol?
options: Diazonium hydrolysis is chosen specifically because it avoids forming any acidic product at all, unlike the Dow process, which is claimed to give an acidic product directly.
The Dow process is actually better suited to lab-scale synthesis because it requires no diazotisation step, while diazonium hydrolysis is exclusively an industrial-scale method.

Diazonium hydrolysis runs under mild, low-temperature aqueous conditions suited to small-scale lab work (unlike the industrial, high-pressure Dow process); once formed, phenol's acidity also lets it be purified by extracting it into aqueous NaOH (as water-soluble phenoxide) and then re-acidifying — a trick that wouldn't work for a simple alcohol.
Phenol's acidity has no bearing on its purification at all; it is purified by fractional distillation only, identically to how any alcohol product would be purified.
questions.explanation: Beyond its mild reaction conditions, diazonium hydrolysis benefits from phenol's acidity at the purification stage: phenol dissolves in aqueous NaOH as the water-soluble phenoxide ion (allowing separation from neutral organic impurities), and can then be regenerated cleanly by acidifying — a purification approach not available for non-acidic alcohols.
questions.hint: Think about what phenol's acidity lets you do to it chemically during work-up that a neutral alcohol wouldn't allow.
distractor_logic: Both routes give the same acidic product, phenol; the routes differ in reaction conditions/scale suitability, not in whether the product itself is acidic.

Reverses the actual practical suitability; the Dow process's extreme pressure/temperature make it an industrial, not lab-scale, method, while diazonium hydrolysis is readily done in ordinary lab glassware.
Dismisses a genuinely useful, acidity-based purification technique that is specific to sufficiently acidic phenols and not applicable to simple alcohols.

questions.question: A mixture of butan-1-ol and 2-methylpropan-2-ol is treated first with PCC, and separately, each with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat. Which correctly predicts the major outcomes?
options: Neither alcohol reacts with PCC or with H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat, since both reagents only work on secondary alcohols.

With PCC, butan-1-ol is oxidised to butanal while 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary, no carbinol C–H) is unreactive; with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat, 2-methylpropan-2-ol dehydrates readily (stable tertiary carbocation) to 2-methylpropene, while butan-1-ol dehydrates more slowly (less stable primary carbocation) toward but-1-ene/but-2-ene.
Under H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat, butan-1-ol dehydrates faster than 2-methylpropan-2-ol, since primary alcohols are generally more reactive in every acid-catalysed process.
PCC oxidises both alcohols equally well to their respective carbonyl compounds, since PCC's reactivity does not depend on alcohol class.
questions.explanation: Oxidation requires a carbinol C–H, absent in tertiary alcohols, so PCC only oxidises the primary alcohol; dehydration reactivity instead follows carbocation stability (3° > 1°), so the tertiary alcohol dehydrates far more readily under acid/heat.
questions.hint: Match each reagent to the structural feature it actually needs: oxidation needs a carbinol C-H; dehydration needs a stable carbocation.
distractor_logic: Factually wrong on both counts; PCC classically oxidises primary alcohols, and H2SO4/heat dehydrates alcohols of every class (tertiary fastest).
Reverses the actual dehydration reactivity order (3° > 2° > 1°, governed by carbocation stability), which is indeed the reverse of SN2 substitution reactivity.
Ignores that PCC (and oxidation generally) requires a carbinol C-H, which is absent in tertiary alcohols.

questions.question: Which two-step sequence correctly converts propene into propan-2-one (acetone)?
options: Step 1: hydroboration-oxidation of propene gives propan-2-ol directly; Step 2: treatment with NaBH<sub>4</sub> gives propan-2-one.
Step 1: ozonolysis of propene gives propan-2-ol directly; Step 2: esterification with acetic acid gives propan-2-one.

Step 1: acid-catalysed hydration (dil. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/H<sub>2</sub>O) of propene gives propan-2-ol (Markovnikov); Step 2: oxidation with acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (or KMnO<sub>4</sub>) gives propan-2-one.
Step 1: dehydration of propene with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives propan-2-ol; Step 2: reduction with LiAlH<sub>4</sub> gives propan-2-one.
questions.explanation: Markovnikov hydration correctly gives the secondary alcohol propan-2-ol; oxidising a secondary alcohol with a strong oxidant like acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> gives the corresponding ketone, propan-2-one.
questions.hint: Step 1 needs to give the correct alcohol (Markovnikov, secondary); step 2 needs a genuine oxidising agent.
distractor_logic: Misapplies hydroboration-oxidation's actual anti-Markovnikov outcome (which would give propan-1-ol, not propan-2-ol) and misuses NaBH4 (a reducing agent) as if it were an oxidant.
Misapplies ozonolysis, which cleaves the C=C bond into two separate carbonyl fragments rather than giving an alcohol, and confuses esterification (giving an ester) with oxidation.
Misapplies dehydration (which removes water from an alcohol to give an alkene, the wrong direction here) and misuses LiAlH4 (a reducing agent) as if it were an oxidant capable of forming a ketone.

questions.question: Which pair of reactions correctly shows that the same alcohol, butan-2-ol, gives different major products depending only on which reagent/pathway is used?
options: Acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>/K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> causes dehydration to but-2-ene, while conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat causes oxidation to butan-2-one.
Both reagent sets give exactly the same product, butan-2-one, since butan-2-ol has only one possible reaction pathway regardless of reagent choice.
Neither reagent set reacts with a secondary alcohol like butan-2-ol; both require a primary alcohol substrate.

With acidified KMnO<sub>4</sub>/K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub> (oxidation), butan-2-ol gives butan-2-one; with conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat (dehydration), the same alcohol instead gives but-2-ene (major, by Zaitsev's rule).
questions.explanation: The very same molecule, butan-2-ol, can be steered toward a ketone (via oxidation) or an alkene (via dehydration) purely by the choice of reagent — illustrating that reagent identity, not just substrate structure, determines the product class.
questions.hint: One reagent set oxidises; the other dehydrates — these are structurally different reaction classes giving different product classes.
distractor_logic: Swaps which reagent performs which reaction; strong oxidants oxidise, while acid/heat dehydrates, not the reverse.
Denies that dehydration (elimination) and oxidation are fundamentally different reaction types giving structurally different product classes (alkene vs ketone).
Factually wrong; both oxidation and acid-catalysed dehydration proceed readily on secondary alcohols like butan-2-ol.

questions.question: Fischer esterification of (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH with acetic acid/H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> gives a poor yield, with elimination as a major side-product. What explains this, and what practical remedy addresses it?
options: Tertiary alcohols readily form stable tertiary carbocations under the acidic conditions, which are prone to E1 elimination (giving an alkene) as a competing side-reaction; using the corresponding acid chloride or anhydride instead (avoiding strongly acidic, carbocation-forming conditions) gives a better-yielding route to the ester.
Tertiary alcohols cannot form esters under any conditions whatsoever, so switching reagents would not help at all.
Switching to a stronger, more concentrated H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> catalyst and higher temperature would fix the poor yield by driving the esterification equilibrium further forward.
The poor yield is unrelated to the alcohol's class; it is caused purely by acetic acid being too weak an acid to esterify any alcohol efficiently, regardless of class.
questions.explanation: The strongly acidic Fischer conditions readily generate the stable tertiary carbocation from (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–OH, which competes by losing a proton (E1) to give 2-methylpropene instead of reacting with acetic acid; the acid chloride/anhydride route avoids strong-acid, carbocation-prone conditions and esterifies more directly.
questions.hint: Think about what a strongly acidic environment does to a tertiary alcohol, quite apart from the intended esterification.
distractor_logic: Factually wrong; tertiary alcohols can be esterified, particularly via the milder acid chloride/anhydride route that avoids the competing elimination pathway.
Actually worsens the problem, since stronger acid and higher temperature further favour carbocation formation and E1 elimination, not the desired substitution/esterification.
Ignores the well-known class-dependent elimination side-reaction and misattributes the problem to acid strength rather than to carbocation-driven elimination specific to tertiary substrates.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: How do the temperature/stoichiometry conditions differ for acid-catalysed intermolecular dehydration of two ethanol molecules (to diethyl ether) versus intramolecular dehydration of one ethanol molecule (to ethene)?
options: Lower temperature (≈413 K) with excess alcohol favours the intermolecular (substitution-type) pathway giving the ether; higher temperature (≈443 K) favours the intramolecular elimination (E1) pathway giving the alkene.
Ether formation and alkene formation are entirely unrelated processes that cannot both arise from the same alcohol and acid catalyst combination.
Both pathways require identical temperature and alcohol concentration conditions, with the outcome depending only on random chance.
Higher temperature favours ether formation, while lower temperature favours alkene formation.
questions.explanation: With excess ethanol at the lower characteristic temperature, one alcohol molecule's oxygen attacks another (protonated) alcohol molecule to give the ether; at the higher temperature, the protonated alcohol instead loses water to form a carbocation that eliminates a proton, giving the alkene.
questions.hint: One of the two characteristic ethanol/H2SO4 temperatures favours a substitution-type (two-molecule) pathway; the other favours a one-molecule elimination pathway.
distractor_logic: Incorrect; both pathways are well-documented outcomes of treating ethanol with conc. H2SO4, differing mainly in the temperature and stoichiometry applied.
Denies the well-established, practically exploited temperature-dependence that differentiates ether formation from alkene formation with ethanol and H2SO4.
Reverses the actual temperature dependence; elimination (alkene) is favoured by the higher temperature, while substitution (ether) is favoured by the milder, lower temperature.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Why is methanol poisoning dangerous, and how does this connect to the oxidation chemistry seen for other primary alcohols?
options: Methanol is toxic because it dehydrates in the body to give formaldehyde gas directly, without any oxidation step being involved.

Alcohol dehydrogenase in the body oxidises methanol stepwise — first to formaldehyde (like a 1° alcohol being oxidised to an aldehyde), then further to formic acid (like the aldehyde-to-acid step) — and it is this formic acid/formaldehyde buildup, not methanol itself, that causes the characteristic toxicity, including optic nerve damage and blindness.
Methanol poisoning has nothing to do with its oxidation chemistry; toxicity results purely from methanol's very high volatility causing suffocation.
Methanol is metabolised by reduction, not oxidation, ultimately being converted to methane gas, which is the toxic species responsible for methanol poisoning.
questions.explanation: Methanol's metabolic pathway mirrors ordinary primary-alcohol oxidation chemistry (alcohol → aldehyde → acid), but here the intermediates themselves (formaldehyde, then formic acid) are what cause the severe toxicity, notably damage to the optic nerve leading to blindness.
questions.hint: Think of methanol's metabolism as the same alcohol-to-aldehyde-to-acid oxidation sequence seen elsewhere in this chapter, just happening inside the body.
distractor_logic: Misattributes the toxic pathway to dehydration/elimination chemistry rather than to the actual, well-documented sequential oxidation pathway.
Ignores the well-established metabolic oxidation pathway (to formaldehyde, then formic acid) that is the actual, medically recognised cause of methanol toxicity.
Misapplies a reduction pathway and invents methane as a toxic metabolite; the actual, medically established pathway is oxidative, producing formaldehyde and then formic acid.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: An unlabeled sample could be 1-butanol, 2-butanol, or 2-methylpropan-2-ol. The Lucas test turns cloudy within 2–5 minutes at room temperature. Which identification is correct, and how does it connect to the broader SN1 reactivity trend in alcohol chemistry?
options: The sample is 2-butanol (secondary); a 2–5 minute turbidity time is the characteristic intermediate rate for secondary alcohols, consistent with the general SN1 reactivity trend (3°>2°>1°) seen throughout alcohol chemistry, including acid-catalysed dehydration.
The 2–5 minute timing is inconclusive and could equally indicate any of the three alcohols, since the Lucas test does not reliably distinguish between them.
The sample is 2-methylpropan-2-ol (tertiary), since tertiary alcohols are known to react over several minutes rather than immediately.
The sample is 1-butanol, since primary alcohols are expected to show turbidity within a similarly short window at room temperature.
questions.explanation: The characteristic Lucas-test timings are: tertiary (immediate), secondary (a few minutes at room temperature, or on gentle warming), primary (slow, needing heat, or effectively no reaction at room temperature) — the 2–5 minute window given here matches a secondary alcohol.
questions.hint: Match the given timing window to the three characteristic Lucas-test speeds: instant, a few minutes, or slow/needs-heat.
distractor_logic: Denies the well-established, reliably distinct timing windows that make the Lucas test a genuinely useful classification tool.
Misassigns the tertiary alcohol's characteristic (immediate, essentially instant) timing to the intermediate window that actually belongs to secondary alcohols.
Misassigns the primary alcohol's characteristic (very slow, requiring heating) timing to the intermediate window that actually belongs to secondary alcohols.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols with Metals and Hydrogen Halides
questions.question: Reactivity toward Na metal follows 1°>2°>3°, while reactivity toward HX/Lucas reagent follows 3°>2°>1° — the exact opposite order for the same three alcohol classes. Why is this not a contradiction?
options: Reactivity with Na metal actually depends on carbocation stability just like the Lucas test, since Na reacts by first ionising the alcohol to a carbocation before losing a hydrogen.

Reactivity with Na depends on how accessible/acidic the O–H hydrogen is (favoured by less steric hindrance and less alkyl electron-donation, i.e. 1°>2°>3°); reactivity with HX/Lucas reagent depends on carbocation stability at carbon (favoured by more alkyl substitution, i.e. 3°>2°>1°) — these probe fundamentally different bonds/mechanisms, so opposite trends are entirely consistent.
The trends run opposite because Na metal and HX are chemically identical in how they interact with alcohols, so any observed difference must be experimental error.
The two trends actually agree (both are 3°>2°>1°), so there is no real opposite-direction relationship to explain.
questions.explanation: These are two different bonds reacting by two different mechanisms: Na/alcohol reactivity is about O–H bond acidity/accessibility (deprotonation, no carbocation involved), while HX/Lucas reactivity is about C–O bond ionisation to a carbocation (SN1) — there is no reason these two, mechanistically unrelated, trends should run the same direction.
questions.hint: Identify which bond is actually being broken in each reaction (O-H versus C-O), and what factor controls the rate for each.
distractor_logic: Misdescribes the Na/alcohol mechanism, which involves loss of H directly from O-H (releasing H2 gas) without any carbocation intermediate, unlike the SN1 pathway relevant to Lucas/HX reactions.
Denies that these are fundamentally different reaction types (deprotonation at O-H versus substitution at C-O), which is exactly why their trends differ.
Misstates the well-established Na-metal reactivity order, which is in fact 1°>2°>3°, opposite to the Lucas/HX trend given in the question.

questions.question: Why is SOCl<sub>2</sub> often preferred over PCl<sub>5</sub> for converting an alcohol to an alkyl chloride, and how does this parallel the reasoning behind choosing PCC over strong oxidants for alcohol oxidation?
options: SOCl<sub>2</sub> and PCl<sub>5</sub> give chemically identical byproducts in every respect, so there is no meaningful practical difference between the two reagents.

SOCl<sub>2</sub> gives only gaseous byproducts (SO<sub>2</sub> and HCl), which escape on their own, leaving a clean product with minimal purification; PCl<sub>5</sub> gives POCl<sub>3</sub> (a liquid) alongside HCl, complicating separation — paralleling how PCC is chosen for the practical benefit of stopping cleanly at one stage, illustrating that reagent choice is often driven by ease of product isolation, not just by whether the core transformation is achievable.
PCl<sub>5</sub> is actually preferred over SOCl<sub>2</sub> in essentially all cases because it reacts faster, and reaction rate is always the dominant consideration in reagent selection.
The comparison to PCC is invalid, since oxidation reagent selection and halogenation reagent selection are governed by completely unrelated principles with no shared logic.
questions.explanation: Both cases illustrate the same broader synthetic theme: a reagent is often chosen not only for whether it can perform the core transformation, but for how easily the desired product can be isolated afterward — SOCl<sub>2</sub>'s fully gaseous byproducts (like PCC's clean, aldehyde-stopping selectivity) make downstream purification far simpler.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to each reagent's byproducts after the reaction, and how that affects how easily you can isolate the product you actually want.
distractor_logic: Incorrect; SOCl2's byproducts (SO2, HCl, both gases) differ meaningfully from PCl5's byproducts (POCl3, a liquid, plus HCl) in ease of removal from the reaction mixture.
Overstates reaction rate as the sole/dominant criterion, ignoring the well-established practical purification advantage of SOCl2's gaseous byproducts, the actual basis for its common preference.
Misses the genuine parallel; both cases illustrate the same broader synthetic principle of choosing a reagent partly for how cleanly the desired product can be isolated afterward.

questions.question: A phenol and a simple alcohol are both treated with Na metal. How do their reactivities compare, and how does this connect to their difference in O–H acidity?
options: Both react with Na to liberate H<sub>2</sub> gas (giving sodium phenoxide or sodium alkoxide respectively), since both have an O–H bond; but because phenol is considerably more acidic than a typical alcohol (due to resonance-stabilised phenoxide formation), phenol reacts somewhat more readily with Na than most alcohols do.
Only alcohols react with Na metal; phenols do not react with Na at all, since their O–H bond is 'aromatic' and behaves completely differently.
Phenol reacts with Na metal much less readily than alcohols do, since resonance delocalisation into the ring makes phenol's O–H bond harder to break, not easier.
Both react with Na metal at identical rates, since acidity differences between phenol and alcohols are too small to have any measurable effect.
questions.explanation: Both possess a genuine O–H bond and react with active metals like Na to release H<sub>2</sub>; phenol's greater acidity (from resonance-stabilised phenoxide formation) means its O–H bond is more easily broken, so it reacts somewhat more readily with Na than a comparable simple alcohol.
questions.hint: Both compounds have an O-H bond and react the same basic way with Na — the question is only about how readily, given their differing acidity.
distractor_logic: Factually wrong; phenol's O-H bond, though more acidic, is still a genuine O-H bond that reacts with active metals like Na, releasing H2 gas, just as alcohols do.
Reverses the actual relationship; resonance stabilisation of the resulting phenoxide ion makes phenol's O-H bond easier, not harder, to break.
Understates the real, exam-relevant acidity difference between phenol and alcohols, which does translate into a difference in reactivity with active metals like Na.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: A mixture contains phenol, benzoic acid, and cyclohexanol. Which extraction sequence (aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, then aqueous NaOH) correctly separates all three, and what does this reveal about their relative acidities?
options: NaOH is used first to extract only cyclohexanol, since alcohols are the most acidic of the three and react preferentially with the weaker base.
NaHCO<sub>3</sub> extracts both benzoic acid and phenol together in the first step, since both are 'acidic' compounds and NaHCO3 is a general-purpose base for all acids.

NaHCO<sub>3</sub> first extracts only benzoic acid (as water-soluble sodium benzoate), since NaHCO<sub>3</sub> is weak enough to deprotonate a carboxylic acid but not phenol; the remaining organic layer is then shaken with NaOH, extracting phenol (as sodium phenoxide) but leaving cyclohexanol (non-acidic) behind — reflecting benzoic acid > phenol > cyclohexanol in acidity.
All three compounds are extracted together by aqueous NaOH in a single step, since NaOH is a strong enough base to deprotonate any organic compound present.
questions.explanation: This sequential extraction exploits a real acidity ladder: benzoic acid (pKa ≈4) is deprotonated even by the weak base NaHCO<sub>3</sub>; phenol (pKa ≈10) needs the stronger NaOH; cyclohexanol (pKa ≈16–18) is not meaningfully deprotonated by either under these mild conditions and stays in the organic layer throughout.
questions.hint: Match each base's strength to which of the three compounds it's actually strong enough to deprotonate.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly identifies cyclohexanol (a non-acidic alcohol under these conditions) as the most acidic component, when it is actually the least acidic and does not get extracted by either aqueous base.
Overlooks that NaHCO3 is a sufficiently weak base to distinguish a genuinely strong-enough acid (benzoic acid) from a much weaker one (phenol), extracting only the former.
Overstates NaOH's reach; cyclohexanol is not acidic enough to be meaningfully deprotonated and extracted by aqueous NaOH under these mild conditions.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Does an ortho/para-directing, ring-activating substituent (like –OCH<sub>3</sub>) also tend to increase phenol's acidity when present on the ring, given that it also activates the ring toward electrophilic substitution?
options: Ring-activating groups have no relationship to acidity at all, since electrophilic substitution and acid-base chemistry are entirely separate topics with no shared electronic basis.
Yes — any ortho/para-directing group by definition also increases phenol's acidity, since both properties come from the same resonance donation.

No — activating, ortho/para-directing groups like –OCH<sub>3</sub> are net electron-donating into the ring, which is exactly the property that activates the ring toward electrophiles AND destabilises the phenoxide's negative charge (opposing delocalisation), so such groups tend to DECREASE acidity even as they increase reactivity toward electrophiles.
–OCH<sub>3</sub> is actually deactivating (not activating) toward electrophilic substitution, so this comparison doesn't even apply to it as an example.
questions.explanation: Ring activation (favoured by electron-DONATING character) and phenoxide-ion stabilisation/acidity increase (favoured by electron-WITHDRAWING character) respond to opposite electronic properties of a substituent, so a strongly activating EDG like –OCH<sub>3</sub> in fact decreases acidity even while boosting reactivity toward electrophiles.
questions.hint: Ask which electronic character (donating or withdrawing) favours ring activation, and which favours phenoxide stabilisation — are they the same?
distractor_logic: Denies that both phenomena trace back to the same underlying resonance/inductive electronic effects of the substituent, even though they respond to those effects in opposite ways.
Incorrectly equates ring activation (favoured by EDGs) with phenoxide-ion stabilisation/acidity increase (favoured by EWGs), which are governed by opposite electronic character.
Factually wrong; -OCH3 is a strong ring activator and ortho/para director in electrophilic aromatic substitution, exactly because of its lone-pair resonance donation.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Place ethanol, phenol, and acetic acid on a rough acidity (pKa) scale, and explain the structural reason phenol sits where it does.
options: Ethanol (pKa ≈16) < phenol (pKa ≈10) < acetic acid (pKa ≈4.8) — phenoxide is resonance-stabilised (more than a simple alkoxide, since the ring absorbs some negative charge) but less so than acetate, where the charge is symmetrically delocalised over two equivalent oxygens, an even more effective stabilisation.
Ethanol is more acidic than phenol, since alkyl groups make the O–H bond in ethanol inherently weaker than the O–H bond in an aromatic phenol.
All three compounds are essentially equally acidic once dissolved in water, since water's levelling effect equalises the acid strength of all weak acids.

Phenol is the strongest acid of the three, stronger even than acetic acid, since aromatic ring delocalisation is inherently more stabilising than delocalisation over two oxygen atoms in a carboxylate.
questions.explanation: Carboxylate's two-oxygen resonance delocalisation is generally more effective at stabilising negative charge than a phenoxide's ring delocalisation, which in turn is far more effective than a simple alkoxide's lack of delocalisation — giving the intermediate acidity ladder ethanol < phenol < acetic acid, matching how each conjugate base's charge is spread out.
questions.hint: Compare how effectively each conjugate base's negative charge is delocalised: not at all, into a ring, or symmetrically over two oxygens.
distractor_logic: Reverses the well-established relative acidity of phenol versus a simple alcohol, driven by the phenoxide's resonance stabilisation that ethanol's alkoxide lacks.
Misapplies the levelling effect, which is relevant mainly for comparing acids stronger than the solvent's conjugate acid, not for distinguishing among these three weak acids.

Reverses the actual relative strength; carboxylate's two-oxygen delocalisation is generally more effective at stabilising negative charge than a phenoxide's ring delocalisation, making acetic acid the stronger acid of the two.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Phenol can be purified from a mixture with neutral anisole by extraction with aqueous NaOH followed by re-acidification. Does the same single-step NaOH extraction also separate phenol from benzoic acid?
options: Anisole (no acidic O–H at all) stays in the organic layer while phenol converts to water-soluble sodium phenoxide, so that separation works; but a single NaOH extraction does NOT separate phenol from benzoic acid, since both are acidic enough to be deprotonated by NaOH and both end up together in the aqueous layer — a weaker base like NaHCO<sub>3</sub> would be needed first to selectively remove only benzoic acid.
Re-acidification after the NaOH extraction step is unnecessary and serves no purpose, since sodium phenoxide is already the desired final product.
Phenol cannot be separated from anisole by any acid-base extraction technique, since both are 'ether-like' oxygen-containing aromatic compounds with essentially identical acidity.
A single NaOH extraction cleanly separates all three compounds (anisole, phenol, benzoic acid) simultaneously into three distinct layers.
questions.explanation: NaOH is strong enough to deprotonate both phenol and benzoic acid, so a single NaOH extraction would pull both into the aqueous layer together; distinguishing phenol from benzoic acid specifically requires a weaker base (NaHCO<sub>3</sub>) that is strong enough for the carboxylic acid but not for phenol.
questions.hint: Check whether NaOH is selective enough to tell phenol and benzoic acid apart, given that both are genuinely acidic.
distractor_logic: Misses the actual point of the extraction technique, which specifically aims to recover the neutral phenol itself (via re-acidification) after purification, not to isolate the phenoxide salt as a final product.
Incorrectly treats phenol (which has an acidic O-H) as chemically equivalent to anisole (which has no O-H at all, only an ether linkage), when they are fundamentally different in acidity.
Overstates what a single-step, single-base extraction can achieve; NaOH deprotonates both phenol and benzoic acid, putting them in the same aqueous layer together, not in separate layers.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Kolbe's reaction on phenol gives salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid). How does the newly installed ortho –COOH group affect the acidity of the phenolic –OH compared to plain phenol?
options: Salicylic acid has no ortho relationship between its two functional groups at all; –COOH and –OH end up meta to each other as the actual major product of Kolbe's reaction.

The ortho –COOH group is a strong electron-withdrawing group that increases the acidity of the adjacent phenolic –OH (compared to plain phenol) via both induction and resonance withdrawal; the ortho relationship also allows intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the two groups, a distinctive feature of salicylic acid's structure.
The –COOH group has no effect whatsoever on the phenolic –OH's acidity, since the two groups react completely independently of one another on the same ring.

The –COOH group actually decreases the phenolic –OH's acidity, since carboxylic acids are generally considered 'ring-deactivating', and this always correlates with decreasing acidity of other ring substituents too.
questions.explanation: –COOH is a strong electron-withdrawing group; positioned ortho to the phenolic –OH (as Kolbe's reaction reliably gives), it increases that –OH's acidity through both induction and resonance, and the close ortho proximity also permits an intramolecular hydrogen bond, a hallmark of salicylic acid's structure.
questions.hint: An electron-withdrawing group ortho to -OH should have a familiar effect on that -OH's acidity — think back to how substituents affect phenol acidity generally.
distractor_logic: Contradicts the well-established ortho-selectivity of Kolbe's reaction, which is precisely why salicylic acid (not a meta isomer) is the characteristic product.
Denies the well-established substituent effect that any electron-withdrawing group (like -COOH) exerts on other acidic/basic groups on the same ring, especially at a nearby (ortho) position.

Incorrectly assumes that 'ring-deactivating' (relevant to electrophilic substitution reactivity) always means 'decreases acidity of other groups'; -COOH, despite deactivating the ring toward electrophiles, still increases the acidity of a nearby -OH group via the same electron-withdrawing character.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Why does controlled, low-temperature bromination of phenol (CS<sub>2</sub> solvent, limited Br<sub>2</sub>) give predominantly p-bromophenol, while excess bromine water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol?
options: CS<sub>2</sub> is used specifically because it is a strong Lewis acid catalyst needed to activate Br<sub>2</sub> toward phenol, analogous to FeBr<sub>3</sub>'s role with benzene.
The solvent and temperature have no real effect on the outcome; the same product (2,4,6-tribromophenol) forms under both sets of conditions regardless of Br<sub>2</sub> stoichiometry.
Excess bromine water actually gives predominantly ortho-monobromination (o-bromophenol) rather than the tribromo product, since ortho is always the kinetically preferred single site of attack.

With excess Br<sub>2</sub> in water, phenol's strongly activated ring undergoes exhaustive substitution at all three available ortho/para positions, giving the tribromo product; with a non-polar solvent (CS<sub>2</sub>) at low temperature and limited (stoichiometric) Br<sub>2</sub>, the reaction is slowed and limited to a single substitution, with sterics/statistics favouring the less-crowded para position over the two ortho positions.
questions.explanation: Both the amount of Br<sub>2</sub> available and the reaction medium control the outcome: excess Br<sub>2</sub> in an activating aqueous medium drives substitution at all three activated positions, while limited Br<sub>2</sub> in a non-polar solvent at low temperature restricts the reaction to a single, sterically-favoured (para) substitution.
questions.hint: Think about two separate variables at play here: how much Br2 is available, and what kind of solvent/temperature is used.
distractor_logic: Misidentifies CS2's role; phenol's ring is already activated and does not need a Lewis acid catalyst for bromination (unlike benzene), and CS2 functions here as a comparatively non-polar solvent, not a catalyst.
Denies the well-documented, practically useful ability to control mono- versus poly-substitution by adjusting solvent, temperature, and Br2 equivalents.
Understates that with excess Br2 in an activating (aqueous) medium, phenol's ring is activated enough to react at all three available ortho/para positions, not stop after a single ortho substitution.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: What is the correct IUPAC name of the major monobromination product of phenol under controlled, low-temperature, non-aqueous conditions?
options: 2,6-Dibromophenol — describes a disubstitution product (both ortho positions), not the intended monobromination product.
2-Bromophenol — ortho substitution is a real minor pathway, but not the major product under these sterically-influenced controlled conditions.
4-Bromophenol — controlled bromination favours the less sterically hindered para position over the two (more crowded) ortho positions; numbering with –OH at C1 places bromine at C4.
3-Bromophenol — places bromine at the meta position, essentially never the major outcome for a strong ortho/para director like –OH.
questions.explanation: Under controlled, limited-bromine conditions, the sterically less hindered para position is favoured over the more crowded ortho positions for the single substitution; in phenol's own numbering (–OH always C1), this bromine sits at C4, giving 4-bromophenol.
questions.hint: Between the two positions –OH directs to, one is less sterically crowded under these controlled, single-substitution conditions.
distractor_logic: Describes a disubstitution product (both ortho positions), not the intended monobromination product asked about under these controlled, limited-bromine conditions.

While ortho substitution is a real, understood minor pathway here, it is not the major product under these controlled, sterically-influenced conditions, which favour the less hindered para position instead.

Misassigns the product to the meta position, when -OH is a strong ortho/para director and would essentially never give a meta-substituted product as the major outcome of simple electrophilic bromination.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: A synthesis plan makes aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) starting from phenol. Which correctly sequences the two key steps involved?
options: Step 1: bromination of phenol with excess Br<sub>2</sub> water gives 2,4,6-tribromophenol; Step 2: substitution of all three bromines with acetate groups gives aspirin.
Step 1: Reimer-Tiemann reaction (phenol + CHCl<sub>3</sub>/NaOH) gives salicylaldehyde directly; Step 2: simple hydration of the aldehyde group gives aspirin directly.
Step 1: direct nitration of phenol with dilute HNO<sub>3</sub> gives a nitrophenol intermediate; Step 2: reduction of the nitro group gives aspirin.

Step 1: Kolbe's reaction (phenol + NaOH, then CO<sub>2</sub> under heat/pressure, then acidify) gives salicylic acid; Step 2: esterification (acetylation) of salicylic acid's phenolic –OH with acetic anhydride gives acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin).
questions.explanation: Kolbe's reaction is the step that installs the ortho –COOH group needed (giving salicylic acid); esterifying its phenolic –OH with acetic anhydride then gives acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) — two well-known, correctly sequenced named reactions.
questions.hint: Aspirin needs both a –COOH group (from one named reaction) and an ester linkage on the phenolic –OH (from a separate esterification step) — which reaction installs the acid group?
distractor_logic: Describes a chemically implausible and unrelated sequence that does not correspond to any real synthetic route to aspirin.
Misidentifies both the correct first reaction (Kolbe's, not Reimer-Tiemann, is needed to install the -COOH group aspirin requires) and invents an implausible 'hydration of an aldehyde' final step.
Describes an entirely unrelated sequence (nitration/reduction) that does not install the carboxylic acid or ester functionality aspirin actually requires.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: A tertiary alkyl halide is an excellent substrate for fast carbocation-based reactions like the Lucas test or acid-catalysed dehydration, yet a poor substrate for Williamson ether synthesis. Why does the same structural feature help in one case and hurt in the other?
options: The same feature — a stable, easily-formed carbocation — is exactly what makes tertiary substrates fast via SN1/E1 (as in the Lucas test or dehydration), but is also exactly what makes them prone to E2 elimination instead of the SN2 substitution Williamson synthesis specifically requires when reacted with a strong, bulky alkoxide base.

Tertiary alkyl halides are actually excellent substrates for Williamson synthesis too, for exactly the same carbocation-related reason they excel in the Lucas test, so there is no real trade-off here.
There is no real connection between these reactions; carbocation stability is relevant only to Lucas test/dehydration chemistry and has no bearing on Williamson synthesis outcomes at all.
Williamson synthesis actually works via the same SN1 mechanism as the Lucas test and dehydration reactions, so tertiary substrates should behave identically well in all three reactions.
questions.explanation: Carbocation-forming ability is an asset when the desired reaction is itself SN1/E1-based (Lucas test, dehydration), but a liability when the desired reaction specifically needs SN2 (Williamson synthesis) — the very feature that speeds one reaction type promotes an unwanted competing pathway in the other.
questions.hint: Ask which mechanism each named reaction actually needs (SN1/E1 versus SN2), then see which mechanism a tertiary substrate naturally favours.
distractor_logic: Incorrect; Williamson synthesis specifically needs SN2 (not SN1/E1), so the same carbocation-forming tendency that helps in Lucas/dehydration chemistry actively hurts (favours elimination over the desired substitution) in Williamson synthesis.
Denies that carbocation-forming tendency (favouring E2/SN1 over SN2) is precisely why tertiary alkyl halides perform poorly in Williamson synthesis specifically.
Misidentifies Williamson synthesis's mechanism, which specifically requires SN2 (backside attack by the alkoxide nucleophile), not SN1, unlike the Lucas test/dehydration.

questions.question: Anisole is cleaved by excess HI to give phenol + methyl iodide. If this mixture is then treated with aqueous NaOH, which component(s) are extracted into the aqueous layer, and why?
options: Both phenol and methyl iodide are extracted into the aqueous layer together, since NaOH is a strong base capable of reacting with any organic compound present.

Only phenol is extracted, as water-soluble sodium phenoxide, since phenol is acidic enough to be deprotonated by NaOH; methyl iodide is a neutral alkyl halide with no acidic proton and stays in the organic layer.
Neither component is extracted, since phenol formed from ether cleavage is somehow less acidic than ordinary phenol prepared by other routes.
Only methyl iodide is extracted into the aqueous layer, since alkyl iodides are generally more water-soluble than phenols.
questions.explanation: This is a simple acid-base extraction: phenol's acidic O–H reacts with NaOH to form water-soluble sodium phenoxide, while neutral methyl iodide (no acidic proton) is unaffected and remains in the organic layer.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two cleavage products actually has an acidic proton for NaOH to react with.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes NaOH reacts with methyl iodide under these conditions in a way that would move it into the aqueous layer; simple NaOH extraction is an acid-base process, and methyl iodide has no acidic proton to react with NaOH this way.
Incorrectly assumes phenol's acidity depends on its synthetic origin; phenol is phenol, regardless of how it was made, and reacts with NaOH the same way every time.

Reverses the actual solubility/reactivity behaviour; methyl iodide is a nonpolar, water-insoluble alkyl halide, while phenol becomes water-soluble specifically upon conversion to its ionic sodium phenoxide salt.

questions.question: A synthesis target is anisole, C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>. Which Williamson synthesis reagent pairing is correct, and why does the swapped combination fail?
options: Both combinations work equally well, since Williamson synthesis simply requires 'a halide and an alkoxide' in any pairing, with no restriction on which partner carries the aryl group.
Neither combination can give anisole; this compound can only be made by O-methylation of phenol using a completely different reagent (dimethyl sulfate), never via classic Williamson synthesis.
Bromobenzene + sodium methoxide is actually the correct (and preferred) combination, since aryl halides are generally more reactive than alkyl halides toward nucleophilic substitution.

Sodium phenoxide (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>ONa) + methyl iodide (CH<sub>3</sub>I) is correct, since the alkyl halide component undergoes the required SN2 attack while the aryl group is supplied as the nucleophile; the swapped combination, bromobenzene (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>Br) + sodium methoxide, would fail because aryl halides do not undergo SN2 substitution at all.
questions.explanation: Williamson synthesis requires the halide component specifically to be SN2-capable; an aryl halide never is, regardless of which nucleophile it's paired with, so the aryl group must instead be supplied as the (already-formed) phenoxide nucleophile, with the alkyl halide (here, methyl iodide) as the electrophile.
questions.hint: Only one of the two groups (aryl or alkyl) can serve as the halide component here — which one is actually capable of SN2?
distractor_logic: Overlooks the fundamental mechanistic requirement that the halide component specifically must be capable of SN2 substitution, which rules out aryl halides regardless of the nucleophile paired with them.
Incorrectly denies that Williamson synthesis (sodium phenoxide + methyl iodide) is in fact a standard, valid method for preparing anisole and similar aryl alkyl ethers.
Reverses the well-established relative reactivity of aryl versus alkyl halides toward SN2 substitution; aryl halides are essentially unreactive via this mechanism, not more reactive.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Ether formation and alkene formation both compete for the same ethanol/conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub> starting material. How does temperature decide which one wins?
options: The two reactions never actually compete in practice, since industrial ether production and industrial alkene production always use two chemically distinct alcohols, never ethanol for both.
Ether formation and alkene formation proceed through completely unrelated, non-competing intermediates, so describing them as 'competing' reactions for the same alcohol is fundamentally incorrect.
Alkene formation is favoured at lower temperature, while ether formation is favoured at higher temperature.

Both reactions start from the same protonated ethanol intermediate; at the lower characteristic temperature (≈413 K) with excess ethanol, a second ethanol molecule's oxygen preferentially attacks that protonated species (intermolecular substitution) to give the ether; at the higher characteristic temperature (≈443 K), the protonated ethanol instead loses water to form a carbocation that undergoes elimination, giving the alkene.
questions.explanation: Both pathways share the same protonated-alcohol starting point; which one dominates depends on temperature and alcohol excess — substitution (ether) at the lower temperature with excess alcohol, elimination (alkene) at the higher temperature.
questions.hint: Both reactions begin from the very same intermediate — a protonated ethanol molecule — before branching one of two ways.
distractor_logic: Factually wrong; ethanol with conc. H2SO4 is the classic textbook example precisely because it demonstrates this same-substrate competition between the two pathways based on temperature.
Denies the well-established shared-intermediate (protonated alcohol) mechanistic picture that makes these two pathways genuine competitors under the same reaction conditions.
Reverses the well-documented temperature dependence; elimination (alkene) is favoured at the higher of the two characteristic temperatures, substitution (ether) at the lower.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Why is salicylic acid, rather than plain phenol or plain benzoic acid, the useful intermediate for making aspirin?
options: Plain phenol alone is actually sufficient to make aspirin directly, without needing any Kolbe's-reaction-derived intermediate like salicylic acid at all.

Salicylic acid uniquely combines a phenolic –OH (needed for the later acetylation/esterification step) AND an ortho –COOH group (part of aspirin's final structure) on the same molecule; plain phenol lacks –COOH entirely, and plain benzoic acid lacks the phenolic –OH needed for esterification, so neither alone can serve as the direct precursor the way salicylic acid (obtainable via Kolbe's reaction) can.
Salicylic acid is chosen for aspirin production for reasons entirely unrelated to its actual functional groups, based purely on historical/traditional pharmaceutical convention.
Plain benzoic acid alone is actually sufficient to make aspirin directly, without needing the phenolic –OH that salicylic acid provides.
questions.explanation: Aspirin's structure requires both a carboxylic acid group and an acetate ester on a phenolic oxygen; only salicylic acid, with its ortho –COOH and phenolic –OH together (installed by Kolbe's reaction), provides both starting points on one molecule.
questions.hint: Check which functional groups aspirin's final structure actually needs, and whether phenol or benzoic acid alone could supply both.
distractor_logic: Overlooks that aspirin's structure specifically requires the -COOH group that only Kolbe's reaction (not plain phenol) installs.
Denies the genuine structural/mechanistic reason (possessing both necessary functional groups) that makes salicylic acid the correct, chemically necessary intermediate.
Overlooks that aspirin's synthesis specifically requires esterifying a phenolic -OH group, which plain benzoic acid (lacking any -OH on the ring) does not have.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Why is acid-base extraction (into aqueous NaOH, then re-acidification) industrially valuable for purifying phenol from the crude cumene-process product mixture?
options: The crude mixture contains phenol alongside acetone and other organic material; because phenol alone (among these) is acidic enough to be selectively extracted into aqueous base as water-soluble sodium phenoxide, this extraction step efficiently separates and purifies phenol before final re-acidification and distillation.

This technique would be equally effective at separating phenol from acetone even if acetone itself were also somewhat acidic, since NaOH extraction doesn't depend on any real acidity difference between the components.
Acetone, not phenol, is the component selectively extracted by aqueous NaOH in this approach, since acetone is described as the more reactive of the two cumene-process products.

This purification technique is never actually used industrially for the cumene process; industrial phenol is purified exclusively by simple fractional distillation, with no acid-base extraction step involved at all.
questions.explanation: Phenol's genuine acidity makes it selectively extractable from a mixture containing non-acidic components like acetone; this acid-base separation is a chemically sound purification step exploiting exactly the same acidity property discussed elsewhere for phenol.
questions.hint: Ask which of the crude mixture's components actually has an acidic proton for NaOH to react with.
distractor_logic: Misunderstands that this technique's entire effectiveness specifically depends on there being a genuine, exploitable acidity difference between the components being separated.
Misidentifies which of the two products would actually be extracted by this specific acid-base technique; acetone has no acidic O-H proton to react with NaOH in this manner.

Overstates the exclusivity of a single purification method, when acid-base extraction (exploiting phenol's genuine acidity) is a real, chemically sound technique broadly applicable to any crude mixture containing phenol alongside non-acidic organic compounds.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Cumene-process phenol is to be converted into anisole. Which sequence correctly applies Williamson synthesis, and what additional reagent is needed?
options: Phenol itself (without first converting it to sodium phenoxide) would react efficiently and directly with methyl iodide to give anisole under simple mixing at room temperature, with no base required.
Anisole formation from phenol would instead require Reimer-Tiemann reaction conditions (CHCl<sub>3</sub>/NaOH), not Williamson synthesis at all, since both reactions use NaOH as a shared reagent.
Anisole can be made directly from cumene-process phenol with no additional reagents at all, since the cumene process's own acetone byproduct can itself serve as the required methylating agent.

Convert phenol to sodium phenoxide (with NaOH), then react with methyl iodide (CH<sub>3</sub>I, an additional reagent not produced by the cumene process itself) via Williamson synthesis to give anisole (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>) + NaI.
questions.explanation: Following the standard Williamson approach, phenol is first deprotonated to the more nucleophilic phenoxide ion, which then displaces iodide from methyl iodide (a reagent that must be sourced separately, not from the cumene process) to give anisole.
questions.hint: Williamson synthesis always needs the alkoxide/phenoxide form, not the neutral alcohol/phenol, reacting with a genuine alkyl halide.
distractor_logic: Overlooks that neutral phenol is too weak a nucleophile for efficient Williamson-type SN2 substitution; deprotonation to the phenoxide ion is needed first, exactly as with any other Williamson synthesis.

Incorrectly conflates two entirely different named reactions (Reimer-Tiemann installs -CHO via a carbene; Williamson synthesis installs an ether via SN2 with an alkyl halide) simply because both happen to use NaOH.
Incorrectly claims acetone (a ketone, not an alkylating agent) can serve as the alkyl halide component of Williamson synthesis, which specifically requires an actual alkyl halide like methyl iodide.

questions.topic: Industrial Preparation (Cumene Process) and Distinguishing Tests/Uses
questions.question: Among phenol, p-cresol, and 4-nitrophenol, which would be extracted from a neutral hydrocarbon solvent using the WEAKEST possible base, and why is this kind of acidity-based selectivity industrially useful?
options: All three phenol derivatives would require exactly the same base strength for extraction, since they share the same core phenolic –OH functional group regardless of ring substituents.

4-Nitrophenol, being the most acidic of the three (strongly electron-withdrawing, resonance-conjugated –NO<sub>2</sub> at para), would be extractable with the mildest base; this acidity-based selectivity is industrially useful for separating specific phenolic compounds from complex mixtures without needing harsh, strongly basic conditions that might degrade other sensitive components.
p-Cresol would be extracted most readily, since methyl-substituted phenols are generally considered the 'most reactive' phenols in industrial separations.
Phenol itself (unsubstituted) would be extracted most readily, since it is the simplest structure of the three and therefore reacts fastest with any base.
questions.explanation: 4-Nitrophenol's strongly electron-withdrawing, resonance-conjugated –NO<sub>2</sub> group makes it considerably more acidic than phenol or p-cresol, so it can be selectively extracted using a weaker base — a useful, mild-condition separation strategy in practice.
questions.hint: Rank the three by substituent electronic effect on acidity first, then ask which one needs the least basic conditions to be deprotonated.
distractor_logic: Ignores the well-established substituent-dependent acidity differences that make some phenols extractable with weaker bases than others.

Incorrectly treats methyl substitution (an electron-donating group that actually DECREASES acidity relative to phenol) as increasing ease of base-extraction, when it should require a STRONGER base than plain phenol, not a weaker one.
Misapplies 'simplest structure' as if it correlated with fastest reaction, when the actual determining factor is each specific substituent's electronic effect on acidity.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: A 2° alcohol's acid-catalysed dehydration produces a carbocation flanked by two different types of β-hydrogens. Which product predominates, and can rearrangement ever complicate even this simple secondary case?
options: Only the less-substituted (Hofmann-type) alkene ever forms from acid-catalysed E1 dehydration, since Zaitsev's rule applies only to base-mediated E2 eliminations.
The less stable carbocation intermediate is always more reactive, so its elimination products always dominate over any more-stable rearranged carbocation's products.

The more substituted (Zaitsev) alkene predominates from direct elimination; additionally, if a hydride/alkyl shift to an adjacent carbon could generate an even more stable (e.g. tertiary-capable) carbocation, that rearranged pathway can compete and give an unexpected alkene, not just the two 'obvious' ones from the original secondary cation.
Hydride shifts are impossible once a carbocation has already formed from a secondary alcohol; only the original two elimination pathways are ever possible.
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule applies to E1 (acid-catalysed) dehydration just as it does elsewhere, favouring the more substituted alkene; but if a 1,2-hydride or alkyl shift can reach an even more stable carbocation from the initially-formed secondary one, that rearranged pathway can compete and even dominate, giving a product not obviously predicted from the starting cation alone.
questions.hint: Don't stop at 'more substituted alkene wins' — check whether an even better carbocation is reachable by a shift first.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly restricts Zaitsev's rule to E2 only; Zaitsev's rule (more substituted alkene favoured) applies to E1 (acid-catalysed dehydration) as well.
Reverses the actual relationship; a MORE stable carbocation (original or rearranged) is generally the kinetically/thermodynamically favoured pathway, not a less stable one.
Denies the well-documented possibility of carbocation rearrangement via hydride/alkyl shifts whenever a more stable cation is accessible, even from an initially secondary carbocation.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Why is PCC in a non-aqueous solvent specifically chosen over aqueous strong-oxidant conditions when the aldehyde product itself would be prone to further oxidation or hydration in water?
options: PCC and aqueous strong oxidants give chemically identical outcomes in every case, with the choice between them being purely a matter of laboratory convenience.
Aqueous strong oxidants like hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> would actually give a better-yielding, purer aldehyde product than PCC, since more vigorous conditions always improve yield.

PCC's mild, non-aqueous, anhydrous conditions avoid both over-oxidation (PCC itself stops at the aldehyde) AND avoid the aldehyde hydrating into a geminal diol in water (which a strong aqueous oxidant could then push on to the carboxylic acid), giving a cleaner, isolable aldehyde.
PCC is chosen purely for cost reasons, with no actual chemical/mechanistic advantage over aqueous strong oxidants for isolating a stable aldehyde product.
questions.explanation: Beyond PCC's own mildness (stopping at the aldehyde), running the reaction in a non-aqueous solvent avoids the aldehyde hydrating to a geminal diol, which a strong aqueous oxidant could otherwise further oxidise toward the carboxylic acid — two separate, complementary reasons the aldehyde stays clean.
questions.hint: Think about two separate risks to the aldehyde product: over-oxidation by a strong reagent, and hydration by water itself.
distractor_logic: Denies the real, mechanistically-grounded difference in selectivity (stopping point) between these two oxidant classes.
Ignores that vigorous aqueous oxidants are exactly what risks over-oxidising the aldehyde further to the carboxylic acid, the opposite of the desired outcome.
Dismisses the genuine chemical rationale (avoiding both over-oxidation and aldehyde hydration) in favour of an unsupported cost-based explanation.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: A molecule contains both a 2° alcohol and a 3° alcohol at different positions. What happens when it is treated with excess PCC?
options: Only the 2° alcohol is oxidised (to a ketone); the 3° alcohol, lacking a carbinol C–H, is untouched by PCC even in excess, giving a hydroxy-ketone product with the 3° –OH still intact.
Neither –OH is oxidised, since having two different classes of alcohol in the same molecule somehow blocks PCC's reactivity toward both entirely.
The 3° alcohol is oxidised preferentially over the 2° alcohol, since more substituted alcohols are generally considered 'more reactive' in every type of reaction, including oxidation.

Both –OH groups are oxidised, the 2° alcohol to a ketone and the 3° alcohol to a more highly oxidised product via a different pathway, since 'excess PCC' implies exhaustive oxidation of every –OH present.
questions.explanation: Oxidation fundamentally requires a hydrogen on the carbinol carbon; the 2° alcohol has one (giving a ketone), while the 3° alcohol has none, so no amount of excess PCC can oxidise it — the product is a hydroxy-ketone with the tertiary –OH untouched.
questions.hint: Excess reagent can't force a reaction that has no mechanistic pathway available — check what each carbinol carbon actually has to offer.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly denies that PCC would still readily oxidise the 2° alcohol present, regardless of the unreactive 3° alcohol elsewhere in the same molecule.

Incorrectly generalises 'more substituted = more reactive' across all reaction types; for oxidation specifically, the trend is the opposite (needs a carbinol C-H, which tertiary alcohols lack), unlike for SN1/E1-type reactions.

Incorrectly assumes excess reagent alone can override the fundamental mechanistic requirement (a carbinol C-H) for oxidation, which the tertiary alcohol simply does not have regardless of how much PCC is used.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: A dehydration could in principle give a more-substituted (Zaitsev) alkene with severe steric strain, or a less-substituted alkene with no such strain. Which generally predominates, and what does this reveal about the limits of Zaitsev's rule?
options: In most ordinary cases the Zaitsev product still predominates, since greater substitution generally correlates with greater alkene stability even with modest steric effects; but Zaitsev's rule is fundamentally a statement about relative alkene STABILITY, and in genuinely severe steric-strain cases the less-strained (even if less substituted) alkene can become the actual major product, showing the rule has real exceptions when strain is severe enough.
Zaitsev's rule has absolutely no exceptions under any circumstances; the more substituted alkene is always the major product regardless of any steric considerations whatsoever.

Alkene stability has nothing to do with degree of substitution at all; Zaitsev's rule is actually based purely on which alkene forms fastest kinetically, unrelated to any thermodynamic stability consideration.
The less-substituted alkene is always the major product in every acid-catalysed dehydration, since steric effects always dominate over substitution-based stability in every case.
questions.explanation: Zaitsev's rule is a generalisation grounded in relative alkene stability (more substitution usually means more stability via hyperconjugation); in the great majority of cases this correctly predicts the major product, but in unusually severe steric-strain cases that stability advantage can be outweighed, showing the rule is not an absolute law.
questions.hint: Ask what Zaitsev's rule is actually a statement ABOUT (stability), then consider what could, in principle, outweigh that.
distractor_logic: Overstates Zaitsev's rule as an absolute law rather than a generalisation based on typical relative stability, which can in principle be outweighed by severe steric strain in unusual cases.

Misattributes Zaitsev's rule's basis; the underlying reason more-substituted alkenes are favoured in ordinary E1 dehydration IS their generally greater relative stability, not a purely kinetic argument disconnected from stability.

Overgeneralises in the opposite direction; in the vast majority of ordinary cases, the more-substituted (Zaitsev) alkene still wins, with severe-steric-strain exceptions being unusual rather than the norm.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: Why does Fischer esterification of a sterically hindered primary alcohol (e.g. neopentyl alcohol, (CH<sub>3</sub>)<sub>3</sub>C–CH<sub>2</sub>OH) proceed more slowly than esterification of an unhindered primary alcohol like ethanol, even though both are formally 1°?
options: Neopentyl alcohol cannot undergo Fischer esterification at all under any conditions, regardless of reaction time or catalyst.
Both alcohols react at identical rates, since Fischer esterification rate depends only on whether the alcohol is 1°, 2°, or 3°, with no further steric sensitivity within the 1° category.

The extreme steric bulk of the tert-butyl group immediately adjacent to the reacting carbon hinders the nucleophilic attack step of Fischer esterification (attack of the alcohol oxygen on the protonated acid's carbonyl carbon), slowing the reaction considerably even though both alcohols share the same simple '1°' classification by carbon-attachment count.
Neopentyl alcohol reacts faster than ethanol, since bulkier alcohols are generally more reactive toward acid-catalysed reactions in general.
questions.explanation: 1°/2°/3° classification only describes the carbinol carbon itself; bulk one carbon further away (like neopentyl alcohol's tert-butyl group) can still sterically hinder the nucleophilic attack step of esterification, slowing the reaction even though the alcohol remains formally primary.
questions.hint: 1°/2°/3° classification looks only at the carbinol carbon — check whether bulk elsewhere nearby could still matter.
distractor_logic: Overstates the steric hindrance as an absolute block rather than simply a rate-slowing factor; the reaction can still proceed, just more slowly.

Ignores that steric bulk immediately adjacent to a reacting centre can matter even within a single formal substitution class, since 1°/2°/3° classification is based on the carbinol carbon alone, not on bulk one carbon further away.
Reverses the actual expected steric effect; bulk near the reacting centre generally slows down (not speeds up) a nucleophilic-attack-dependent mechanism like Fischer esterification.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: PCC reliably stops primary-alcohol oxidation at the aldehyde stage, while hot KMnO<sub>4</sub> continues to the acid. Would running KMnO<sub>4</sub> cold and dilute instead reliably achieve PCC-like selectivity?
options: Cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> reliably and cleanly stops at the aldehyde stage for primary alcohols, making it functionally interchangeable with PCC in essentially all synthetic contexts.
KMnO<sub>4</sub> cannot oxidise primary alcohols at all under any conditions, hot or cold, concentrated or dilute; only PCC is capable of oxidising a primary alcohol in the first place.
The distinction between PCC and KMnO<sub>4</sub> is purely about reaction rate, with no real difference in where each reagent actually stops along the oxidation pathway.

Not reliably — even cold, dilute KMnO<sub>4</sub> is generally still too strong/unselective an oxidant to cleanly stop at the aldehyde stage in typical practice; PCC (or similar mild chromium(VI) oxidants) remains the standard choice specifically because KMnO<sub>4</sub>'s fundamental oxidising strength, not merely concentration or temperature, tends to drive the reaction toward the acid.
questions.explanation: PCC's selectivity comes from its inherent (mild) oxidising character, not merely from running it under gentle conditions; simply diluting/cooling a fundamentally strong oxidant like KMnO<sub>4</sub> is not a dependable way to reproduce that same stopping-point selectivity, which is why PCC (or PDC) remains the standard choice when the aldehyde specifically must be isolated.
questions.hint: Ask whether an oxidant's stopping point is really just about concentration/temperature, or about something more fundamental to the reagent itself.
distractor_logic: Overstates the reliability of concentration/temperature control alone for achieving PCC-like selectivity with KMnO4, which is not the standard, dependable approach used in practice for this specific selectivity goal.

Factually wrong; KMnO4 (hot, acidic/concentrated) is a standard, well-established oxidant for primary alcohols, just one that typically proceeds all the way to the carboxylic acid rather than stopping at the aldehyde.
Denies the real, well-established selectivity/stopping-point difference between these two reagent classes, reducing it to an unrelated rate-only distinction.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: A molecule has one 2° and one 3° –OH group, and only limited (sub-stoichiometric) dilute acid catalyst is available. Which –OH dehydrates preferentially?
options: Both –OH groups dehydrate at exactly the same rate regardless of class, since the limited amount of catalyst available affects both groups identically and simultaneously.
Neither –OH group dehydrates at all unless a full stoichiometric or excess amount of acid catalyst is provided.

The tertiary –OH dehydrates preferentially, since it forms its carbocation intermediate fastest (lowest activation energy) among the two, consistent with the general 3°>2°>1° dehydration reactivity order established for isolated alcohols.

The secondary –OH dehydrates preferentially, since secondary carbocations are generally considered more 'balanced' or 'moderate' in reactivity and thus statistically favoured under limited-catalyst conditions.
questions.explanation: Since acid is catalytic (regenerated, able to act repeatedly), the reactivity difference between the two sites still matters under limited-catalyst conditions: the tertiary site's faster carbocation formation lets it react preferentially with whatever catalyst becomes available.
questions.hint: Remember that a catalyst is regenerated after use — it isn't 'used up' on one site only.
distractor_logic: Ignores that carbocation stability differences between the two classes would still create a genuine kinetic preference, even under catalyst-limited conditions.

Misunderstands the catalytic nature of the acid in this reaction; a catalyst is regenerated and can act on multiple substrate molecules sequentially, with the more reactive site reacting preferentially.
Invents an unsupported 'balanced reactivity' rationale that contradicts the well-established, more straightforward reactivity order (3°>2°>1°) based on carbocation stability.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: A molecule could undergo either intramolecular dehydration (forming a cyclic ether, if a second –OH is favourably positioned) or intermolecular esterification (with an external carboxylic acid also present). Which pathway generally dominates when both are geometrically possible?
options: Both pathways are always equally likely regardless of ring size, since the underlying acid-catalysed chemistry is fundamentally the same whether the reacting groups are in the same molecule or different molecules.

Cyclic ether formation is actually impossible under any acid-catalysed conditions, since ether formation was previously described only as an intermolecular process between two separate alcohol molecules.

The intramolecular cyclic ether-forming pathway typically dominates when a favourable ring size (5- or 6-membered) is accessible, since intramolecular reactions are generally strongly kinetically favoured over the corresponding intermolecular reaction, due to the much higher effective concentration of the reacting groups when tethered within one molecule.

Intermolecular esterification always dominates over any possible intramolecular pathway, regardless of ring size or geometry, since intermolecular reactions are inherently faster than intramolecular ones.
questions.explanation: A favourable intramolecular cyclisation (especially forming a 5- or 6-membered ring) benefits from a much higher effective local concentration of the reacting groups than an intermolecular reaction ever could, generally making it the kinetically dominant pathway when geometrically accessible.
questions.hint: Think about 'effective concentration' — two groups tethered in the same molecule are always 'right there' for each other.
distractor_logic: Ignores the substantial effective-concentration/entropic advantage that intramolecular reactions generally have when a favourable ring size is geometrically accessible.

Overgeneralises a specific earlier example (intermolecular ether formation from two separate simple alcohol molecules) into an absolute rule, when intramolecular cyclic ether formation from an appropriately-positioned diol is a well-known, related process.

Reverses the well-established general kinetic advantage that favourable intramolecular reactions (especially those forming 5- or 6-membered rings) typically have over the corresponding intermolecular version.
