questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: The same strong oxidant (e.g. hot acidified K<sub>2</sub>Cr<sub>2</sub>O<sub>7</sub>) gives completely different outcomes depending on whether it's applied to a 1°, 2°, or 3° alcohol. Why, given that the reagent and conditions are identical each time?
options: The outcome depends entirely on the SUBSTRATE's structure (how many C–H bonds are on the carbinol carbon: two for 1°, one for 2°, zero for 3°), not on any change in the reagent; the oxidant removes available carbinol C–H bonds progressively, illustrating that reagent strength alone doesn't determine outcome — substrate structure is equally essential.
The oxidant itself somehow changes its chemical identity/strength depending on which alcohol class it's mixed with, becoming weaker for tertiary alcohols and stronger for primary alcohols.
Reaction time, not substrate structure, is the only variable that determines the final product for all three alcohol classes with this oxidant.

All three alcohol classes actually give the identical final product (the corresponding carboxylic acid) with this strong oxidant, with any apparent product differences being due to incomplete reactions.
questions.explanation: The reagent is constant throughout; what changes is the substrate's own available chemistry — specifically how many carbinol C–H bonds each class has to offer for progressive oxidation. A tertiary alcohol's complete lack of one is a structural, not a kinetic, limit.
questions.hint: The reagent doesn't change between the three cases — so look for what's different about each substrate instead.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly attributes a changing reagent identity/strength to what is actually a constant, unchanging reagent reacting differently due to substrate structural differences, not due to any change in the oxidant itself.
Extending reaction time cannot substitute for the structurally absent carbinol C-H bond that the oxidation mechanism fundamentally requires.

Incorrectly claims tertiary alcohols can reach a carboxylic-acid-type product with more reaction time, when their complete lack of a carbinol C-H is a genuine, insurmountable structural limit on this oxidation pathway.

questions.topic: Reactions of Alcohols: Esterification, Dehydration and Oxidation
questions.question: A mixture of a 1° and a 3° alcohol is treated simultaneously with BOTH PCC and conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat added together to the same flask. What outcome is expected?
options: Both alcohols would undergo oxidation only, since PCC is present and oxidation always takes priority over dehydration whenever both reagent types are available together.

Both alcohols would undergo dehydration only, since conc. H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat is present and dehydration always takes priority over oxidation whenever both reagent types are available together.

The 1° alcohol is predominantly oxidised by PCC to the corresponding aldehyde (PCC needs a carbinol C–H, present in 1° but not 3°), while the 3° alcohol, immune to PCC, instead undergoes acid-catalysed dehydration (favoured by H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>/heat and its very stable tertiary carbocation) to give an alkene — two different products from the one combined-reagent flask, each reagent acting on the substrate it's actually suited to.

No reaction occurs for either alcohol, since combining an oxidising agent (PCC) and a strong acid (H<sub>2</sub>SO<sub>4</sub>) in the same flask causes them to neutralise/deactivate each other completely.
questions.explanation: Each reagent reacts with whichever substrate is actually suited to it: PCC can only oxidise the primary alcohol (which has a carbinol C–H), while the tertiary alcohol, immune to PCC, is instead dehydrated by the acid/heat present — the two reactions proceed in parallel on their respective substrates.
questions.hint: Ask separately: which reagent can actually act on the 1° alcohol, and which can act on the 3° alcohol?
distractor_logic: Same core error as above, but reversed; PCC specifically cannot oxidise the tertiary alcohol at all (no carbinol C-H), so dehydration would be the only viable pathway for that substrate regardless of PCC's presence.

Incorrectly assumes one reagent's reactivity universally overrides the other's, when in fact each reagent reacts with whichever substrate is actually suited to it, and both reactions can occur in parallel.

Overstates an incompatibility between these two reagents; there's no fundamental chemical reason PCC and H2SO4 would completely neutralise each other's distinct modes of reactivity toward the two different substrates present.

questions.question: Rank three disubstituted phenols by acidity: 2,4-dinitrophenol, 2,4-dimethylphenol, and 2-nitro-4-methylphenol (one of each substituent).
options: 2,4-Dinitrophenol > 2-nitro-4-methylphenol > 2,4-dimethylphenol — two electron-withdrawing nitro groups combine for the strongest acidifying effect; two electron-donating methyl groups combine for the strongest acidity-decreasing effect; the mixed compound falls in between these two extremes.
2,4-Dimethylphenol > 2-nitro-4-methylphenol > 2,4-dinitrophenol — the reverse order.
All three are equally acidic, since disubstitution effects always cancel out regardless of which specific groups are involved.
2-Nitro-4-methylphenol > 2,4-dinitrophenol > 2,4-dimethylphenol — ranking the mixed-substitution compound above the doubly-EWG-substituted one.
questions.explanation: Two EWGs (dinitro) combine for the strongest acidifying effect; two EDGs (dimethyl) combine for the strongest acidity-decreasing effect; a compound with one of each falls between these two extremes.
questions.hint: Sort by how many electron-withdrawing versus electron-donating groups each compound has, then place the mixed case between the two 'pure' extremes.
distractor_logic: Reverses the entire order, effectively treating EWGs as acid-weakening and EDGs as acid-strengthening.
Ignores the real, substituent-dependent acidity differences that clearly distinguish these three specific compounds.
Incorrectly ranks the mixed-substitution compound above the doubly-EWG-substituted one, when two EWGs should outdo a mix of one EWG and one EDG.

questions.question: Both o-nitrophenol and p-nitrophenol have –NO<sub>2</sub> at a position with direct resonance access to the phenoxide oxygen, yet o-nitrophenol is sometimes found to be slightly less acidic than the para isomer. Why?
options: Steric and geometric factors at the crowded ortho position (bulky –NO<sub>2</sub> next to –OH/–O<sup>–</sup>, possibly twisting –NO<sub>2</sub> slightly out of ring coplanarity) can modestly reduce –NO<sub>2</sub>'s resonance effectiveness compared to the sterically unencumbered para position, giving o-nitrophenol slightly lower acidity than the para isomer despite both having a formally available resonance pathway.
o-Nitrophenol's lower acidity is due to –NO<sub>2</sub> acting as an electron donor specifically when in the ortho position, reversing its usual electron-withdrawing character.
The acidity difference between the two isomers has nothing to do with sterics/geometry at all; it is entirely due to random experimental variation with no real underlying cause.
o-Nitrophenol is actually more acidic than p-nitrophenol in all cases, with no exceptions, since ortho substituents are inherently stronger than para substituents in every respect.
questions.explanation: Steric crowding at the ortho position can subtly twist –NO<sub>2</sub> out of perfect coplanarity with the ring, reducing how effectively its resonance withdrawal reaches the phenoxide oxygen, compared to the geometrically unhindered para position.
questions.hint: Both positions offer a resonance pathway in principle — but is that pathway equally UNOBSTRUCTED at both positions?
distractor_logic: Incorrectly claims -NO2 changes its fundamental electronic character based on position; it remains electron-withdrawing at ortho, just potentially with reduced resonance effectiveness due to geometric factors.
Denies a real, chemically grounded (if subtle) steric/resonance-overlap explanation for the observed difference.
Overstates ortho superiority as an absolute rule; steric/geometric factors can in fact modestly reduce an ortho substituent's effectiveness compared to para.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Would phenol (pKa ≈10) be substantially deprotonated by aqueous ammonia (NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> pKa ≈9.25), a much weaker base than NaOH?
options: The extent of deprotonation is unrelated to the relative pKa values of phenol and ammonium; it depends only on the concentration of ammonia used.
Phenol is completely, quantitatively deprotonated by aqueous ammonia, exactly as it would be by NaOH, since ammonia is basic enough to react with any acidic compound to completion.

Only to a small/partial extent — since phenol's pKa is close to, but somewhat higher than, ammonium's pKa, the equilibrium phenol + NH<sub>3</sub> ⇌ phenoxide + NH<sub>4</sub><sup>+</sup> lies only modestly toward products, unlike the essentially complete deprotonation phenol undergoes with a much stronger base like NaOH.
Phenol does not react with aqueous ammonia at all, since ammonia is too weak a base to deprotonate any phenol under any circumstances.
questions.explanation: Because phenol's pKa (≈10) is close to ammonium's pKa (≈9.25), the acid-base equilibrium lies only modestly toward the phenoxide/ammonium side — giving partial, not complete, deprotonation, unlike phenol's essentially complete reaction with the much stronger base NaOH.
questions.hint: Compare phenol's pKa directly to ammonium's pKa — how close are they, and what does that imply for the equilibrium position?
distractor_logic: Ignores the fundamental acid-base equilibrium principle that relative pKa (not just concentration) determines the position of the deprotonation equilibrium.
Ignores that the EXTENT of an acid-base reaction depends on the relative pKa's of the acid and the conjugate acid of the base used, not simply on whether the base is 'basic enough' in a binary sense.
Understates ammonia's basicity; being reasonably close in pKa to phenol, ammonia CAN achieve a measurable, if partial, deprotonation.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: A phenol bears both a –NH<sub>2</sub> group (strong EDG by resonance) and a –NO<sub>2</sub> group (strong EWG by resonance) at two different ortho/para-accessible positions. Which effect dominates the net acidity relative to unsubstituted phenol?
options: The two effects always exactly cancel regardless of which specific positions are involved, giving a compound with identical acidity to unsubstituted phenol in every such case.
Having both an EDG and an EWG present simultaneously makes the compound's acidity completely unpredictable and impossible to reason about using electronic effects at all.
–NH<sub>2</sub> always dominates over –NO<sub>2</sub> regardless of relative resonance strength, since amino groups are inherently 'stronger' directors in all electronic contexts.

The net effect depends on the relative magnitude of the two competing resonance effects; since –NO<sub>2</sub> is generally a considerably stronger resonance-withdrawing group than –NH<sub>2</sub> is a resonance-donating group (when similarly positioned), the compound would typically be expected to be MORE acidic than unsubstituted phenol overall.
questions.explanation: –NO<sub>2</sub>'s resonance-withdrawing strength generally exceeds –NH<sub>2</sub>'s resonance-donating strength when both are similarly positioned, so the net effect on acidity is expected to favour an increase relative to unsubstituted phenol, even though qualitative (not exact numerical) reasoning is what's available without more specific data.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two groups is generally the STRONGER electronic effect, not just whether both effects exist.
distractor_logic: Overstates a precise, always-exact cancellation that is not generally true; the two groups' effects are not necessarily of equal magnitude.
Denies that qualitative reasoning about relative substituent strength is possible; while exact quantitative prediction needs more data, a qualitative prediction is still reasonable.
Incorrectly asserts a universal dominance for -NH2 without justification; in terms of resonance-withdrawing/donating strength specifically for acidity purposes, -NO2 is generally the stronger effect.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Kolbe's reaction specifically requires sodium PHENOXIDE (not neutral phenol) as the reactive species. How does phenol's own acidity make this practically achievable with an ordinary base like NaOH?
options: Phenoxide and phenol are equally good nucleophiles/reactive species for these reactions, so there would be no practical reason to specifically require pre-formed phenoxide.
Phenol's acidity is completely irrelevant to Kolbe's reaction; the reaction works identically well whether starting from neutral phenol or pre-formed phenoxide, with no practical difference.

Phenol's meaningful acidity (pKa≈10) means it CAN be efficiently and essentially completely converted to phenoxide by a reasonably strong base like NaOH — exactly what Kolbe's reaction requires as the actual nucleophile; a much less acidic compound (like a simple alcohol, pKa≈16-18) would need a stronger, more specialised base (like NaH or a metal) for the same complete deprotonation.
A less acidic compound would actually be more easily converted to its conjugate base form than a more acidic one, reversing the actual relationship between acidity and ease of deprotonation.
questions.explanation: Because phenol's pKa is comfortably below water's (NaOH's conjugate acid), NaOH can essentially completely convert phenol to phenoxide — the actual nucleophile Kolbe's reaction (and Williamson synthesis) requires; a much weaker acid like a simple alcohol would need a considerably stronger base to achieve the same complete deprotonation.
questions.hint: Compare phenol's pKa to water's pKa (NaOH's own conjugate acid) — is the gap large enough for essentially complete deprotonation?
distractor_logic: Denies the real, well-established difference in nucleophilicity between neutral phenol (a weak nucleophile) and phenoxide (a much stronger, more available nucleophile).
Denies the well-established requirement for pre-forming the phenoxide (the actual nucleophile) in this reaction, which depends directly on phenol's meaningful acidity.
Reverses the fundamental relationship between acid strength and the ease/completeness of deprotonation by a given base.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Would phenol be extracted from a neutral solvent by aqueous sodium carbonate (Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub>, a base of roughly comparable strength to NaOH for this purpose, though somewhat weaker), similar to extraction with NaOH?
options: The choice of base for extracting phenol has nothing to do with relative acid/base strength comparisons at all; any aqueous base, however weak, would extract phenol equally well given enough time.

Yes, generally — phenol (pKa≈10) is a weaker acid than carbonic acid's relevant ionisation (pKa≈6.3), so Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is a strong enough base for this purpose, and phenol would generally be extracted by aqueous Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> similarly to how it's extracted by NaOH.

Phenol cannot be extracted by Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> under any circumstances, only by NaOH specifically, since Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is considered 'too weak' a base for phenol regardless of the actual relative pKa comparison.
Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is actually a stronger base than NaOH, so it would extract phenol even more efficiently and completely than NaOH would.
questions.explanation: Comparing phenol's pKa (≈10) to carbonic acid's relevant pKa (≈6.3) shows Na<sub>2</sub>CO<sub>3</sub> is a sufficiently strong base to deprotonate phenol effectively, so it can serve a similar extraction role to NaOH in this context.
questions.hint: Compare phenol's pKa to the pKa of carbonic acid (Na2CO3's conjugate acid) — is Na2CO3 strong enough for phenol specifically?
distractor_logic: Denies the fundamental acid-base equilibrium principle that a base's strength (relative to the acid being extracted) determines whether/how completely the extraction actually occurs.
Overstates a rigid reagent-specific requirement rather than reasoning from the actual relative acid/base strength comparison, which shows Na2CO3 is a sufficiently strong base for this purpose.
Reverses the actual relative base strength of these two common laboratory bases; NaOH is generally considered the stronger of the two.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Titrating phenol with standardised aqueous NaOH gives a usably sharp endpoint, despite phenol being considerably weaker than a typical carboxylic acid. Why does this still work?
options: The titration endpoint's pH would be identical for phenol and a carboxylic acid, since the endpoint always occurs at pH 7 regardless of which acid is being titrated.
Phenol cannot be titrated with NaOH at all using standard acid-base indicators, since indicators only work for strong acid/strong base titrations.

Even though phenol (pKa≈10) is weaker than a typical carboxylic acid (pKa≈4-5), it is still acidic enough relative to NaOH (conjugate acid water, pKa≈15.7) to give a large enough equilibrium constant for the neutralisation to proceed essentially to completion at the equivalence point, giving a usably sharp endpoint, even though that endpoint's exact pH is somewhat more basic than a stronger acid's would be.
A sharp titration endpoint requires the acid being titrated to be at least as strong as a typical carboxylic acid; phenol's titration with NaOH would NOT show any usable endpoint at all.
questions.explanation: Phenol's pKa gap from water (roughly 5-6 units) is still large enough to give an equilibrium constant favouring essentially complete neutralisation at the equivalence point, producing a usable, if somewhat more basic, titration endpoint than a stronger acid would give.
questions.hint: A 'sharp enough' endpoint just needs a large enough equilibrium constant for the neutralisation — how big is phenol's pKa gap from water?
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes titration endpoints are always at neutral pH 7; the equivalence-point pH for a weak acid/strong base titration is actually somewhat basic, with a weaker acid giving an even more basic endpoint pH.
Overstates a limitation of acid-base indicators; appropriately chosen indicators can and are used for weak acid/strong base titrations including phenol.
Understates that phenol's substantial pKa gap from water/NaOH's conjugate acid pair is still large enough (roughly 5-6 pKa units) to give a usably complete, sharp-enough titration reaction.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Phenol is not stable to strongly basic aqueous conditions the way anisole is. Does this mean phenol is chemically degraded by prolonged base exposure, unlike anisole?
options: No — phenol's genuine acidity simply keeps it in its deprotonated (sodium phenoxide) form throughout, a reversible acid-base equilibrium, not decomposition; anisole, lacking any acidic proton, remains chemically unchanged throughout the same exposure — the real distinction is 'reversibly deprotonated' versus 'entirely unreactive', not that phenol is somehow degraded.
Yes — phenol is genuinely chemically decomposed/degraded by prolonged exposure to aqueous NaOH, breaking down into unidentified byproducts, unlike the fully stable anisole.
Anisole is actually the less stable of the two under strongly basic aqueous conditions, since ethers are generally considered more reactive than phenols toward nucleophilic attack by hydroxide.
Both phenol and anisole are equally affected (either both decompose or both remain fully unchanged) by prolonged exposure to aqueous NaOH.
questions.explanation: Phenol's behaviour under base is simple, reversible deprotonation to phenoxide (fully recoverable by re-acidification), not decomposition; anisole, having no acidic proton, is simply unreactive throughout, so the real contrast is reversible-ionisation versus complete-inertness, not stability versus instability.
questions.hint: Ask whether phenol's change under base is reversible (and recoverable) or genuinely destructive.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly frames simple, reversible acid-base deprotonation as if it were irreversible chemical decomposition; phenol is fully recoverable by re-acidification, indicating no actual degradation occurred.
Reverses the actual relative reactivity; anisole's ether C-O bonds are not readily cleaved by aqueous hydroxide under ordinary conditions, unlike phenol's simple, reversible acid-base behaviour.
Denies the real, acidity-based distinction between the two compounds' behaviour toward aqueous base.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: 2,6-Di-tert-butylphenol is less acidic than expected from a simple 'tert-butyl is a mild EDG' analysis alone. Why?
options: 2,6-Di-tert-butylphenol's acidity is identical to unsubstituted phenol, since tert-butyl groups have no measurable electronic or steric effect on a phenol's acidity in any documented case.
2,6-Di-tert-butylphenol is actually more acidic than phenol, not less, since having two substituents at both ortho positions always increases acidity regardless of their electronic character.
The decreased acidity is due purely to steric effects, with tert-butyl's electronic character having no measurable influence on acidity at all in this specific case.

While tert-butyl's modest electron-donating character contributes somewhat to decreased acidity as any EDG at ortho would, the bulk of TWO tert-butyl groups at both ortho positions can ALSO sterically hinder effective solvation/stabilisation of the phenoxide oxygen (or otherwise disrupt optimal resonance/solvation geometry), providing an additional, largely steric contribution to the observed decrease beyond what electronics alone would predict.
questions.explanation: Both effects contribute: tert-butyl's modest electron donation decreases acidity somewhat (as any ortho EDG would), and the severe steric bulk of two such groups at both ortho positions can further hinder effective phenoxide stabilisation/solvation, adding an extra decrease beyond the purely electronic contribution.
questions.hint: Consider two separate contributions here: the electronic character of tert-butyl, AND the sheer bulk of having two of them at both ortho positions.
distractor_logic: Denies the well-documented, measurable decrease in acidity actually observed for this specific bulky, doubly-ortho-substituted phenol.

Incorrectly assumes ortho substitution always increases acidity; the effect fundamentally depends on the substituent's electronic character, and tert-butyl is electron-donating, which decreases acidity.

Denies that tert-butyl's genuine (if modest) electron-donating character still contributes to the observed decrease, treating the effect as purely steric when it is more accurately a combination of both factors.

questions.topic: Acidity of Phenols and Factors Affecting Acid Strength
questions.question: Phenol is the conjugate acid of a WEAKER base (phenoxide) than ethanol is of ethoxide. Does this mean phenoxide is a weaker nucleophile than ethoxide in an SN2 reaction?
options: Phenoxide is actually a stronger nucleophile than ethoxide, since the resonance stabilisation that makes phenol more acidic also somehow makes phenoxide more reactive as a nucleophile, not less.
Phenoxide and ethoxide are equally good nucleophiles in all SN2 reactions, since both carry an identical formal negative charge on oxygen regardless of what stabilises that charge.

Yes — phenoxide, as the conjugate base of the stronger acid (phenol), is correspondingly a weaker base/nucleophile than ethoxide; it is still perfectly usable in Williamson synthesis, but generally reacts somewhat more slowly/less readily as a nucleophile in SN2 reactions than a comparably-sized simple alkoxide, consistent with the general inverse relationship between conjugate acid strength and conjugate base reactivity.
Nucleophilicity and basicity are entirely unrelated properties with no general correlation, so no prediction about phenoxide's relative nucleophilicity can be made from its relative basicity at all.
questions.explanation: The resonance delocalisation that stabilises phenoxide (and makes phenol more acidic) also makes that same negative charge LESS available/reactive toward an electrophile, consistent with the general inverse relationship between how stabilised (weakly basic) a conjugate base is and how nucleophilic it tends to be.
questions.hint: Think about what resonance stabilisation does to how 'available' a lone pair/negative charge actually is for attacking something else.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes resonance stabilisation (which lowers phenoxide's basicity/reactivity by spreading out and stabilising its negative charge) would instead increase its nucleophilic reactivity; a more stabilised species is generally a weaker, not stronger, nucleophile.
Ignores that the degree of charge stabilisation/delocalisation directly affects how reactive/available that charge is for a subsequent nucleophilic attack.
Overstates the disconnect; while nucleophilicity and basicity aren't always perfectly correlated, the general inverse relationship is still a reasonable, commonly-used qualitative predictor here.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: A phenol bears an EWG at the META position (e.g. 3-nitrophenol). Where does Kolbe's carboxylation still occur, given that –OH directs to its own ortho/para positions regardless of the meta substituent?
options: Instead ortho/para to the nitro group specifically, since –NO<sub>2</sub>'s own (meta-directing) preference would override –OH's directing influence entirely.
No reaction occurs at all once any second substituent is present on the ring, regardless of its position or electronic character.

Carboxylation occurs equally at all available ring positions with no preference at all, since having two substituents with potentially competing directing preferences creates complete non-selectivity.

Still predominantly ortho to –OH (i.e. C2 or C6 relative to –OH at C1), since –OH remains the dominant director toward its own ortho/para positions regardless of a meta-positioned second substituent's own directing preference; the meta-nitro group would somewhat reduce the overall rate but not change WHICH positions –OH directs to.
questions.explanation: A far stronger activator like –OH (direct resonance donation) remains the dominant director for where new substitution occurs, regardless of a second, meta-positioned, more weakly influential substituent's own directing tendency for further substitution relative to itself.
questions.hint: Ask which substituent is the STRONGER director overall, not just which one is 'closer' to the new substitution.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly assumes the second substituent's own directing preference (for substitution relative to itself) somehow overrides the first group's (-OH's) directing influence, when -OH remains the dominant director.
Overstates that any second substituent entirely blocks the reaction; Kolbe's reaction can still proceed, just potentially more slowly with an EWG present.
Denies that -OH, as by far the stronger director in this system, still exerts a dominant, predictable directing influence despite the second substituent's presence.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Phenol is brominated in non-aqueous CCl<sub>4</sub> at low temperature with only 1 equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub>, favouring monobromination. Does the solvent choice (aqueous vs non-aqueous) itself change whether ortho or para product dominates, under similarly controlled (1 equiv, low temp) conditions?
options: Solvent polarity has no effect whatsoever on Br<sub>2</sub>'s reactivity as an electrophile toward phenol; a polar versus non-polar medium makes literally zero difference to reaction rate or mechanism.
Non-aqueous CCl<sub>4</sub> conditions give exclusively para product with zero ortho product formed, while aqueous conditions give exclusively ortho product with zero para product formed.

Using 1 equivalent of Br<sub>2</sub> in any solvent always gives the same exhaustive tribromination product (2,4,6-tribromophenol) regardless of stoichiometry, since phenol's ring is so strongly activated.

Not fundamentally — both approaches can achieve predominantly monobromination when Br<sub>2</sub> is limited to 1 equivalent, regardless of solvent polarity; solvent choice mainly affects reaction RATE and the electrophile's exact character, while the ortho/para product ratio (typically favouring para due to sterics) is influenced more by temperature and steric factors than by aqueous versus non-aqueous solvent choice itself.
questions.explanation: The key controllable variable for mono- versus poly-substitution is Br<sub>2</sub> stoichiometry (1 equivalent versus excess), not solvent polarity per se; solvent mainly modulates rate/electrophile character, while the para-favoured (with some ortho) product mix arises mainly from steric and temperature factors common to both solvent systems.
questions.hint: Separate two different variables here: how much Br2 is used (stoichiometry), versus what kind of solvent it's dissolved in.
distractor_logic: Overstates that solvent polarity is entirely irrelevant, when in reality it does modestly affect Br2's polarisation/reactivity and thus reaction rate, even if the qualitative activation/directing pattern remains similar.

Overstates an absolute, all-or-nothing product distinction between solvent systems that doesn't reflect the more realistic picture of a major/minor product mixture under controlled monobromination conditions in either solvent system.
Incorrectly ignores that limiting Br2 stoichiometry (to 1 equivalent) is precisely the controllable variable that restricts the reaction to monobromination, regardless of which solvent is used.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Reimer-Tiemann specifically uses strong base (concentrated NaOH), not a weaker base like NaHCO<sub>3</sub>. Why won't a weaker base work for this specific reaction?
options: Concentrated NaOH is needed not to deprotonate CHCl<sub>3</sub> at all, but purely to neutralise the HCl byproduct formed later in the mechanism, with its base strength being otherwise irrelevant to the carbene-generating step itself.
Any base, regardless of strength, would work equally well for this reaction, since the choice of NaOH over a weaker base is purely a matter of historical convention with no real mechanistic basis.

A weaker base like NaHCO<sub>3</sub> would actually work just as well, or even better, for generating dichlorocarbene, since weaker bases are generally considered 'gentler' and less likely to cause unwanted side reactions.

Generating the trichloromethide anion (CCl<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>) from CHCl<sub>3</sub> requires deprotonating a relatively weakly acidic C–H bond; only a sufficiently strong base like concentrated NaOH can achieve this at a useful rate/extent, whereas NaHCO<sub>3</sub> is not basic enough to meaningfully deprotonate CHCl<sub>3</sub>, so the essential first step (needed before α-elimination can generate the carbene) simply wouldn't occur to any useful extent.
questions.explanation: The crucial, base-strength-dependent step is deprotonating CHCl<sub>3</sub> itself (a relatively weak C–H acid) to form CCl<sub>3</sub><sup>–</sup>, the precursor that then loses Cl<sup>–</sup> to generate the carbene; a base too weak to achieve that initial deprotonation cannot get the mechanism started at all.
questions.hint: Trace the mechanism back to its very first step — what does that step actually require of the base?
distractor_logic: Misidentifies which step in the mechanism actually requires strong base; the crucial, base-strength-dependent step is the initial deprotonation of CHCl3 itself, not simply mopping up a later byproduct.
Denies the genuine mechanistic requirement for a sufficiently strong base to deprotonate the comparatively weakly acidic CHCl3 C-H bond in the first place.
Incorrectly assumes 'gentler is always better' without regard to whether the base is actually strong enough to accomplish the specific, required deprotonation step at all.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Would the Reimer-Tiemann reaction work on anisole (methoxybenzene) the way it works on phenol, given that anisole's ring is also activated (methoxy is o,p-directing) but anisole has no free phenolic O–H?
options: Anisole reacts even more readily than phenol under Reimer-Tiemann conditions, since methoxy is a stronger activating group than hydroxyl in electrophilic aromatic substitution generally.
The reaction works equally well on anisole as on phenol, giving an analogous ortho-formylated product, since both compounds have an activated, oxygen-substituted aromatic ring.

No — the reaction specifically requires the phenOXIDE ion (from NaOH deprotonating phenol's O–H) as the actual reactive species coordinating with the incoming carbene; anisole, having no acidic O–H to deprotonate, cannot form the analogous reactive intermediate, even though its ring is independently activated toward electrophilic substitution in a general sense.
Neither phenol nor anisole can undergo the Reimer-Tiemann reaction at all; this reaction is only theoretical and has never actually been demonstrated on any real substrate.
questions.explanation: The Reimer-Tiemann mechanism is understood to specifically require the phenoxide ion (not just any activated ring) as the reactive species; anisole cannot form this because it has no acidic O–H to deprotonate, so the reaction does not proceed the same way on it.
questions.hint: Ask what the reaction actually needs BEYOND simple ring activation — is that requirement something anisole can meet?
distractor_logic: Misapplies a general electrophilic-substitution-activation comparison to this SPECIFIC named reaction, which has an additional structural requirement beyond simple ring activation strength.
Overlooks that the specific Reimer-Tiemann mechanism is understood to require the phenoxide ion, not just any activated ring, a requirement anisole cannot meet.
Factually wrong; the Reimer-Tiemann reaction on phenol (giving salicylaldehyde) is a well-established, real, classic reaction.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol, pKa≈0.4) is extremely acidic. Would it, unlike plain phenol, be readily deprotonated by a weak base like aqueous NaHCO<sub>3</sub>?
options: Both picric acid and plain phenol would be equally, completely deprotonated by NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, since both share the same core phenolic –OH functional group.

Yes — being comparable in strength to many mineral acids, picric acid would be readily and essentially completely deprotonated even by weak NaHCO<sub>3</sub> (conjugate acid carbonic acid, pKa≈6.3, still far higher than picric acid's pKa); in sharp contrast, plain phenol (pKa≈10) is NOT significantly deprotonated by the same weak base, since phenol's pKa is well above carbonic acid's.
Neither picric acid nor plain phenol would react meaningfully with NaHCO<sub>3</sub>, since NaHCO<sub>3</sub> is considered a 'weak' base unsuitable for deprotonating any phenolic compound.

Plain phenol would actually be more readily deprotonated by NaHCO<sub>3</sub> than picric acid, since simpler, less-substituted molecules are generally considered more reactive in acid-base chemistry.
questions.explanation: Picric acid's dramatically lower pKa (≈0.4, far below carbonic acid's ≈6.3) means even a weak base like NaHCO<sub>3</sub> readily deprotonates it, while phenol's higher pKa (≈10, above carbonic acid's) means the same weak base fails to meaningfully deprotonate phenol.
questions.hint: Compare both compounds' pKa values directly against carbonic acid's pKa (≈6.3), NaHCO3's own conjugate acid.
distractor_logic: Ignores the enormous pKa difference (about 9.6 units) between these two specific compounds, which translates into a dramatically different extent of reaction with the same weak base.
Incorrectly generalises NaHCO3 as universally too weak for ALL phenolic compounds, when picric acid's much lower pKa makes it readily deprotonatable even by this comparatively weak base.
Reverses the entire relationship; picric acid, not phenol, is the dramatically stronger and more readily-deprotonated acid of the two.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Kolbe's reaction classically uses sodium phenoxide specifically. Could the identity of the alkali metal counter-ion (sodium vs potassium vs lithium) plausibly matter for the reaction's characteristic ortho-selectivity?
options: Kolbe's reaction cannot be performed with any alkali metal counter-ion other than sodium; potassium and lithium phenoxides are entirely unreactive toward CO<sub>2</sub> under Kolbe's reaction conditions.
The counter-ion's identity is completely and absolutely irrelevant to Kolbe's reaction's mechanism or outcome in every conceivable respect, since only the phenoxide oxygen's own chemistry matters.
Using a potassium or lithium phenoxide instead of sodium phenoxide would completely reverse Kolbe's reaction's selectivity, giving exclusively para product instead of ortho.

Plausibly yes, at least in principle — if the proposed mechanism for ortho-selectivity does rely on some coordination/chelation between the phenoxide oxygen, the metal counter-ion, and the incoming CO<sub>2</sub>, then the counter-ion's size/coordinating ability could influence how effectively that proximity effect operates, though sodium is the specific, classically-studied counter-ion for this reaction.
questions.explanation: If a coordination/chelation-based explanation for ortho-selectivity is accepted, then the metal counter-ion's own coordinating properties are a mechanistically reasonable (if subtle) factor to consider, even though sodium is the classically used and studied case for this reaction.
questions.hint: Think about WHY ortho-selectivity is proposed to occur in the first place, and whether the counter-ion plays any role in that proposed explanation.
distractor_logic: Factually overstated; other alkali metal phenoxides would generally be expected to still be reactive nucleophiles toward CO2, even if specific regioselectivity details might differ somewhat.

Overstates an absolute irrelevance for the counter-ion, when if a coordination/chelation-based mechanism for ortho-selectivity is indeed operative, the counter-ion's properties could plausibly play at least some role.

Overstates a specific, dramatic reversal effect that is not established; the general expectation is ortho-selectivity, though the degree of selectivity conceivably might vary somewhat with different counter-ions.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Resorcinol (benzene-1,3-diol) has TWO –OH groups, each independently directing ortho/para to itself. Where does Kolbe's reaction carboxylation preferentially occur?
options: Resorcinol cannot undergo Kolbe's reaction at all, since having two –OH groups on the same ring is structurally incompatible with the reaction's mechanism.
Carboxylation occurs completely randomly across all six ring positions with absolutely no preference, since having two different directing –OH groups creates total directing conflict.
Only ONE of the two –OH groups (arbitrarily chosen) would actually exert any directing influence at all, with the second –OH group's presence somehow completely disabling its own directing effect.

Predominantly at the ring position that is simultaneously ortho/para-favourable relative to BOTH –OH groups at once, since a position reinforced by both directors together is generally more strongly activated than one favoured by only one of the two.
questions.explanation: With two independently ortho/para-directing groups present, ring positions activated by BOTH directors simultaneously are generally the most strongly activated overall, making them the preferred site for the incoming electrophile.
questions.hint: Look for a ring position that satisfies BOTH hydroxyl groups' own ortho/para directing preference at the same time.
distractor_logic: Overstates a structural incompatibility that isn't actually present; multiple activating -OH groups on the same ring generally make it, if anything, even MORE reactive toward electrophilic substitution, not unreactive.
Denies that positions reinforced by both directors (rather than opposed by them) would still be expected to be more strongly activated than other positions, even with two directing groups present.
Incorrectly assumes one hydroxyl group's directing effect is simply switched off by the presence of a second one, when in reality both groups independently contribute their own directing influence.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: After dichlorocarbene attacks the ortho position of the phenoxide ring in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, is the immediate product already an aromatic dichloromethylphenol, or is there an intermediate step first?
options: The ring never loses its aromaticity at any point during this mechanism; the carbene simply substitutes for a ring hydrogen directly and instantaneously with no disruption to the aromatic system whatsoever.

There is an intermediate step: the initial carbene attack temporarily disrupts the ring's aromaticity (forming a non-aromatic cyclohexadienone-type intermediate); a subsequent proton shift restores aromaticity (bearing the –CHCl<sub>2</sub> group), which is THEN hydrolysed by the aqueous base to the final aldehyde, –CHO — tracking this sequence correctly is what lets you predict the final product is an aromatic aldehyde, not some non-aromatic dichloro-containing species.
The final hydrolysis step (converting –CHCl<sub>2</sub> to –CHO) is optional and can be skipped, with dichloromethyl-substituted phenol itself being an equally valid 'final product'.
The dichlorocarbene attack directly installs the –CHO group in a single step with no intermediate species at all.
questions.explanation: Like any electrophilic aromatic substitution, carbene attack first disrupts aromaticity (a Wheland-type intermediate), which then loses a proton to restore the aromatic ring (now bearing –CHCl<sub>2</sub>); only the SUBSEQUENT hydrolysis step converts that –CHCl<sub>2</sub> group into the final –CHO of salicylaldehyde.
questions.hint: Think about how electrophilic aromatic substitution generally proceeds in stages — attack, then re-aromatisation — and apply that same pattern here.
distractor_logic: Misrepresents the actual mechanism of electrophilic aromatic substitution generally, which does involve a temporarily non-aromatic intermediate before re-aromatisation.
Incorrectly treats the hydrolysis step as optional, when it is in fact a standard, essential part of the overall Reimer-Tiemann sequence for reliably obtaining the aldehyde product.

Understates the genuine, multi-step nature of electrophilic aromatic substitution mechanisms generally, which is directly relevant to correctly tracking what species are actually present before the final hydrolysis step.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Phenol brominates with Br<sub>2</sub> alone (no catalyst); benzene needs FeBr<sub>3</sub>. Would toluene (a weaker activator than –OH, via hyperconjugation only) also need a catalyst?
options: Toluene, being activated by –CH<sub>3</sub> just like phenol is activated by –OH, would also require no catalyst for bromination, exactly like phenol.

Toluene would actually need an even stronger catalyst than benzene itself requires, since alkyl-substituted rings are somehow less reactive toward electrophilic substitution than unsubstituted benzene.

Yes — toluene, though activated, is considerably less strongly activated than phenol (hyperconjugative/inductive –CH<sub>3</sub> donation is much weaker than –OH's direct resonance donation), so it still requires a Lewis acid catalyst like FeBr<sub>3</sub> for bromination, unlike phenol, which needs none; the DEGREE of activation matters, not just whether a ring is activated at all.
Whether a catalyst is needed for bromination has nothing to do with a substituent's activating/deactivating strength; it depends only on the size of the substituent group present on the ring.
questions.explanation: Only a sufficiently STRONGLY activated ring (like phenol's, via direct resonance donation) eliminates the need for a catalyst entirely; toluene's much more modest hyperconjugative/inductive activation, while real, is not enough to achieve the same catalyst-free reactivity.
questions.hint: Not all 'activated' rings are activated to the same DEGREE — compare how strong -OH's activation is versus -CH3's.
distractor_logic: Incorrectly equates the strength of activation from a weak activator with that of a much stronger activator, when only sufficiently strongly activated rings eliminate the need for a catalyst.
Reverses toluene's actual electronic character; -CH3 IS a (mild) activating, ortho/para-directing group, making toluene somewhat more reactive than benzene, not less.
Ignores the genuine electronic (not size-based) basis for why some rings need a catalyst for bromination and others do not.

questions.topic: Electrophilic Substitution Reactions of Phenols (Kolbe's, Reimer–Tiemann and Related Reactions)
questions.question: Both Kolbe's reaction and the Reimer-Tiemann reaction require converting phenol to its phenoxide ion first. Would either reaction work efficiently starting from phenol's methyl ether (anisole) instead?
options: Both reactions would work equally well on anisole as on free phenol, since anisole's ring is still activated in a general electrophilic-substitution sense, which is all that either reaction actually requires.
Reimer-Tiemann would work on anisole but Kolbe's reaction would not, for the reverse (and equally incorrect) reasoning.
Kolbe's reaction would work on anisole but Reimer-Tiemann would not, since Kolbe's reaction is claimed to depend only on ring activation while Reimer-Tiemann specifically requires the phenoxide ion.

Neither reaction would work as intended on anisole, since both specifically require the phenoxide ion (from deprotonating a free phenolic –OH) as the reactive species that positions/attracts the respective electrophile; anisole has no such deprotonatable –OH, so pre-converting phenol to its methyl ether would actually PREVENT both reactions from proceeding via their normal mechanisms.
questions.explanation: Both named reactions are understood to proceed via a phenoxide-ion-mediated mechanism, not merely 'any activated ring'; since anisole has no free phenolic –OH to deprotonate, neither reaction can proceed the normal way starting from it.
questions.hint: Ask the SAME question (does this reaction need the phenoxide ion specifically?) for both named reactions, not just one.
distractor_logic: Overlooks that both specific named reactions have an additional mechanistic requirement (the phenoxide ion specifically) that anisole, lacking a free phenolic -OH, cannot satisfy.
Same core error as above, reversed; both reactions genuinely require the phenoxide ion, so both would fail to proceed normally on anisole, not just one of them.
Incorrectly singles out only one of the two reactions as requiring the phenoxide ion, when in fact both reactions are understood to proceed via phenoxide-ion-mediated mechanisms.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: A secondary alkyl halide (e.g. isopropyl bromide) is used with a primary alkoxide (sodium ethoxide) in an attempted Williamson synthesis. Does this behave more like the 'good' (primary) or 'poor' (tertiary) end of the suitability spectrum?
options: A secondary alkyl halide behaves identically to a tertiary halide, with elimination completely dominating and essentially no ether product forming at all.
Secondary alkyl halides cannot react with alkoxides via any mechanism (SN2 or E2) at all, making this combination entirely unreactive.

It falls in an intermediate position: SN2 substitution can still occur to a useful extent (the alkoxide can still access the secondary carbon for backside attack), but competing E2 elimination becomes more significant than with a primary halide, so yields are generally lower/less clean, though usually still synthetically workable, unlike the essentially-failed tertiary case.
A secondary alkyl halide behaves identically to a primary halide, with elimination being a negligible side-reaction in both cases.
questions.explanation: A secondary substrate sits genuinely between the two extremes: SN2 is still accessible (unlike for tertiary substrates), but competing E2 elimination is more significant than for a primary substrate, generally giving a lower, though still workable, ether yield.
questions.hint: Don't round secondary substrates to either extreme — they genuinely behave as an intermediate case.
distractor_logic: Overstates the similarity to tertiary halides; secondary substrates, while more elimination-prone than primary ones, still generally allow a useful, workable degree of SN2 substitution.
Factually wrong; secondary alkyl halides do react with strong bases/nucleophiles like alkoxides, via a mixture of SN2 and E2 pathways, not zero reaction.
Understates the genuinely increased (even if not dominant) competing elimination that occurs with secondary substrates compared to primary ones.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: For synthesising sec-butyl tert-butyl ether, both possible Williamson synthesis groups (sec-butyl, tert-butyl) are more hindered than a simple primary group. Which reagent pairing is still the better (if imperfect) choice?
options: sec-Butoxide + tert-butyl halide would be the better pairing, since using the smaller alkoxide is always preferred regardless of which specific group ends up as the halide component.
Both pairings would give identical yields, since the overall molecular hindrance is the same regardless of which specific group is assigned as the alkoxide versus the halide.
Since neither group is a simple primary halide, Williamson synthesis cannot be used at all for this target molecule under any reagent pairing.

Sodium tert-butoxide (the more hindered group, as the alkoxide/nucleophile) + sec-butyl halide (the comparatively less hindered group, though still secondary, as the electrophile) — expected to give a higher yield than the reverse pairing (sec-butoxide + tert-butyl halide, which would suffer severely from the tertiary halide's strong elimination tendency), though overall yield by either pairing would likely be modest.
questions.explanation: The Williamson rule (bulkier group as nucleophile, less hindered group as electrophile) still applies in relative terms even when neither choice is ideal: pairing tert-butoxide with the comparatively less-hindered sec-butyl halide is expected to outperform the reverse pairing, which would suffer badly from the tertiary halide's strong elimination tendency.
questions.hint: Even between two imperfect options, apply the same underlying rule: which group should be the electrophile undergoing backside attack?
distractor_logic: Reverses the fundamental Williamson rule; the MORE hindered group should be the alkoxide (nucleophile), not the halide (electrophile), since a hindered electrophile most severely promotes competing elimination.
Ignores that the ROLE each group plays (nucleophile alkoxide vs. electrophile halide undergoing backside attack) matters independently of overall molecular bulk.
Overstates an absolute failure; while yields would likely be modest given that even the 'better' halide choice here is secondary, some useful degree of SN2 substitution would still be expected.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Ether cleavage by excess HI often gives little to no reaction at room temperature, even for an ether that would eventually cleave upon heating. Why, and how does this connect to alcohol dehydration also needing heat?
options: Ether cleavage is thermodynamically unfavourable at room temperature and only becomes favourable at higher temperature, which is why heating is required, rather than heating simply overcoming a kinetic barrier.

Ether cleavage by HI has essentially zero activation energy and would be expected to proceed instantaneously and completely even at room temperature; any lack of reaction must be due to insufficiently concentrated HI, unrelated to temperature.

Ether cleavage, like acid-catalysed alcohol dehydration, has a meaningful activation energy barrier (for protonating the ether oxygen and then breaking the C–O bond); at room temperature the rate may simply be too slow to observe significant product in a reasonable time, even though the reaction is thermodynamically favourable — heating supplies the energy needed for a practical rate, exactly as with dehydration.
There is no meaningful difference in ether cleavage extent between room temperature and heated conditions for any ether; this reaction is temperature-independent, unlike dehydration.
questions.explanation: Both reactions share the same underlying pattern: a genuinely favourable reaction can still be kinetically slow at room temperature due to an activation-energy barrier, and heating simply supplies the energy needed to reach a practical reaction rate, not to make an otherwise-unfavourable reaction favourable.
questions.hint: Ask whether heat is needed because the reaction is unfavourable at low temperature, or because it's simply too SLOW at low temperature.
distractor_logic: Misattributes the role of heat to a change in thermodynamic favourability rather than to providing energy to overcome a kinetic activation-energy barrier for an already-favourable reaction.
Denies that a genuine kinetic (activation-energy) barrier exists for this reaction, incorrectly attributing all rate limitations to reagent concentration alone.
Denies the well-established, practically significant temperature-dependence of ether cleavage reaction rate, and incorrectly claims no meaningful parallel exists to dehydration.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Tetrahydrofuran (THF, a 5-membered cyclic ether) is treated with excess HI. How does the outcome differ structurally from cleaving an acyclic ether like diethyl ether?
options: THF's ring cleavage gives a cyclic (not open-chain) product, since breaking a ring bond somehow preserves the ring's closed structure in a different form.
THF and diethyl ether behave identically under HI cleavage, both giving two separate small-molecule products directly.

THF's ring-opening initially gives a SINGLE open-chain product bearing both an iodide and a hydroxyl at the two former ring-oxygen-attached ends (4-iodobutan-1-ol), rather than immediately splitting into two separate small molecules the way diethyl ether does; the two carbons stay connected through the rest of the ring's carbon skeleton even after one C–O bond breaks.
THF does not react with excess HI at all, since cyclic ethers are entirely resistant to the ether-cleavage reaction that acyclic ethers undergo.
questions.explanation: Because both ends of the broken C–O bond in a cyclic ether remain connected through the rest of the ring's carbon skeleton, breaking just one C–O bond opens the ring into a single bifunctional (iodo-alcohol) molecule, rather than splitting it into two separate fragments as happens with an acyclic ether.
questions.hint: Before cleavage, both 'ends' of a cyclic ether's C-O bonds are already connected to each other through the rest of the ring — does breaking just one bond change that?
distractor_logic: Misunderstands basic ring-opening logic; breaking one bond of a ring converts it into an open chain, not into a different cyclic structure.
Overlooks the structural consequence of the ether oxygen being part of a ring; cleaving one C-O bond in a cyclic ether does not create two separate molecules the way it does for an acyclic ether.
Factually wrong; cyclic ethers, including THF, are well known to undergo ring-opening cleavage reactions with strong hydrogen halides like HI, just with a structurally different outcome.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: A chiral secondary alkyl halide, (R)-2-bromobutane, is reacted with sodium methoxide via Williamson synthesis. What configuration is expected at that stereocentre in the ether product?
options: Stereochemistry is entirely irrelevant to this reaction and cannot be predicted at all, since ether products are claimed to never retain any stereochemical information from their starting alkyl halide.
The product would be a racemic mixture (equal amounts of (R)- and (S)-configured ether), since SN2 reactions are claimed to always scramble stereochemistry completely.

Inverted configuration relative to the starting halide (predominantly the (S)-configured ether), since SN2 substitution proceeds with backside attack of the nucleophile, causing a Walden inversion at the reacting stereocentre.
The product retains the same configuration as the starting halide (still (R)-configured), since substitution reactions are generally assumed to proceed with retention of configuration by default.
questions.explanation: Williamson synthesis proceeds via SN2, which is characterised by a single, predictable backside attack causing inversion (not retention or racemisation) at the reacting carbon — a direct, textbook stereochemical consequence of this mechanism.
questions.hint: Recall which specific mechanism (SN1 or SN2) Williamson synthesis uses, and what THAT mechanism predicts stereochemically.
distractor_logic: Denies that SN2 reactions have a well-established, predictable stereochemical outcome (inversion) that can and should be used to predict the product's configuration.
Incorrectly applies an SN1-type racemisation outcome (relevant to a planar carbocation intermediate) to an SN2 reaction, which instead proceeds with a single, predictable inversion, not racemisation.
Reverses the well-established stereochemical outcome of SN2 substitution specifically, which proceeds with INVERSION, not retention, due to the mechanism's backside-attack geometry.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Why is phenol's greater acidity (versus a simple alcohol) practically relevant to reliably generating phenoxide with NaOH alone for Williamson synthesis, when a simple alcohol usually needs a stronger base/reactive metal instead?
options: Simple alcohols are actually MORE completely deprotonated by NaOH than phenol is, reversing the claimed relationship.

Phenol and simple alcohols are equally well and completely converted to their respective conjugate bases by NaOH, so there is no practical difference in nucleophile-generation reliability between the two.
The completeness of alkoxide/phenoxide formation by a given base has nothing to do with relative pKa values at all; it depends only on the concentration of base used.

Because phenol (pKa≈10) is considerably more acidic than a simple alcohol (pKa≈16-18), NaOH (conjugate acid water, pKa≈15.7) can essentially completely deprotonate phenol to phenoxide, but would only very incompletely deprotonate a simple alcohol — which is part of why simple alcohols are more often converted to alkoxides using stronger bases/reactive metals (like Na metal), while phenol can be reliably and completely converted to phenoxide by NaOH alone.
questions.explanation: Comparing each compound's pKa to water's own pKa (NaOH's conjugate acid) shows NaOH is strong enough to essentially completely deprotonate phenol but not a simple alcohol, explaining the different base choices practically used to generate each nucleophile reliably for Williamson synthesis.
questions.hint: Compare each compound's pKa against water's pKa (≈15.7, NaOH's own conjugate acid) to see how complete each deprotonation would be.
distractor_logic: Reverses the actual relative acidity of phenol versus a simple alcohol; phenol, not the alcohol, is the more acidic (and therefore more completely NaOH-deprotonated) of the two.

Ignores the substantial pKa gap between phenol and a typical alcohol relative to water/NaOH's own conjugate acid-base pair, which does translate into a real difference in how completely each is deprotonated.
Denies the fundamental acid-base equilibrium principle (relative pKa determines extent of deprotonation) that actually explains this practical difference.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: 4-Chlorobutan-1-ol has both a C–Cl electrophile and a free –OH in the same molecule. If treated with base and a separate external sodium ethoxide nucleophile, is there a competing INTRAmolecular reaction to consider?
options: The intended intermolecular reaction with external ethoxide would always dominate completely, with no competing intramolecular cyclisation occurring at all, since intermolecular reactions are inherently favoured over intramolecular ones in every case.

No reaction (intramolecular or intermolecular) would occur at all, since having both a halide and a hydroxyl group in the same starting molecule makes the molecule completely unreactive toward any nucleophilic substitution.

Yes — under basic conditions, the molecule's own internal alkoxide (once its –OH is deprotonated) could attack its own internal C–Cl intramolecularly, forming a cyclic ether (tetrahydrofuran here); this intramolecular cyclisation would generally be expected to dominate over the intended intermolecular reaction with external ethoxide, since favourable ring-forming intramolecular reactions (especially 5- or 6-membered rings) are typically much faster than the analogous intermolecular reaction.
Both the intramolecular and intermolecular pathways would occur at exactly equal rates, giving a precise 50:50 mixture of the cyclic ether and the intended acyclic ether product.
questions.explanation: This substrate's own internal nucleophile and electrophile are ideally positioned to react with each other, forming a favourable 5-membered ring; such intramolecular cyclisations are generally much faster than the corresponding intermolecular reaction, due to the much higher effective local concentration of the reacting groups.
questions.hint: Check what ring size would form if the molecule's own –OH (once deprotonated) attacked its own C–Cl — is that a favourable size?
distractor_logic: Reverses the well-established general kinetic advantage that favourable intramolecular cyclisations, especially those forming 5- or 6-membered rings, typically have over the corresponding intermolecular reaction.

Denies that the molecule's own internal nucleophile/electrophile pair remains just as chemically reactive as if they were in two separate molecules, and if anything MORE likely to react given their favourable proximity.
Understates the substantial kinetic advantage that a favourable intramolecular cyclisation (forming a 5-membered ring here) typically has over the corresponding intermolecular process.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: Benzyl methyl ether (C<sub>6</sub>H<sub>5</sub>–CH<sub>2</sub>–O–CH<sub>3</sub>) is cleaved by HI. Its benzylic carbon is formally 'primary' by substitution-counting, yet cleavage there can still compete via SN1. Why?
options: Benzyl methyl ether cannot be cleaved by HI at all, since the aromatic ring completely blocks any reactivity at the adjacent benzylic C–O bond.

Despite being formally primary by carbon-substitution counting, the benzylic carbon can still stabilise a carbocation effectively via resonance delocalisation into the attached aromatic ring, making SN1-type cleavage there competitive or dominant (giving benzyl iodide + methanol) — illustrating that simple 1°/2°/3° counting alone isn't always sufficient; resonance stabilisation (as at a benzylic position) is an important additional factor.
The methyl (not benzylic) carbon would be the one to form a stabilised carbocation in this molecule, since methyl carbocations are inherently more stable than benzylic carbocations.

Benzyl methyl ether behaves identically to a simple primary-primary ether, cleaving via SN2 at the methyl carbon exclusively, since the benzylic carbon is still formally 'primary' and therefore cannot access any SN1-type pathway.
questions.explanation: Resonance stabilisation from the adjacent aromatic ring makes a benzylic carbocation surprisingly stable despite the carbon being formally 'primary' by simple substitution-counting, so cleavage there can proceed competitively (or dominantly) via SN1, giving benzyl iodide.
questions.hint: Simple 1°/2°/3° counting misses one important stabilising factor here — what's special about being right next to an aromatic ring?
distractor_logic: Factually wrong; benzylic ethers are well known to undergo ether cleavage, often readily, due to the very same benzylic-stabilisation effect that makes this position reactive.

Reverses the actual, well-established relative stability of methyl versus benzylic carbocations; a benzylic carbocation, stabilised by ring resonance, is considerably more stable than an unstabilised methyl carbocation.

Ignores that resonance stabilisation from the adjacent aromatic ring can make a formally-primary benzylic carbocation surprisingly stable and accessible, despite the simple substitution-counting rule.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: For making a SYMMETRICAL ether like diethyl ether, is Williamson synthesis or acid-catalysed intermolecular dehydration the more practical choice, and does this change for an UNSYMMETRICAL target?
options: Acid-catalysed dehydration is always preferred over Williamson synthesis for making ANY ether, including unsymmetrical ones, since it is claimed to be a simpler one-step process regardless of the target ether's symmetry.

For a symmetrical ether, acid-catalysed intermolecular dehydration is often simpler/more direct (no need to separately prepare an alkoxide AND a separate alkyl halide from the same alcohol); Williamson synthesis becomes comparatively more essential specifically for UNSYMMETRICAL ethers, since dehydration of two different alcohols would give an uncontrolled statistical mixture of all three possible ethers, while Williamson synthesis gives a clean, controlled outcome.

Williamson synthesis is always preferred over acid-catalysed dehydration for making ANY ether, symmetrical or not, since Williamson synthesis is claimed to be inherently faster and higher-yielding in every single case.
Both methods give identical yields and selectivity regardless of whether the target ether is symmetrical or unsymmetrical, so the choice between them is purely arbitrary.
questions.explanation: For a symmetrical target, simple acid-catalysed dehydration of one alcohol avoids the extra step of separately preparing an alkyl halide; for an unsymmetrical target, dehydrating two different alcohols would give an uncontrolled statistical mixture, making Williamson synthesis's clean, controlled two-precursor approach the practically necessary choice.
questions.hint: Ask what acid-catalysed dehydration of TWO DIFFERENT alcohols mixed together would actually give as products.
distractor_logic: Overlooks that acid-catalysed dehydration of two different alcohols would give an uncontrolled statistical mixture of three possible ethers, making it a poor choice specifically for unsymmetrical targets.
Overstates a universal preference for Williamson synthesis, when for simple symmetrical ethers specifically, direct acid-catalysed dehydration is often the simpler, more practical choice.
Ignores the genuine, practically important distinction in suitability between these two methods depending specifically on whether a symmetrical or unsymmetrical ether is the target.

questions.topic: Preparation and Reactions of Ethers (Williamson Synthesis and Cleavage)
questions.question: PCC's deliberate mildness (stopping cleanly at the aldehyde) is valued in synthesis. How does an ether's general inertness toward common reagents connect to this same broader synthetic principle?
options: There is no meaningful connection between PCC's oxidation selectivity and an ether's use as a protecting group; these are completely unrelated concepts with no shared underlying principle.

Just as PCC's mildness is valued specifically because it leaves other parts of a molecule untouched while achieving one selective transformation, an ether's general inertness toward most common reagents makes it useful as a way to temporarily 'protect' an alcohol's reactivity (by converting –OH to –O–R) during other synthetic steps, then later 'deprotecting' it (e.g. via HI cleavage) when needed — both illustrate that a deliberate LACK of reactivity can itself be a useful, selectivity-providing property.
Ethers are actually just as reactive as alcohols toward most common reagents, so their use as 'protecting groups' is a misconception with no real chemical basis.
PCC's mildness and an ether's inertness are connected, but only because both are examples of reagents/groups that are simply 'too unreactive to be useful for anything'.
questions.explanation: Both examples share the same underlying synthetic logic: deliberately choosing something (a reagent or a functional-group transformation) specifically for what it does NOT react with, in order to achieve overall selectivity in a multi-step synthesis — PCC leaves the rest of a molecule untouched while oxidising cleanly; an ether protects an alcohol's reactivity until it's deliberately removed again.
questions.hint: Both examples involve deliberately choosing something for what it WON'T do, in service of a larger synthetic goal.
distractor_logic: Misses the genuine shared theme (deliberately choosing a reagent or functional group specifically for what it does NOT react with, in order to achieve overall synthetic selectivity) connecting these two seemingly different examples.
Denies the well-established, genuinely useful relative inertness of the ether functional group compared to a free alcohol, which is precisely why ethers are valued as protecting groups in synthesis.

Mischaracterises both examples as generally 'not useful' rather than correctly recognising that their SELECTIVE lack of reactivity toward specific conditions is precisely what makes each one deliberately, purposefully useful in synthesis.
